auch Wasser/ so auß dem Kalch der Erden/ den wir nicht sehen/ mögen ein solche Hitz empfahen. Ab diesem Kalch soll sich kein Philosophus verwundern: dann die Wunderwerck in den Ber-gen seind also groß und treffenlich/ als die auff der Erden. Dann wo so vil Mineralia ligen/ von Kakimiis, Margasithen, Thalck, Plumosis, &c. nit möglich ist/ daß sie ohn Kalch zergehen mögen durch ihr eigen Natur und Krafft: Warumb solten dann die Wasser/ die dadurch lauffen/ nit kalchmässig werden? Wo nun solche Kalch und Mineralia ligen/ und ein heimlicher Wassergang/ der an den tag begert/ durch solche Regiones lauffen müste/ so muß er sich vereinigen mit disen Mineralibus, und muß empfahen die Hitz und Arth derselbigen/ demnach an den tag/ und behalt also sein Hitz die er innwendig empfangen hat. Wiewol offtmals ein solcher gewermter Cataract so weitt zu lauffen hatt/ daß er möchte erkalten/ oder deß halben theils/ mehr oder weniger/ wie es sich begebe: Auß dem offtmals entspringt/ daß die Wasser so heiß nicht kommen/ als heiß sie geboren werden/ oder ettwann der Kalch wenig ist/ nicht sehr starck/ darauß dann die Bäder eins heisser und kelter/ dann das ander geht. Diese Bäder empfahen die arth des Kalchs an sich/ ettwann auß der Magnetischen arth/ ettwann vom Asphalto, ettwann vom Carabe des schwartzen/ ettwann von der Sulphurischen arth/ der verbrennt ist von jhm selbs/ welcherley Gattung dasselbig ist/ also hangt ein entlenete Krafft im selbigen Wasser.

<sig>Pp iij</sig>

also waters, which may receive such heat from the lime of the earth that we do not see. A philosopher should not be astonished by this lime, for the wonders in the mountains are as great and excellent as those upon the earth. For where so many minerals lie, of <term>kakimii</term> <gloss>alum salts</gloss>, <term>margasites</term> <gloss>pyrites</gloss>, <term>talc</term>, <term>plumose alum</term>, etc., it is not possible that they could dissolve without lime through their own nature and power. Why then should the waters that flow through them not become lime-like? Now, where such lime and minerals lie, and a hidden watercourse, which seeks the day, must flow through such <term>regiones</term> <gloss>regions</gloss>, it must unite with these minerals and must receive the heat and nature of the same, subsequently [emerging] to the day, and thus retains the heat it received inwardly. Although such a warmed <term>cataract</term> <gloss>waterfall/channel</gloss> often has such a long distance to run that it might cool down, or by half, more or less, as it happens, it often occurs from this that the waters do not emerge as hot as they were born, or sometimes the lime is little, not very strong, from which one bath becomes hotter and another colder than the next. These baths receive the nature of the lime upon themselves, sometimes from the <term>magnetic</term> nature, sometimes from <term>asphalto</term> <gloss>bitumen</gloss>, sometimes from the black <term>carabe</term> <gloss>amber</gloss>, sometimes from the <term>sulphuric</term> nature, which is burned by itself, whatever kind that may be; thus a borrowed power hangs in the same water.

### CHAPTER II.

<note>An ornamental drop-cap 'D' depicts floral and foliage motifs.</note>In the same manner, there are other origins of certain baths that do not emerge from the aforementioned causes but from another power, as you then see the fire-mountains, coal-mountains, which have the <term>Aetnean</term> nature (like Mount Aetna) within them, which are upon the earth and burn, and yet their body is solely stone and earth, and they cannot be extinguished by any rain or water. Similarly, just as such a miracle occurs outside, so too such burning natures exist as much within the earth as outside it. For the outer ones do not receive the origin from the outside, but from the <term>centro der Erden</term> <gloss>center of the earth</gloss>, that is, from the middle, following a stream or passage,

Our daily lives are visible, tangible, comprehensive evidences of things unseen and unknown which can be wholly felt or believed only on the abstract planes of consciousness. The most beautiful thoughts are often unrevealed because the thinker has no words to express them; most glorious melodies are lost to the world because the one who feels them is incapable of expressing them musically.

Man's vehicles of expression must always limit the life and while he may dream on forever beautiful dreams, if he does not properly attune his instrument he dreams for himself alone, and oftimes he cannot even formulate clearly within his own mind the dreams which fill his soul.

Vibration is caused by the animation of substances and the setting of air or ether in motion. Every word that comes out of our mouths is toned by the mouth. It is changed and often ruined by the shape of the teeth, the position of the tongue, and the quality of the sound-box at the back of the mouth. As the rates of vibration pass out of the throat into the various chambers of the head and chest they produce the various tones which we admire or dislike. Wherever there is impediment in the natural expression of vibration we have the so-called nasal tone, which is out of tune because it isn't nasal, and the passages being stopped up inhibits the flow of the vitalized energies. The results of developing the cavities in the head and chest are the building of resonant tones which striking the ear-drum in a harmonious way we recognize as melodies and harmonies, and every known tone is the result of air in motion passing through chambers differing from each other in two things. First, size, shape, and location; second, the quality of the material forming their walls.

In the beginning it is said that man was created through the outbreathing of God, who, as He outpours the vibrations from the celestial sound-box of cosmos, becomes the great Father principle of creation for He is sending forth the sparks of life from

<column-break/>

His own mouth. These strike matter and the various combinations of these two forces produce the differentiation in form, shape, and quality. All the varying expressions of life in form of which we can conceive are the result of motion striking the lack of motion, the result being spiritual, mental, or physical harmonies or sounds, which are tuned according to the sounding board of cosmic root substance upon which these harmonies strike in their search for expression.

The same sound wave we hear in a cornet passes also through the bass horn but the notes of the latter are heavier and deeper and in many ways different, the only cause being that the general form, magnitude, and orifices of the two instruments are different in size and shape. The same setting in motion of atmosphere takes place and the same noted energy is used in drawing the bows of both a cello and a violin but the result of the action differs on account of the difference in the instruments.

In the spiritual things of life the same principle is true. Man is completely limited by the quality of the instrument upon which he is seeking to play the celestial harmonies. There are no two individuals who ever have been or ever will be exactly the same in their thoughts, desires, and actions, and these in turn mold the instrument of matter into an expression of their own quality which results in the distinct individuality of specie. In spiritual things we find a perfect analogy, for the spiritual waves of living substances in motion are molding eternally their own keyboard into an expression of themselves and this keyboard is in turn defining and limiting the expression of its own creator.

Spirit or God is an intelligent force which being creative itself bequeathes the power of creation upon everything which expresses it. Man is a creator every time he animates substances and he animates certain substances with every expression of active energy, mental, physical, or spiritual. Whenever he speaks or even thinks the result is a chain of vibratory waves

# BESCHRYVING
# VAN
# NEDERLAND,
### En aengrensende Landen.

<margin>Fol. A.</margin>
<margin>Naem van Nederland.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter N containing a landscape with a building and figures.</image-desc>
Nederland, by ſommige van wegens ſyne uytſtekende voortreffelijckheit, het Oog der Noordſche Wereldt genoemt, is in 17 Provincien verdeelt; die yder al over eenige hondert jaren hare byſondere Vorſten hadden, van doorluchtige edele af-komſten, de ſelvige ſoo wel in Vrouwelijke als Mannelijke linien erfelijk beſittende.
<margin>De 17. Provincien.</margin>
Deſe 17. Provincien zijn vier Hertogdommen, als *Brabant, Limburg, Lutzenburg, Gelderland*; ſeven Graafſchappen, als *Vlaenderen, Artois, Henegouwen, Holland, Zeeland, Namen, en Zutphen*; het Marquiſaet van 't Heilige Rijk; met de Heerlijkheden van *Friesland, Mechelen, Utrecht, Over-ijssel, en Groningen*.
<margin>Be-paling.</margin>
Dit Nederland is bepaelt met de Eems (een vermaerde Rivier, het Land van Benthem en Westphalen, de Landen van Gulick en Cleve, de Bisdommen van Keulen en Trier, het Hertogdom van Lotharingen, en het Koninkrijk van Vrankrijk tot de mond van de Rivier de Aa, die ſich in de Zee by Grevelingen ontlast, en voorts word het van de Noord-Zee om-geſpoelt.
<margin>De groote van dit Land.</margin>
Het begrijpt in 't rond omtrent 340. Neerlandſche mijlen, daer in meer dan 200. bemuerde Steden zijn te tellen, boven de welke noch wel 150. die Stadts recht en Privilegien hebben, met over de 6300 Dorpen, behalven ontallijke Gehuchten, Heeren-Huifen, Sloten en Kasteelen.
<margin>Lucht en Grondt.</margin>
De Lucht van deſe Landen, hoewel doorgaens wat vochtigh en grof, word nochtans geſond, en bequaem tot de voort-teeling gehouden; want als de Inwoonders ſich niet in een ongeregelde ſtyl van leven overlaegden, bekomen sy in 't gemeen grooten ouderdom, gelijk dat meeſt blijkt in de Kempen binnen Brabant, waer de Lieden, om d'onvruchtbaerheit des lands, ſober leven, en kloek in 't arbeiden, dikwils hooge jaren bereiken. De Somer is er lustig en heel vermakelijk, niet geplaght door ondragelijke hitte, maer wel gematigt. De winters zijn ſomstijds lang, hard, en fel, als d'Oostenrijk of Noordſche winden waejen: maer wanneer daer weder Weste of Zuide winden opkomen, ſoo verandert de koude haestig in warmte en regen. Selden worden daer vyerige teekenen in de Lucht geſien; en weinige quade buyen, of aerdbevingen worden hier gevoelt: want de vochtigheit van de Lucht, ende laegte van het aerdrijk konnen dat ſchier niet lyden.
<margin>Landts-ge-legenheyt.</margin>
De Lands-douwe is bykans over al effen en plat, met weinigh heuvelen, en veel min bergen voorzien, behalven in Lutzenburg, Limburg, Namen, en ſommige quartieren van Henegouwen. In vele plaetſen is het ſandachtigh, als in de groote Heyden binnen Brabant, Vlaenderen, Gelderland, en Over-ijssel: en meeſt langs de Zee-kant, als in Holland en Zeeland, heeft het hooge Sandbergen, diemen gewoonlijk Duinen noemt, ſchudden tegen de woedende Zee.
<margin>Vruchtbaerheit.</margin>
Voorts is het doorgaens wel beboet, en ſeer vruchtbaer in alderhande gewas. In Walſch-Vlaenderen, Artois, Henegouwen, en Zeeland valt overvloedig veel ſchoone Terw, die in Gelderland mede niet ontbreekt. Wat de boomvruchten belangt, daer waſſen over al vele Peeren, Appelen, Pruimen, en Kerſen, welke laeſte, van Plinius ſelf gepreſen worden. Moerbeſien, Perſen, Abrikooſen, Okernoten, Haſelnoten, en Miſpelen zijn 'er overvloedig. In ſommige quartieren vallen ook eenige Kastanien, Vijgen, Granaet-appelen, Oranje, Limoonen, Olijven, en diergelyke edele vruchten waſſen daer niet wel van wegen de koude, maer worden hier over-

<column-break/>

vloedig uit Spangien en andere vremde Landen gebragt. Boomen tot timmerhout en brandhout vind men hier velerlei, en met namen veele Linde-boomen, welker kolen ſeer bequaem zijn om buypoeder te maken. Sy hebben ook eenen boom, die deſe landen ſchyne eigen te weſen, Abeelen genoemt, en is een ſoort van witte Populier. De hof of moes-kruiden vallen hier te lande ſoo goet en ſchoon, en miſchien beter als in Italien.
Oſſen, Koeijen, Schapen, en andere gedierten, tot 's menschen onderhoud bequaem, worden in deſe Landen met groote menigte gevonden, van ſeer goede ſmaeck, en ſoo tam, door de ionrigheit des luchts, dat de dieren daer niet veel wilder zijn, dan de Oſſen in Indien. Het vee ſet hier dapper voort, en vermenigvuldigt wonderlijk in korten tijt. De paerden zijn 'er ſterk, ſchoon en groot, voorneemlijck in Vlaenderen, Holland, Zeeland, en Friesland, tot alle oeffeningen bequaem, byſonder tot den Oorlog. Met boter, kaas, melk is 'er geen land in eenen boecken des werelts ſo ſeer begaeft, en aldermeest het Graafſchap van Holland.
De rivieren, die met menigten door deſe landen loopen, zijn ſchoon en groot, waer van de voorneemſte zijn, de Rijn, de Maes, de Schelde, en de Loir. Op de hooge landen in Nederland verciert zag vele ſchoone luſtige Boſchjes, waer ran het beroemſte is dat van Ardennen. Alle deſe boſch-lantiën zijn vol van allerlei wild, als Herten, Hinden, Daſſen, Rhees, wilde Verken, Haſel, Konijnen. Men heeft daer ook allerhande Gevogelte, als Patrijsen, Reigen, Swanen, Oyevaers, Ganſen, Enden, Hoenders, Kalkoenen, Faſanten, Duyven, Snippen, Patryſſen, Quikkels, en wat voor kleine vogelkens niet? Roofvogels zijn 'er yet menigte.
<margin>Aert der In-woonderen.</margin>
Het volk van Nederland is doorgaens groot, ſterk, blank, en wel gemaekt, aerdende in elk Landſchap wat na hare gebuuren. Sy zijn dappere en grootmoedige Krijgs-lieden, ſoo te voet als te paerde; van ſunderlinge kloeckheit in de Zee-vaert, ſeer genegen tot koophandel, weer op haer gastvrije land gegrond en geſlicht is. Sy zijn ſeer vernuftig, guetig, en behendig om iet uit te vinden, en daer beneffens ſeer arbeitſaem en neertigh om 'tgeent sy gevonden en geleert hebben in 't werk te ſteken, en door geduerige oeffening dat meerder te verbeteren. Het Boek-drucken, Oly onder Verwen te mengen, het Glaſs-hyven of allerhande konſteyen op Glas te bakken, het bereiden van veelderlei Lakenen, Stoffen, Lyawaten, zijn alle hare vonden. Haren aert is wat koel en gematigt in al 't guue ſy ter hand nemen.
De Vrouwen, ſchoon, wel gemaekt, en fraey op haer leden, zijn ook ſeer vriendelijk, beleeft, en bevallig in al haer doen en laten, hare kuyſheit en eerbaerheit ſorgvuldigh bewarende, waerom ſy ook van hare Ouders en Echte-genooten in groote weerde worden gehouden, maer vryelijk by alle geſelſchappen verkeeren. De Nederlanders oude en moederlijke Tael (behalven in de Walſche quartieren, als Artois, Henegouwen, Walſch-Brabant, en Walſch-Vlaenderen; daer men gebroken Franſch ſpreekt) is Duits, een Tael in oudheit, rijkdom, en volkomenheit alle andere overtreffende, maer moeijelijk om in een kort tijdt recht te leeren; daer ſy nochtans lichtelijck andere vremde Talen leeren. Sy zijn godvrugtige lieden, en onder de eerſte die het Evangelium Jeſu Christi hebben aengenomen. Deſe Landen zijn nu in tweën verdeelt, waer van het eene boort onder de Konink van Spangien, en het ander beſeten word by de Staten Generael der vrye Vereenigde Nederlanden. Nu ſullen wy voortgaen tot yder van die in 't byſonder.

# DESCRIPTION
# OF
# THE NETHERLANDS,
### And neighboring Lands.

<margin>Fol. A.</margin>
<margin>Name of the Netherlands.</margin>
<meta>Ornamental initial letter N containing a landscape with a building and figures.</meta>
The Netherlands, called by some the Eye of the Northern World because of its outstanding excellence, is divided into 17 Provinces; each of which had its own particular Princes for some hundreds of years, of illustrious noble descent, possessing the same hereditarily in both female and male lines.
<margin>The 17. Provinces.</margin>
These 17. Provinces are four Duchies, such as *Brabant, Limburg, Luxembourg, Gelderland*; seven Counties, such as *Flanders, Artois, Hainault, Holland, Zeeland, Namur, and Zutphen*; the Marquisate of the Holy Empire; with the Lordships of *Friesland, Mechelen, Utrecht, Over-ijssel, and Groningen*.
<margin>Boundaries.</margin>
This Netherlands is bounded by the Ems (a famous River), the Land of Bentheim and Westphalia, the Lands of Jülich and Cleves, the Bishoprics of Cologne and Trier, the Duchy of Lorraine, and the Kingdom of France to the mouth of the River Aa, which discharges itself into the Sea by Gravelines, and furthermore it is washed by the North Sea.
<margin>The size of this Land.</margin>
It comprises in circumference about 340 Netherlandish miles, in which more than 200 walled Cities are to be counted, besides which there are still 150 that have City rights and Privileges, with over 6300 Villages, besides countless Hamlets, Manor-houses, Chateaus and Castles.
<margin>Air and Soil.</margin>
The air of these lands, although generally somewhat moist and heavy, is nevertheless held to be healthy and suitable for procreation; for if the Inhabitants did not overload themselves with an irregular style of living, they generally attain great old age, as is mostly apparent in the Campine within Brabant, where the People, because of the infertility of the land, live soberly, and being quick in labor, often reach high years. The Summer is pleasant and very enjoyable, not plagued by unbearable heat, but rather moderate. The winters are sometimes long, hard, and fierce, when the Austrian or Northern winds blow: but when Western or Southern winds arise, the cold changes suddenly into warmth and rain. Seldom are fiery signs seen in the Air; and few bad storms or earthquakes are felt here: because the humidity of the Air and the lowness of the terrain can hardly sustain that.
<margin>Geography.</margin>
The terrain is almost everywhere even and flat, provided with few hills and far fewer mountains, except in Luxembourg, Limburg, Namur, and some quarters of Hainault. In many places it is sandy, as in the great Heaths within Brabant, Flanders, Gelderland, and Over-ijssel: and mostly along the Sea-side, as in Holland and Zeeland, it has high Sand-hills, which one usually calls Dunes, [acting as a] shield against the raging Sea.
<margin>Fertility.</margin>
Furthermore, it is generally well cultivated, and very fertile in all kinds of crops. In Walloon-Flanders, Artois, Hainault, and Zeeland, an abundance of fine Wheat falls, which is also not lacking in Gelderland. As far as fruit from trees is concerned, many Pears, Apples, Plums, and Cherries grow everywhere, which last are praised even by Pliny. Mulberries, Peaches, Apricots, Walnuts, Hazelnuts, and Medlars are abundant there. In some quarters also some Chestnuts fall; Figs, Pomegranates, Oranges, Lemons, Olives, and similar noble fruits do not grow well there because of the cold, but are here

<column-break/>

brought in abundance from Spain and other foreign Lands. Trees for timber and firewood one finds here of many kinds, and by name many Linden-trees, whose coals are very suitable for making gunpowder. They also have a tree that seems to be peculiar to these lands, called Abelen, and is a kind of white Poplar. The garden or pot-herbs fall here in the land as good and fine, and perhaps better than in Italy.
Oxen, Cows, Sheep, and other animals, suitable for man's maintenance, are found in these Lands in great multitudes, of very good taste, and so tame, through the mildness of the air, that the animals there are not much wilder than the Oxen in India. The cattle breed well here, and multiply wonderfully in a short time. The horses are strong, fine and large, especially in Flanders, Holland, Zeeland, and Friesland, suitable for all exercises, especially for War. With butter, cheese, milk, there is no land in the world so well endowed, and most of all the County of Holland.
The rivers, which run through these lands in multitudes, are fine and large, of which the most important are, the Rhine, the Meuse, the Scheldt, and the Loire. On the high lands in the Netherlands, nature adorns many fine pleasant little woods, of which the most famous is that of the Ardennes. All these woodlands are full of all kinds of game, such as Harts, Hinds, Badgers, Roes, wild Boars, Hares, Rabbits. One has there also all kinds of Fowl, such as Partridges, Herons, Swans, Storks, Geese, Ducks, Chickens, Turkeys, Pheasants, Pigeons, Snipes, Quails, and what small birds not? Birds of prey are in great multitude.
<margin>Nature of the Inhabitants.</margin>
The people of the Netherlands are generally tall, strong, fair, and well-made, leaning in each Landscape somewhat to their neighbors. They are brave and magnanimous Soldiers, both on foot and on horseback; of singular cleverness in Sea-navigation, very inclined to trade, which is grounded and established upon their hospitable land. They are very ingenious, clever, and agile to invent something, and besides that very industrious and diligent to put what they have found and learned into work, and by constant practice to improve that further. Book-printing, mixing Oil with Paints, Glass-blowing or baking all kinds of arts on Glass, the preparation of many kinds of Cloths, Fabrics, Linens, are all their inventions. Their nature is somewhat cool and moderate in all that they take in hand.
The Women, beautiful, well-made, and graceful in their limbs, are also very friendly, polite, and charming in all their conduct, carefully preserving their chastity and modesty, why they are also held in great value by their Parents and Husbands, but freely move in all company. The Netherlanders' old and motherly Language (except in the Walloon quarters, such as Artois, Hainault, Walloon-Brabant, and Walloon-Flanders; where one speaks broken French) is German <note>original: "Duits" (referring here to the Dutch language, historically termed "Diets" or "Duits")</note>, a Language in antiquity, richness, and perfection surpassing all others, but difficult to learn correctly in a short time; although they nevertheless easily learn other foreign Languages. They are pious people, and among the first who have accepted the Gospel of Jesus Christ. These Lands are now divided into two, of which one belongs under the King of Spain, and the other is possessed by the States General of the free United Netherlands. Now we shall proceed to each of them in particular.

O sweet admonitions, O discourse sweeter than nectar itself,
Or if anything appears sweeter,
How calmly you call your servant, O most gentle Father.
When with your fingers you gave the law-bearing old man <note>referring to Moses</note> the precepts described on the high mount Sinai,
The rock was seen to be consumed by rapid fire,
The earth shook with terror, the very ether shuddered.
With a terrible sound, the heavens echoed from all sides;

The men were stunned, the crowd struck with fear,
Like those astonished, they stood without any senses.

Ingenijs tellus etiam est fœlicibus apta,
Aonias celebrent quæ pietate Deas.
Hæc etenim nobis genuit iam terra Poetam,
Quo uix hoc nostro tempore maior erit.
Namque bonos facili uersus effundit auena,
In numeros coeunt uerba soluta suos.
Cum sit in hac igitur natus regione Lutherus,
Ingenio est etiam præditus ipse bono.
Vrbs, quæ prima dedit genito cunabula Sponso,
Est sita florenti gramine, Lucha, solo.
Nam locus ille uiret pratis ita pulcher amœnis,
Aurea ut Agricolis Uissa uocetur ibi.
Hunc Unstrot fluuius liquidis præterfluit undis,
Qui lacus à fuso sanguine nomen habet.
Namque Bonifacius riuum prostrauit ad illum,
Agmina uictrici per sua bella manu.
Ut niger in toto manarit flumine sanguis,
Atque cruor puras commacularit aquas.
Eius ibi pater ad summos euectus honores,
Legibus exequitur publica iura datis.
Is bonus est Iudex, placidis qui pectora uerbis,
Mulcet, et officio fungitur arte suo.
Et cum sit sapiens causas inquirit honestas,
Atque fauet studijs hac ratione bonis.
Ipse suum natum Musis mandauit alendum,
Ubera dum Matris sugeret ore puer.
Sub quibus ille diu multos permansit in Annos,
Aonias uenerans sedulitate deas.
Mars ubi Saxonicis Musas exterruit oris,
Mouit ut horrendo tristia bella sono.
Impiger ipse domi patria non mansit in urbe.
Longinquas potius uidit in orbe plagas.
Namque iuuat uarias hominum cognoscere terras,
Inde potest iuuenis discere multa rudis.

The land is also suited for happy minds,
Which celebrate the Aonian <note>Muse-related/Pierian</note> goddesses with piety.
For this land has now produced for us a poet,
Than whom there will scarcely be a greater in our time.
For he pours forth good verses with an easy pipe,
And loose words gather into their own meters.
Since Luther was therefore born in this region,
He himself is also endowed with a good talent.
The city which first gave the newborn groom his cradle
Is situated on flourishing grass, Lucha, in the soil.
For that place is green with such beautiful meadows,
That it is called the golden <term>Uissa</term> <gloss>a local river</gloss> by the farmers there.
The river Unstrot flows past this with liquid waves,
Which has its name from spilled blood.
For Bonifacius struck down an army at that stream,
Through his own wars with a victorious hand.
So that black blood flowed in the whole river,
And gore stained the pure waters.
His father there, raised to the highest honors,
Executes public rights according to given laws.
He is a good judge, who soothes hearts with calm words,
And performs his duty with his skill.
And since he is wise, he investigates honest causes,
And favors good studies in this way.
He himself entrusted his son to be nourished by the Muses,
While the boy was still sucking his mother's milk.
Under whom he remained for many long years,
Venerating the Aonian goddesses with diligence.
When Mars frightened the Muses on Saxon shores,
As he moved sad wars with a horrendous sound.
The restless one did not stay at home in his native city.
He saw far-off regions of the world instead.
For it pleases one to know the various lands of men,
From which a raw youth can learn many things.

malice of an act, but can also sometimes free an act from moral malice entirely. But those things which are known to be sins must not be done so that goods may result. Nor can you object that a good work turns out evil because of an evil intention. Therefore, by the power of opposites, an evil work becomes good because of a good intention. While an evil work arises from any defect whatsoever, that which deserves the name of 'good' must have nothing vicious found within it, since true good is born from an integral cause and all required goods. A perfect number demands all units for its own perfection, but with the loss of even a single unit, it is rendered imperfect: so a good and perfect work requires all causes to be good for its own goodness; if even one is missing, then the good lapses into evil.

Nor are there lacking most evident examples, from which it appears that one should by no means judge the quality and condition of a work from the mere intention of the agent.

It was prohibited in the law of the Lord that anyone other than a priest should offer sacrifices. However, when Saul, the first King of Israel, saw danger being prepared for him by the Philistine enemies, and the Prophet Samuel was still delayed, Saul himself offered burnt offerings to the Lord at Gilgal, in order to appease Him and to keep Him favorable to himself and the people. This intention was good, but was the work also good? *You have acted foolishly,* it is said in 1 Samuel, Chapter 13, verse 13, *and you have not kept the commandments of the Lord your God, which He commanded you.*

the derivative words, *ill*, and *he knew*¹. If then we use the two proper words, there is formed this sentence, in plain prose indeed, but expressive of the poet’s meaning,—*He was knowing and skilled in many things, but to know all those things was to him an evil.*—It is evident then, that if much knowledge was to him an evil, what knowledge he had was worthless, and he himself was some worthless fellow; supposing any credit to be due to the conclusions from our past reasonings.

ALC. And I think, Socrates, it is their due: for I should hardly give credit to any other rational conclusions, if I denied it to those.

Soc. And you think rightly too. But in the name of Jupiter, let us proceed. For you see, how great are the perplexities attending the subject in which we are engaged; you see also, what the nature is of those perplexities. And you seem to me to have a share in them yourself; as you never rest from changing your thoughts over and over again upon this subject; discarding the opinions, which you had before so ardently embraced, and continuing no longer in the same mind. Should the God then, to whom you are going to make your prayers, appear to you, now after all our conclusions; and should he ask you, before you had presented any petition whatever to him—whether or no your desires would be satisfied, if you obtained any of those dominions mentioned in the beginning of our argument;—or should he leave to yourself the naming of what you wished for;—in which way, think you, could you best avail yourself of this opportunity? whether in accepting any of the grants offered you, or in naming some other thing you wished for?

ALC. Now, by the gods, Socrates, I should not know what to say to such a proposal. Indeed, I think, that it would be rash in me to make any decisive answer at all; and that great caution is absolutely requisite in such a case; to prevent a man from praying unwarily for things evil, while he imagines them to be good; and from doing as you said, soon afterwards recanting his choice, and praying to be delivered from what he had before prayed to have.

---

¹ We have here a specimen of Plato’s uncommon skill in philosophical or universal grammar. It appears, not only by his deducing the adverb ΚΑΚΩΣ, *ill*, from the substantive noun ΚΑΚΟΝ, *evil*, but also by (what shows a much deeper theory of words, considered as the parts of speech,) his deriving ΗΠΙΣΤΑΤΟ, *he knew*, a verb of the indicative mode, from the infinitive, or most general verb, ’ΕΠΙΣΤΑΣΘΑΙ, *to know*. See Mr. Harris’s Hermes, b. i. ch. xi. and viii.—S.

If, then, we use the two proper terms, the sentence reads as follows, in plain prose yet expressing the poet’s meaning: *He was knowing and skilled in many things, but to know all those things was to him an evil.* It is evident, then, that if much knowledge was an evil to him, the knowledge he had was worthless, and he himself was a worthless fellow, assuming any credit is due to our previous reasoning.

Alc. And I think, Socrates, it is due; for I should hardly give credit to any other logical conclusions if I denied it to those.

Soc. And you think rightly. But in the name of Jupiter, let us proceed. You see how great are the perplexities surrounding the subject we are engaged in; you also see the nature of those perplexities. And you seem to have a share in them yourself, as you never rest from changing your mind on this subject—discarding the opinions you had previously embraced so ardently, and never staying in the same frame of mind. If the God to whom you are going to pray were to appear to you now, after all our conclusions, and ask you—before you had offered any petition—whether your desires would be satisfied if you obtained any of those dominions mentioned at the beginning of our argument, or if he should leave it to you to name what you wished for, how do you think you could best avail yourself of this opportunity? Would you accept any of the grants offered, or name something else entirely?

Alc. Now, by the gods, Socrates, I should not know what to say to such a proposal. Indeed, I think it would be rash for me to make any decisive answer at all. Great caution is absolutely necessary in such a case to prevent a man from praying unwarily for evil things while imagining them to be good, and from doing as you said—soon afterward recanting his choice and praying to be delivered from what he had previously prayed to have.

Christ also dwells in Christians through the purity of body and soul, just as the Apostle says to the Corinthians, 1: "Know you not that you are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in you?" For the temple of God is holy, which you are. As if he said: if you are holy, that is, pure in heart and soul, then God dwells in you. For holiness befits the house of the Lord in the length of days, Psalm 92. Thirdly, Christ dwells in Christians through visceral charity, whence John says in his first epistle, 4: "God is charity, and he that abides in charity abides in God, and God in him." It is a delightful thing that God should dwell in us through charity, and we in Him. But what is charity? Charity is God, and to love Him with one's whole heart, not merely through the motion of the mouth. There are many who appear to love God with their mouth, but their kidneys <note>a biblical metaphor for the seat of inner desires</note> are far from Him; whence Jeremiah 12 says: "You are near to their mouth, and far from their kidneys." As if to say: their mouth pretends to speak of charity, but their desires seek the most shameful pleasures. There are also many who profess to love their neighbors with their mouth, but they plot guile and snares in their hearts. Of such, Jeremiah 9 says: "With his mouth he speaks peace with his friend, and secretly he lays snares for him." Fourthly, Christ dwells in Christians through graceful humility, whence Isaiah 57 says: "Because the high Lord dwells with the contrite and humble of spirit." The Virgin Mary herself says that not so much because she was most pure, but rather because she was most humble, she merited to conceive the Son of God, as she herself testifies in Luke 1: "He has regarded the humility of His handmaid." She does not say "chastity," though she was most chaste, but "humility." Fifthly, Christ dwells in Christians through the solidity of fear, whence the Apostle says to the Colossians 3: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom." By the wisdom of the Lord, he signifies what Ecclesiasticus 1 says: "The fullness of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." Hence, therefore, Christ dwells in those who fear Him. For everyone who fears the Lord neglects nothing of His will. Pray, therefore, to the Lord that He may deign to dwell in the hospice of our hearts so that we may also merit to be received by Him into the eternal tabernacles. May He grant this to us.

st moisture, and the two larger ones close their mouths one with the other, and the two others, a little smaller, are similarly locked, included, and surrounded by these two larger ones; and furthermore, two others, somewhat smaller, are included and surrounded by these second ones, like the layers of an onion. We must imagine the eye to be composed in this way, regarding its tunics and its humors. And finally, the two others, also smaller, are included and surrounded by these two to constitute sight in the animal. 

¶ The first tunic of the eye is called the <term>conjunctiva</term> <gloss>the membrane covering the white of the eye</gloss>, and it is the largest, which holds all the others together. The entire substance of the eye joins outside that black portion which appears in the eye, which does not extend there; it has its beginning from the membrane that covers the bone of the head on the outside, called the <term>almocatim</term> <gloss>the pericranium or membrane covering the skull</gloss>. Thus, through this tunic, the eye is bound and suspended from the cranium. 

¶ The second tunic, according to the front part, is called the <term>cornea</term> <gloss>horny layer</gloss> because it has the color of a lantern horn, and in the back part, it is the <term>sclera</term> <gloss>hard outer layer</gloss>, that is, hard and thick. Even though it has two names, it is nonetheless one, surrounded by the first one already mentioned according to all its parts on the outside. That part in front, which is uncovered by the <term>conjunctiva</term> <gloss>the membrane covering the white of the eye</gloss>, has its origin immediately under the bone of the head which is called the <term>dura mater</term> <gloss>the outer membrane of the brain</gloss>. Through this tunic, the eye is also bound to the cranium, as has been said of the <term>conjunctiva</term> <gloss>the membrane covering the white of the eye</gloss>. 

¶ The third tunic is called the <term>uvea</term> <gloss>the vascular coat of the eye</gloss> in the front parts because it resembles a grape grain, and in the posterior part, the <term>secundina</term> <gloss>a membrane enveloping the fetus</gloss>, that is, like the membrane that wraps the creature in the mother’s womb. It originates from the membrane that immediately covers the substance of the brain, called the <term>pia mater</term> <gloss>the inner membrane of the brain</gloss>. Through this tunic, the eye is bound and fixed to the head. 

¶ The fourth tunic, according to the front part, is called the <term>aranea</term> <gloss>spider-web-like membrane</gloss> because it is like a spider's web, and according to the posterior part, it is called the <term>retina</term> <gloss>net-like membrane</gloss>, fashioned like a net. It has its origin from two nerves that are called optic nerves, which thicken in the anterior part of the head. One comes to one eye and the other to the other, and from them, some threads separate, from which this tunic is woven, and also from some veins and arteries. 

¶ Beyond these tunics, there are three humors. The first is called the <term>albugineous humor</term> <gloss>the clear, watery fluid of the eye</gloss>, made in the manner of an egg white, placed between the <term>aranea</term> <gloss>spider-web-like membrane</gloss> and the <term>cornea</term> <gloss>horny layer</gloss>, which surrounds the tunic called the <term>uvea</term> <gloss>the vascular coat of the eye</gloss>. This <term>uvea</term> <gloss>the vascular coat of the eye</gloss> floats in that humor, and beyond that humor is the <term>aranea</term> <gloss>spider-web-like membrane</gloss>. Afterward follows the second humor, called the <term>crystalline humor</term> <gloss>the lens of the eye</gloss>, which is the most principal part of the eye, placed precisely in the middle as the place in which sight is produced. Maka sembah Bendahara, "Daulat Tuanku Syah Alam, belum lagi, tetapi segala pegawai dan pertuanan muda-muda sudah hadir patik kerahkan, mana titah patik junjung."

Maka titah Baginda, "Segeralah Mamak Bendahara menyambut anak Raja itu!"

Maka Bendahara pun menyembah, lalu ke luar, duduk di balai gendang, menyuruhkan segala pegawai dan pertuanan pergi menyambut Raja itu. Setelah sampai, sekalian oran gitu lalu naik menghadap Raja Jolan itu, serta berdatang sembah segala pegawai itu, "Adapun patik sekalian datang ini dititahkan oleh paduka ayahanda menyambut Tuanku, naik bermain-main ke darat."

Maka kata Raja Jolan, "Baiklah, kita pun sudah sedia hendak menghadap duli yang dipertuan."

Maka Raja Jolan pun turun dari bahteranya, lalu naik ke atas gajah, berjalan masuk ke dalam negeri, diiringkan oleh segala pegawai dan pertuanan sekalian: penuh sesak sekalian orang Melaka melihat anak Raja itu, terlalu ramai sepanjang jalan. Hatta maka Raja Jolan pun sampailah ke balai gendang, lalu turun dari atas gajahnya berjalan masuk. Maka Patih Karma Wijaya pun datang menyembah, lalu naik berjalan bersama-sama. Maka tatkala itu Baginda pun sudah keluar dihadap oleh Bendahara dan Laksamana dengan segala pegawai dan pertuanan sekalian, penuh sesak, bertindih-tindih lutut duduk. Maka Raja Jolan pun berjalan naik, lalu duduk menyembah. Maka titah Baginda, "Silakanlah anakku duduk dekat ayahanda di sini!"

Maka Raja Jolan pun bangkit duduk bertimbalan dengan Bendahara Paduka Raja. Maka segala persembahan Raja Jolan pun disambut oranglah, dibawa masuk ke dalam istana. Maka sirih pada jorong emas pun datanglah. Maka titah Baginda, "Makanlah sirih, Anakku!"

Maka jorong itu pun disambut oleh Raja Jolan, serta menyembah, lalu makan sirih itu. Maka titah Baginda, "Berapa hari anakku datang ini di laut?"

Maka sembah Raja Jolan, "Daulat Tuanku, karena banyak empat patik singgah bermain-main, segenap pulau dan kuala, jadi lama patik di laut."

Maka titah Baginda, "Manatah segala raja-raja berangkat itu, tiada bermain-main berburu segenap pulau?"

Seketika duduk maka hidangan pun diangkat orang beriring-iring, seerti di dalam tulisan rupanya orang menyandang tatapan itu. Maka Raja Jolan pun makan sehidangan dengan Bendahara Paduka Raja.

The Bendahara replied, "Long live your Majesty, not yet, but all the officials and the young nobles are present as I ordered; I await your command."

The King commanded, "Quickly, Uncle Bendahara, welcome the Prince!"

The Bendahara bowed, then went out to the music pavilion, ordering all the officials and nobles to go and welcome the King. Upon arriving, they all boarded to meet Raja Jolan and stated, "We have come here under the command of the Prince's father to welcome you to come ashore and play."

Raja Jolan said, "Very well, I am ready to face the King."

Raja Jolan descended from his vessel, mounted an elephant, and walked into the city, followed by all the officials and nobles. The people of Melaka were packed to see the Prince, and the streets were very crowded. Raja Jolan reached the music pavilion, descended from his elephant, and walked inside. <term>Patih Karma Wijaya</term> <gloss>a high official</gloss> came to bow and accompanied him inside. At that moment, the King was already out, attended by the Bendahara and Laksamana along with all the officials and nobles; it was packed, with people sitting knee to knee. Raja Jolan walked up and sat down to bow. The King said, "Please, my child, sit near your father here!"

Raja Jolan rose and sat opposite the Bendahara Paduka Raja. The gifts brought by Raja Jolan were received and taken into the palace. Betel on a golden tray was brought. The King said, "Eat the betel, my child!"

The tray was received by Raja Jolan, who bowed and ate the betel. The King asked, "How many days have you been at sea, my child?"

Raja Jolan replied, "Long live your Majesty, because I stopped many times at various islands and estuaries to play, I spent a long time at sea."

The King said, "Where are all the kings who go traveling, not stopping to hunt on every island?"

After a while, food was brought out in procession. Raja Jolan ate from the same tray as the Bendahara Paduka Raja.

A scias principium eius non fuisse ex putrido sanguine, sed ex cholera rubra perusta in melancholiam conuersa. Quod si synocha acuitur et mouetur in phlegmate, sicut in horis sanguinis, scias generari ex sanguine iuncto phlegmati falso: et proprie post terminum suum completum mutabitur vel in quotidianam, vel tertianam, licet magis affinis sit tertianae, et quotidianae, propter calorem. Si vero tertiana phlegmatica mouetur, et acuitur sicut in horis cholerae rubrae, minus est periculosa: mutabitur enim in quotidianam: de quotidiana vero fit quartana: et aliquando reddit tertianam. Quod si quartana moueat et acuatur in horis phlegmatis, principium eius fuit falsi phlegmatis, quod versum in choleram rubram incenditur, et vertitur in melancholiam: sicut viride lignum vertitur in viuum carbonem, deinde in cinerem. Quod si synocha mouetur in horis cholerae nigrae, et minus grauis passio, et aeger est piger, et grauis, et illa infirmitas habet partem non solum ex bono sanguine, sed etiam ex putrido: et proprie post terminum suum completum veniet infirmus in quartanam. Si vero tertiana acuitur et mouetur in horis melancholiae, subito vertitur in quartanam. Quod si quartana mouetur in horis illis, firma est et propria, nec mutatur in aliam propter praedictas passiones: omnes enim aliae habent moueri et acui secundum praedictas horas, et earum naturam et rationem: et secundum motum, et acutionem ipsarum, bene discernetur et tactu, et pulsu, sicut ex praedictis horis.

<margin>Al. magis est.</margin>
De Cognitione Aegritudinis secundum Planetam, Diem, et Horam.

Scire etiam medicum decet planetam et signum, in quo aeger aegrotare coepit, et tempus finem diem et horam. Nam si infirmitas fuerit ex signa et planetas, sed accidentaliter ex acutione signi et planetae esset, habet aliam distinctionem. Si vero medicus nesciuerit infirmitatem per numerum, idest per naturam signi et planetae, perscrutetur pulsum et horas, vt dictum est.

De Qualitate et Efficacia Planetarum in septem Climata.

A Sferut etiam physici omnia in terris firmari et compleri secundum cursum et operationem superiorum corporum: quorum operatio omnis summi Creatoris virtute consistit. Elementa igitur quatuor, signis duodecim, et septem planetis iuncta sunt: et eorum causa, quatuor habet temporum mutationes: secundum quas humana, et omnium subiectorum natura mouetur et acuitur: per quam motionem et acutionem passiones fiunt. Haec autem mutatio est vniuersalis omnibus mundanis. Est et alia mutatio ex natura terrae specialiter et planetarum constans in diuersis regionibus. Quadrifidus enim orbis etiam in septem diuisus est partes secundum septem planetas, qui per astrolabium discernuntur. Sciendum est tamen partes illas septem non esse contiguas, sed in toto mundo diuisas. Terra enim illa, quae est frigida et sicca in quarto gradu, sub potestate est Saturni, qui eiusdem est naturae. Quae vero frigida est et sicca in primo gradu, sub louis imperio, qui eiusdem est naturae, et qui etiam affinitatem habet cum natura rerum omnium maximeque ad gaudium pertinentium. Sed quae calida in secundo, humida in primo, sub Martis ditione est, et suae naturae conuenit eiusdem. Sed quae est calida et sicca in quarto, Soli conuenit et concedit. Quae autem calida et humida in primo gradu, sub Mercurio. Quae vero humida, in primo, frigida in secundo, habens aliquantulum temperamenti calidi, Veneri subiacet. Sed quae frigida et humida in primo gradu, Lunae conuenit. Quaeque autem singulae terrarum partes sui retinent planetae qualitates: accidentaliter tamen in naturam vertuntur planetae alterius: terra enim, quae ex planetae natura proprie frigida seu calida esse debet, in contrariam vertitur naturam et complexionem. In complexionibus ergo praefatis, deinde etiam in altitudine, et profunditate, et erectione, et casu, et harmonia cuiusque planetae conuenire debet, ad cuius similitudinem composita est, et inde omne corpus fanum vel aegrum est. Vnde Andronicus peripateticus asserit nos esse secundum nostram voluntatem: et extra nostram voluntatem ambulamus: et etiam contra nostram voluntatem, quando nostra anima ducimur, vel quando accidentaliter ex natura corporis, aut irae furore, aut alio impetu mouemur. Monet etiam secundario aut cogente natura corporis ad malum cognitionem reddere: sicut enim musicus nequit chorda falsa sonitum reddere, sic anima prauum corpus, scilicet libidinosum vel aliud, ratione sui nequit regere: et symphonia instrumenti artificis animae, idest corporis displicet. Andronicus igitur commotiones planetarum, et compositiones merito asserit veras: et cetera vitia non esse naturalia animae: nec animam ex natura corporis constare, quod quidam voluere. Si enim eiusdem esset naturae, nil repugnaret quin anima rationibus spiritualibus subderet corpus, scilicet ieiuniis, et ceteris virtutibus corporis vitia subderet. Et ideo dicit Plato in logica, dum iuuentus est per sensum et rationem mundata ab omni prauitate corporis, cognoscetis omnem virtutem: omnis enim prauitas extra naturam. At aliis elementis corpore composito, ipsum corpus animam mouet: quod eorum contrahit qualitates. Dicit Hippocrates in Physica, quod terra est apposita generare naturam corporum. Est autem vt terra alia dulcis et temperata, ita et homines eius dulces et mansueti. Et ideo anima mandat eis per phantasiam suam omnem bonam operationem. Est et alia terra per naturam planetae acuta: vnde eius homines veniunt bellicosi. Et quia operatio corpore materia ligata est quatuor elementis, ideo dicit Plato, quod ratio conuenit ex superioribus, et ministrat homini spiritualem intellectum, secundum quem discernet superiora et inferiora, vera et falfa in theoria,

<margin>In lib. de natu. hum. com. 1. t. 31. 1. 31. g. idest fere in li. de natu. pueri ad medium, et ad principium libri 4 de morb.</margin>

you know its beginning was not from putrid blood, but from red choler scorched and turned into melancholy. But if synocha is sharpened and moved in phlegm, as in the hours of blood, you know it is generated from blood joined to false phlegm: and properly after its term is completed, it will be changed either into a daily or a tertian, although it is more akin to the tertian and daily, because of the heat. But if a phlegmatic tertian is moved and sharpened as in the hours of red choler, it is less dangerous: for it will be changed into a daily: but from the daily it becomes a quartan: and sometimes it renders a tertian. But if a quartan moves and is sharpened in the hours of phlegm, its beginning was false phlegm, which being turned into red choler is ignited, and is turned into melancholy: just as green wood is turned into live coal, then into ash. But if synocha moves in the hours of black choler, and the passion is less grave, and the sick person is lazy and heavy, and that infirmity has a part not only from good blood, but also from putrid: and properly after its term is completed, the sick person will come into a quartan. But if a tertian is sharpened and moved in the hours of melancholy, it is suddenly turned into a quartan. But if a quartan is moved in those hours, it is firm and proper, nor is it changed into another because of the aforementioned passions: for all others have to be moved and sharpened according to the aforementioned hours, and their nature and reason: and according to the motion and sharpening of them, it will be well discerned both by touch and by pulse, as from the aforementioned hours.

<margin>Al. <note>Alternatively:</note> it is more.</margin>
On the Cognition of Sickness according to the Planet, Day, and Hour.

It also behooves the physician to know the planet and the sign in which the sick person began to be sick, and the time, end, day, and hour. For if the infirmity were from signs and planets, but accidentally from the sharpening of a sign and planet, it has another distinction. If, however, the physician does not know the infirmity by number, that is, by the nature of the sign and planet, let him investigate the pulse and the hours, as has been said.

On the Quality and Efficacy of the Planets in the seven Climates.

Physicians also investigate that all things on earth are fixed and completed according to the course and operation of the superior bodies: the operation of which entirely consists in the virtue of the highest Creator. The four elements, therefore, are joined to the twelve signs and seven planets: and because of them, the year has four changes of seasons: according to which the nature of humans and of all subject things is moved and sharpened: through which motion and sharpening, passions are made. This change, however, is universal to all worldly things. There is also another change from the nature of the earth specially and the planets, consisting in diverse regions. For the fourfold orb is also divided into seven parts according to the seven planets, which are discerned by the astrolabe. It must be known, however, that those seven parts are not contiguous, but divided throughout the whole world. For that earth, which is cold and dry in the fourth degree, is under the power of Saturn, which is of the same nature. But that which is cold and dry in the first degree is under the empire of Jupiter, which is of the same nature, and which also has an affinity with the nature of all things, and especially those pertaining to joy. But that which is hot in the second, humid in the first, is under the dominion of Mars, and agrees with the same of its nature. But that which is hot and dry in the fourth agrees with and yields to the Sun. That which is hot and humid in the first degree is under Mercury. That which is humid in the first, cold in the second, having a little of hot temperament, is subject to Venus. But that which is cold and humid in the first degree agrees with the Moon. And whatever individual parts of the lands retain the qualities of their planet: accidentally, however, they are turned into the nature of another planet: for the earth, which should properly be cold or hot from the nature of the planet, is turned into the contrary nature and complexion. In the aforementioned complexions, therefore, then also in the altitude, and depth, and erection, and fall, and harmony of each planet, it ought to agree, to the likeness of which it is composed, and from there every body is healthy or sick. Whence Andronicus the Peripatetic asserts that we are according to our will: and we walk outside our will: and also against our will, when we are led by our soul, or when we are moved accidentally from the nature of the body, or the fury of anger, or some other impetus. He also warns that the nature of the body secondarily or compellingly renders knowledge: for just as a musician cannot render sound from a false string, so the soul cannot govern a depraved body, that is, a libidinous one or other, by reason of itself: and the symphony of the instrument of the artist, that is, the soul, displeases the body. Andronicus therefore deservedly asserts the commotions of the planets and the compositions to be true: and that other vices are not natural to the soul: nor that the soul consists of the nature of the body, which some have wished. For if it were of the same nature, nothing would hinder the soul from subjecting the body to spiritual reasons, that is, subjecting the vices of the body to fasts and other virtues. And therefore Plato says in his logic, while youth is cleansed by sense and reason from all depravity of the body, you will know every virtue: for all depravity is outside nature. But the body being composed with other elements, the body itself moves the soul: which contracts their qualities. Hippocrates says in his Physics, that the earth is set to generate the nature of bodies. But as some earth is sweet and tempered, so also are its men sweet and gentle. And therefore the soul commands them through its phantasy <gloss>imagination/mental impression</gloss> every good operation. There is also another earth sharp by the nature of the planet: whence its men become warlike. And because the operation of the body is bound to matter by the four elements, therefore Plato says that reason agrees from the superiors, and ministers to man a spiritual intellect, according to which he will discern the higher and the lower, the true and the false in theory,

and the REDEEMER of the same from the superfluities against pure Nature; the SON of the macrocosm: MAGNESIA.

Who, when he has suffered Physico-Chemically for the Salvation of the aforementioned greater (a) world; he descended to the depths of his most Physico-artificial sepulcher; by the Third Operation of the same honest art often mentioned, he rose from the dead, without stain and Corruption.

He ascended to the heavens of Plus-perfection and Clarification: he sits at the right hand of the power and virtue of the macrocosm, the almighty Parent; in crystalline serenity and the redness of a carbuncle; whole, in Body, Spirit, and Soul, as if Quint-Essential:

Thence he comes physico-artificially to judge the healthy and the sick, both of the micro- and macrocosm.

At whose arrival all fruits of all Elements, such as Vegetables, Animals, and Minerals, must be examined, tested, and judged in their Bodies, Spirits, and Souls.

And they render (each in its own way) testimony, either of their own goodness or of their malignity.

And the good that is in them goes into the state of glorification; but that which is evil, into the fire of consumption.

gently solicited with his sight, he disturbed with his hearing, and whose presence the messenger had barely moved, the authority of the one sending shook with all its weight. For what wonder is it if, with a gentle movement and pious affection, God turned the virgin to himself as a servant in his mother, and turned her to himself as a parent? Yet her viscera were troubled, and her very condition trembled when her creator, God, whom the whole creation does not contain, received and hid himself within the human breast. The same author. For even when she saw the angel, her mind, as a virgin's, trembled and was astonished; in his entry, she felt the entry of divinity. The temple of the human body was troubled, and the narrowness of the carnal dwelling was moved when the whole magnitude of God was hidden in the virginal breast. He undoubtedly resumed man from the womb of the woman, he who formed the virgin from the body of man. Ambrose, on Luke, Book II. The virgin should indeed tremble and fear at all entries of men, and revere all their addresses. Therefore, let women learn to imitate the modesty of one placed there. Let the virgin love to avoid the wantonness of words. Mary also feared the angel’s salutation. Jerome to Oceanus. The angel found Mary alone in her private quarters, not speaking with a lover, and she feared the entry of a male. You who are a furnace of malice, why do you desire to be greeted frequently by a man? Bernard, as above. Virgins who are truly virgins are usually fearful, and they avoid not only what is to be feared, but they also fear even safe things, knowing they carry a precious treasure in earthen vessels, and that it is a very arduous task to lead a celibate life in the flesh. Moreover, they hold all things new or sudden as suspect traps and deem everything plotted against them. Therefore, Mary was troubled at the word of the angel, but not perturbed. "I was troubled," says David, "and I did not speak, but I thought of the ancient days, and I had the eternal years in my mind." Similarly, therefore, Mary was troubled and did not speak, but was thinking what manner of salutation that might be. Peter the Bishop, as above. For to

<column-break/>

respond is of human ease; to think, however, is of the greatest weight and mature judgment. Bernard, as above. Therefore, she was troubled by virginal modesty, and not perturbed by strength; she was silent and thought with prudence. The prudent virgin knew indeed that the angel of Satan often transforms himself into an angel of light, but because she was simple and humble, she did not suspect any such thing at all of the holy angel, and therefore she was thinking what this salutation might be. The same author in a sermon on the Assumption. Undoubtedly, she deemed herself unworthy of an angelic salutation, and perhaps by meditating on such things in her mind, she was thinking, "Whence this to me, that the angel of my Lord should come to me?" Gloss on Luke. Elizabeth blushes at her guilt, but Mary blushes at modesty. In a woman, modesty is added; in a virgin, the grace of modesty is increased.

<meta>A decorative initial 'A' featuring floral flourishes.</meta>
The angel, therefore, looking at Mary the virgin and easily perceiving the various thoughts she was revolving within herself, consoles the fearful, confirms the doubtful, and familiarly calling her by name, kindly persuades her not to fear. Peter the Bishop, as above. For while he exhorts her to bear in herself the whole glory of the deity, lest the subtle sand of our body succumb under such a great weight of the celestial structure, and the slender branch be broken while carrying the fruit of the whole human race, he consoles her by dispelling her fear, saying: "Do not fear, Mary." Behold, the dignity of the virgin is announced by her name. For Mary is called "Lady" in Hebrew. Therefore, the angel calls her "Lady" as the mother of the Lord. As if to say, "Trembling stems from servitude, which the authority of the fruit of your own womb makes you be called Lady and commands." Augustine, as above. "Do not therefore fear from my aspect, O mother of my Lord. For I have come as a minister of your conception—not that I might interfere with your virginity."

<summary>This page details the emotional and intellectual response of the Virgin Mary to the Annunciation, emphasizing her modesty, prudence, and the angel's reassuring address to the "Lady" of heaven.</summary>
<keywords>Annunciation, Virgin Mary, Angel Gabriel, Modesty, Prudence, Theology</keywords>

172          THE WAY

refuse them. But because he penetrates the depths of hearts, he rarely grants them these graces, because he does not see them disposed to want to drink from his chalice <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 20:22, signifying the willingness to share in the suffering of Christ.</note>. That is why, my daughters, the sign of your advancement in virtue will be if each of you believes herself so much the worst of all that her actions make it known to others—for their good and for their edification—that she truly has this sentiment in her heart; and not if she has more sweetness in Prayer <note>"Oraiſon" specifically refers to "mental prayer," a focused, interior conversation with God central to Carmelite spirituality.</note>, more raptures, more visions, and other favors of this nature that God grants to souls when it pleases him. For we will not know the value of these goods until the next world. But humility is a currency that is always in circulation <note>original: "a toûjours cours" — Meaning it is always valid and accepted as legal tender in the spiritual economy.</note>, a guaranteed income, and a non-redeemable annuity <note>"rente non rachetable" refers to a permanent financial investment that provides a steady stream of income and cannot be arbitrarily cancelled or bought back.</note>; whereas the rest is like money lent to us for a time and which can be asked back from us. Is it a solid humility, a true mortification, and a great obedience to not fail in any way in what your Su-

<summary>Saint Teresa explains that true spiritual progress is measured by genuine humility and a sense of one's own unworthiness, rather than by mystical visions or "sweetness" in prayer. She compares humility to a stable, permanent currency, while spiritual favors are merely temporary loans from God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the human soul as a microcosm and the internal struggle of the creative forces during formation.</meta>

# OF THE NATURE OF THINGS, CHAPTER I.

A prepared lute-play <note>original: "Lautenspiel"; a lute or musical instrument</note>, upon which the spirit of the will strikes; whichever strings he hits, they sound according to their own property. Within the human mind lies the signature <note>The "Signature" refers to the outward mark or character that reveals the inner essence of a thing</note> quite artfully prepared, according to the Being of all beings <note>original: "Wesen aller Wesen"; a term for the Divine Essence or the totality of existence</note>. Nothing more is lacking to man than the skillful Master who can play his instrument—that is, the true Spirit of the high power of Eternity. If that same Spirit is awakened in man, so that it moves in the center of the mind, then it strikes the instrument of the human form. Then the form goes forth with the resonance in the Word from the mouth. Just as his instrument was tuned <note>original: "gezogen"; literally "drawn" or "strung"</note> at the time of his incarnation <note>original: "Menschwerdung"; the process of becoming human or being formed in the womb</note>, so it sounds, and such is his knowledge. The inner reveals itself in the resonance of the Word, for that is the mind’s natural knowledge of itself.

Man indeed has all the forms of all three worlds <note>The three worlds typically refer to the dark fire-world, the light love-world, and the outer visible world</note> lying within him, for he is a complete image of God or of the Being of all beings. Only in his incarnation is the order established within him. For there are three master-builders <note>original: "Werckmeister"</note> in him who prepare his form, namely the threefold *fiat* <note>Latin: "let it be done"; the creative command of God</note>, according to the three worlds. These are in a wrestling match for the form, and the form is then figured according to that wrestling; whichever master retains the upper-regiment <note>The dominant rule or authority</note> and prevails in the essence <note>original: "Essentz"</note>, according to that will the—

<summary>This page uses the metaphor of a lute to describe how the human mind and voice reveal an individual's inner spiritual signature. It explains that man contains the essence of three worlds, which compete to shape his character during his formation.</summary>

<keywords>microcosm, signature of things, incarnation, three worlds, master-builders, spiritual music, divine essence, human formation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the moralizing conclusion to the biography of Rhea Ilia (the mother of Romulus and Remus), who was forced into the Vestal Virgins by her uncle. The author uses her story to transition into a broader critique of forcing young women into religious life for family convenience or financial greed.</meta>

...ignominious exclusions, and flights, and finally, a dishonorable state <note>original: "dehonestas." Here implying the dishonor of a family unable or unwilling to provide a dowry.</note> seeks to nourish those whom integrity might have sustained; or the greedy man <note>original: "avarus"</note> seeks to join them to husbands. Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher. This citation serves to provide moral authority to the author's argument for self-knowledge and restraint.</note> says: let the madmen know, then, if they do not wish to measure the strength of others by their own, that virgins must be dedicated to God not in ignorance, not as little children, and not under compulsion. 

Indeed, they should first be raised holily from infancy in their father’s house, imbued with integrity and commendable character; advanced in age; and knowing what they do and understanding their own minds; of their own will and not by force, taking up the yoke of perpetual virginity <note>original: "virginitatis"</note>, which I believe is very rarely found. But it is far better for there to be a small number of such women than to profane the sanctuary of God with a seductive multitude <note>original: "multitudine illecebri"</note>.

<summary>The author concludes a moral reflection on the story of Rhea Ilia, arguing that perpetual virginity should only be undertaken by mature women of their own free will, rather than being forced upon children by greedy or dishonorable families.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual journey, picking up from the previous page's metaphor of the merchant who braves the sea for profit. It shifts from the anxiety of the journey to the ultimate reward of inner transformation and divine sonship.</meta>

# Homily XIV.

the merchant rejoices when he makes a profit, but is nonetheless anxious and afraid of murderers and the spirits of wickedness, lest through negligence he lose his labor anywhere: until he comes into the kingdom of heaven, into the city of Jerusalem which is above. For this reason, let us also pray to God from the heart, that he may cause us to put off the **old man** <note>a biblical term (from the Greek 'palaios anthropos') referring to the sinful, unregenerate nature of a person before spiritual rebirth</note>, and that he may cause us to put on the **heavenly Christ** from this time forth, so that we, rejoicing and being guided by him, may live in all tranquility. For the Lord said, when he wished to give us an abundant taste of the kingdom, **Without me you can do nothing.** But through the <margin>John 15:5</margin> service of the Apostles he can also enlighten many people (for those who were otherwise creatures nourished their fellow-brothers) and can make a brother or a son of Christ, and something more excellent than other humans: for these made holy the heart and the understanding, likewise the thoughts, in order to behold God with steadfast eyes: who secretly gave life, and was helpful to the heart, commending himself to it. For when someone dedicates and surrenders his secrets—namely, the understanding and the thoughts—to God, not busying himself with any other matter or idle thought, but constraining himself with force: then the Lord makes this person a partaker of the mysteries and secrets in greater holiness and purity: and gives himself as a heavenly food and as a spiritual drink. Just as if someone who has much property, many servants and sons, fed his servants with one kind of food, and his own sons born of his seed with another <note>The original Dutch repeats "andere spijse" (other food) for both, but the context implies a distinction in quality or status between the servants' rations and the sons' inheritance.</note>: for the sons are the father's heirs, and they eat with him as being almost equal to their father: Even so Christ, who is the True Lord, has created all things, and feeds the evil and the ungrate- <meta>catchword: ungrate-</meta>

<summary>This page explores the transition from being a mere creation to becoming a 'son of Christ' through the total surrender of one's inner thoughts and intellect to God. It uses the metaphor of a father providing a special, intimate nourishment to his heirs to describe the spiritual food Christ offers to the faithful.</summary>
<keywords>Homily XIV, Jerusalem above, old man, heavenly Christ, John 15:5, Apostles, spiritual nourishment, divine sonship, purity of heart</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the spiritual macrocosm and microcosm. Having previously established that seeds and angels contain the potential of all things within them through "enfolding," the author now moves to the ultimate source of this power: the divine nature of God as the center and circle of all existence.</meta>

## ON SIGNATURES.

...established and elevated, can do so much better and more quickly. He who diligently considers this **Central** or **Circular Philosophy** <note>Central or Circular Philosophy refers to a mystical way of understanding the world where the physical circumference of reality is understood by looking into its spiritual center or source.</note> with his intellect and the purified eye of the mind, will not find it difficult to believe that an Angel or the Great Celestial can include the entire Firmament in a <term>Gamaæa<gloss>original: *Gamaæa*; a talisman or stone naturally or artificially marked with celestial signs, believed to hold the power of the stars</gloss></term>, or even the whole world in his fist. Since, however, an Angel is the perfect and absolute image of **GOD**, and <term>enfolds<gloss>original: *complicet*; the philosophical concept that all the complexity of the universe exists in a unified, simplified state within the divine mind</gloss></term>, holds, and possesses all things in his **Abyss**, it must not be denied that the first and supreme Cause, existing from itself and depending on itself, enfolds all things with itself invisibly and spiritually in its Abyss; indeed, all things exist in the **Fontal Unity** in the simplest manner. For all created things were produced by Him, who is all in all, namely the First and last cause of all things:

<margin>
Nothing Divine is dark.
The dark Beginning.
The Dark Light.
</margin>

Not from pre-existing matter, nor did He take anything from another, nor receive anything abundantly from outside Himself. For whatever the inferior Power can do and possesses, as was said above, this same thing the superior Power can do and possesses, but much more excellently, effectively—indeed, superexcellently.

<margin>
God, ineffable and unnamable, is marked as a **Trigram** in nature, a **Tetragram** in the Law, and a **Pentagram** in grace. This is the state of future blessedness.
</margin>

For there is no comparison of the infinite to the finite, or of the Creator to the Creature. God is the **Center and Circle** of Himself, dwelling in Himself, that is, in the **Abyss of Infinity** (which the Hebrews call <term>Ein Sof<gloss>original: *Eoſuph*; a Hebrew Kabbalistic term meaning "the infinite" or "without end," describing God before any self-manifestation</gloss></term>, the incomprehensible infinity) where for eternity no place, no beginning, and no end can be investigated or even thought of. He was made neither by another nor by Himself: for He could not be made by another, because He had no one prior to Himself—otherwise He would not be the first cause—nor did He make Himself, for from nothing, nothing is made. Therefore He always was (and this is the essential **Ineffable Tetragrammaton** <note>original Greek: *τετραγράμματον*, meaning "four-lettered," referring to the sacred Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note> name, on account of His tremendous majesty...

<note>This page discusses the regulation of liveries—badges or signs of affiliation—to prevent the formation of private armies, and addresses the unlawful seizure of land through royal grants.</note>

# First <note>referring to the first year of the reign</note>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence discussing the consequences for those who do not follow the requirements for letters patent</note> such desert to the King as those who have not signed of their own will, being left to the benefit of the letters patent granted to them in this part. <margin>Item</margin> Item, to maintain and nourish love, peace, and quiet of all parties throughout the realm, it is ordained and established by the King and the lords spiritual and temporal and the commons together in full parliament, that no lord, of whatever estate or condition he be, shall use or give any <term>livery</term> <gloss>uniform or badge of affiliation</gloss> of a sign of company to any knight, esquire, or valet within the realm aforesaid. Always providing that my said lord the King may give his honorable livery only to the temporal lords as it shall please him. And furthermore, the King may give his said honorable livery to his household knights and esquires, and also to his knights and esquires who are of his retinue and take from him their annual fee for term of life. And beyond this, it is accorded and assented by the King and the lords and commons, that knights and esquires shall not in any way use the said liveries in their neighborhoods or counties where they are resident or dwelling, nor anywhere within the realm outside the presence of the King. And if anyone does the contrary to this, and is duly convicted, he shall pay a ransom and fine at the King’s will. And if any knight or esquire does the contrary, and is duly attainted, he shall forfeit his said livery as a fee forever. And no valet called a <term>yeoman</term> <gloss>a servant or attendant in a noble household</gloss> shall take or use any livery of the King or of any other lord, upon pain of imprisonment and making fine and ransom at the King’s will. Provided always that the Constable and Marshal of England for the time being, with their said knights and esquires, may use the said livery of the King on the frontiers and the marches of the realm in time of war. And provided also that all those who wish to travel and pass across the sea to foreign parts to seek honors may use <margin>vii</margin> the livery of those parts without being in any way aggrieved or impeached for it. And furthermore, it is accorded and assented that no Archbishop, Bishop, Abbot, or Prior, nor any other man of Holy Church or temporal man of whatever estate or condition he be within the said realm, shall give any livery of cloth to anyone, but only to his household servants and officers and those who are of their counsel, both spiritual and temporal, under pain of making fine and ransom at the King’s will. And these ordinances and statutes shall begin to take effect from the feast of Candlemas <note>February 2</note> next coming. <margin>Item</margin> Item, at the grievous complaint of the said commons made in the said parliament, that many of the lieges of my said lord the King have been ousted and dispossessed of their lands and tenements, despite their right and title, as much by <term>disseisin</term> <gloss>wrongful dispossession</gloss> with force upon the King of England as by false suggestion made to him, the said lands and tenements have been granted to various persons by letters patent made thereof. Thus, by color of the said grants and letters patent, the tenants and rightful possessors of the said tenements in many counties are disseised and ousted directly to their great damage and against the course of the common law, without due process of law. <meta>This page continues the technical instructions for preparing the ingredients mentioned on the previous page. Although the catchword provided from the previous page was "Hor," the text here begins with "de," completing the word "alcalisade" (alkalized) from the end of page 117.
