upon the earth, and the <term>Turba</term> <gloss>disorder or turmoil</gloss> pressed in alongside it. God wanted to partly destroy this <term>Turbam</term> <gloss>disorder</gloss> in forty days and nights. If the source of water had not opened up, the source of fire would have risen out of the <term>Turba</term>. Thus, the Great Flood was in part a benevolent act of God, preventing the fire from swallowing the earth before its time because of sin. As Peter says in 1 Peter 3, eight souls were saved through the water.

87. Question: What does the drunkenness of Noah signify?

Answer: The story is to be read in Genesis 9. Noah's drunkenness signifies that we carry all animal-like qualities within us, as God gave Job to understand through the image of the <term>Behemot</term> <gloss>Behemoth</gloss>. Since we have animalistic lust stuck deep within us, we did not feel shame before God. We only despise the heavenly image and elevate the earthly. God does not count this corrupted nature against us, but rather shows His love to the ungodly in the death of His Son. Romans 5.

88. Question: Why were the languages confused at the Tower of Babel?

Answer: Nimrod had Babel as the beginning of his kingdom. There, the arts spread because they had one language, which is why they began to build the tower... <note>The text breaks off here to continue on the next page.</note>

a <term>Corrosiff</term> <gloss>corrosive or caustic substance</gloss>, now tell me: in what way must you bring it to that state? Otherwise, it is no corrosive. If it is possible to make bad out of good, then it is also possible to make good out of bad.

No one should punish or criticize a thing if they do not recognize its <term>transmutation</term> <gloss>transformation from one state to another</gloss>, and if they do not know what harm or good it may do.

Geh nach der Stadt, sagte Johann, und überbringe dem Grafen Rosenschild die schöne Uhr, die du verfertigtest. Bleib einige Tage in der Stadt, und erhole dich ein wenig. Gottlieb trug die Uhr nach der Stadt; begab sich aber gleich den andern Tag wieder zurück. Es dämmerte schon, als er an den Wald kam, und es war finstere Nacht, als ihn der Weg bis in die Mitte des Forstes führte. In tiefen Gedanken wandelte Gottlieb seine Wege, als er gähling ein jammerndes Geschrey verunglückter Menschen hörte, die um Hilfe riefen, Gottlieb eilte den Lärmen nach, und erblickte bey dem Schein einiger Fackeln, daß eine Kutsche von Räubern angehalten wurde, und ein schönes Frauenzimmer lag ohnmächtig in den Armen eines Räubers, der sie fortschleppte. Gottlieb eilte dem Verwegnen nach, stürzte ihn zu Boden, und rettete die Dame. Wie ein tollsinniger wüthete er unter den Mördern, und schlug sie in die Flucht, obwohl er selbst tödlich durch einen Schuß verwundet wurde.

pages.translation:
<meta>continues from previous page: Gottlieb senses the end of his life, but his master tries to comfort him.</meta>
Master John made every effort to talk his Gottlieb out of these imaginings, but Gottlieb did not become any more cheerful.

Go to the city, John said, and deliver the beautiful watch you finished to Count Rosenschild. Stay in the city for a few days and recover a little. Gottlieb carried the watch to the city, but he returned the very next day. It was already dusk when he reached the forest, and it was dark night by the time his path led him into the middle of the woods. Gottlieb walked his way lost in deep thought, when he suddenly heard the piteous cries of unfortunate people calling for help. Gottlieb rushed toward the noise and saw, by the light of a few torches, that a carriage had been stopped by robbers. A beautiful young lady lay unconscious in the arms of a robber who was dragging her away. Gottlieb rushed after the daring man, threw him to the ground, and saved the lady. Like a madman he raged among the murderers and put them to flight, although he himself was mortally wounded by a gunshot.

tribus qui étaient au service de l'empire, soit au corps des clients attachés à la maison du souverain. Les cadis remplissaient alors les mêmes fonctions que, de nos jours, on confie aux vizirs dans le Maghreb : ils sortaient à la tête des armées pour faire les campagnes d'été, et ils avaient la direction des affaires les plus importantes, affaires qui ne se confient qu'à des hommes auxquels la puissance de leur famille donne les moyens d'exécution. Ceux qui entendent parler de ces faits tombent souvent dans l'erreur, parce qu'ils assimilent un ordre de choses à un autre qui en diffère.

Ce genre de méprise est très-commun de nos jours, surtout parmi les (musulmans) espagnols peu éclairés. Cela tient à l'extinction de tout esprit de corps chez eux, changement amené, il y a plusieurs siècles, par la ruine de la puissance arabe dans ce pays et par la chute de la dynastie qu'elle y avait fondée. Délivrés de la domination des Berbers², peuples chez lesquels a toujours existé un vif sentiment de nationalité, ces Arabes ont perdu l'esprit de corps et d'assistance mutuelle qui mène à la puissance, et ne conservent que leurs généalogies. Tombés au rang des peuples soumis qui ne se prêtent aucun secours les uns aux autres, subjugués par la force, abreuvés d'humiliations, ils s'imaginent qu'avec de la naissance et un emploi dans le gouvernement, on parvient facilement à conquérir un royaume et à gouverner les hommes. Vous trouverez, chez eux, jusqu'aux hommes de métier et aux simples artisans qui rêvent le pouvoir et qui cherchent à le saisir. Celui qui a vu de près l'état des tribus dans le Maghreb, l'esprit de corps qui les anime, les empires qu'elles ont fondés et la manière dont ces peuples et ces tribus établissent leur domination, ne se laisse guère tomber dans de pareilles erreurs et se trompe rarement dans l'appréciation de ces matières.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
tribes who were in the service of the empire, or to the body of clients attached to the sovereign's house. At that time, <term>qadis</term> <gloss>Islamic judges</gloss> fulfilled the same functions that are entrusted to <term>viziers</term> <gloss>ministers or high officials</gloss> in the Maghreb <gloss>Northwest Africa</gloss> today. They went out at the head of armies to conduct summer campaigns, and they directed the most important affairs. These matters are only entrusted to men whose family influence provides the means for execution. Those who hear of these facts often fall into error because they equate one order of things with another that differs from it.

This kind of mistake is very common today, especially among the less enlightened Spanish Muslims <note>referring to the inhabitants of Al-Andalus</note>. This is due to the extinction of all <term>asabiyyah</term> <gloss>esprit de corps or social solidarity</gloss> among them. This change was brought about several centuries ago by the ruin of Arab power in that country and by the fall of the dynasty it had founded there. Delivered from the domination of the Berbers <margin>Page 49</margin> <note>Specifically, the Almoravids and their successors, the Almohades. The latter belonged to the Masmuda tribes who lived in the Moroccan Atlas range. The former were part of the Lemtuna and other Berber tribes who lived in the great desert between Senegal and Timbuktu.</note>, peoples among whom a lively sense of nationality has always existed, these Arabs have lost the spirit of unity and mutual assistance that leads to power. They retain only their genealogies. Having fallen to the rank of subject peoples who offer no help to one another, subjugated by force, and saturated with humiliations, they imagine that with noble birth and a government job, one can easily conquer a kingdom and govern men. You will find among them even tradesmen and simple artisans who dream of power and seek to seize it. Anyone who has closely seen the state of the tribes in the Maghreb, the <term>asabiyyah</term> that animates them, the empires they have founded, and the way these peoples and tribes establish their domination, will hardly fall into such errors and will rarely be mistaken in evaluating these matters.

sine lege erant quasi sine lege essemus omnibus omnia factus sum: ut omnes facerem salvos. Quid igitur actio in se nec turpis: nec honesta: sed modus agendi actioni tribuit cognometum. Pari lege eiuscemodi imagines venerandi opus in se quidem paruipendendum est: nisi quatenus mens quae sub solius creatoris imperio degere licet interno ipso idolorum cultu se creaturae praebet obnoxiam. Idcirco cum ad solum creatoris misterium internam. Imaginis venerationem transtulerint manente ritu qui ab extra: ipsa effrenata ac stolida multitudo quieuit: et si forte imbecilles inde periclitentur: vastasque in erroris voraginem ruant: nil tamen scandali et turpitudinis hinc sospiti mente erumpit. Ex hoc vnius consule tamen censere audio: modo orthodoxa iac christi fide ad plenitudines redacta non iniuria: imo condens et laudabile factu esset (nisi longeue forte consuetudinis luxus remitteretur) templa: oraculaque a sanctorum sculptilibus exuta construeret: siquidem ad yperbolicos et ethereos sanctorum spiritus hominum mentes extolleret no corporeas manu factas imagines: quae et de scandali periculo infirmos eriperet. Insuper obtrectantium iudeorum latratibus silentium imponeret: ac plures eorum: quos preteritis imaginibus cultus repellit ad piam christi religionem amplectendam perduceret. In singulis tamen ad sacra et inconcussa ecclesiae: quae a non errante spiritu regitur edicta me confero: cum illa pergo: cum illa sapio: viuo et requiescam in secula.

<meta>continues from previous page: the coupling with a woman is in itself neither foul nor honorable, but it is made wicked if by the desire of lust, if without marriage, if knowing her when she is polluted by men</meta>
who were without law, as if we were without law, and I became all things to all men so that I might save all <note>original: "sine lege erant quasi sine lege essemus omnibus omnia factus sum: ut omnes facerem salvos." This is a reference to the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:22.</note>. What then is an action in itself? It is neither shameful nor honorable; rather, the mode of acting attributes the name to the action. By an equal law, the work of venerating images of this kind is in itself to be valued little, except insofar as the mind, which should live under the authority of the Creator alone, makes itself subject to a creature through that internal worship of idols. Therefore, when they transferred the internal veneration of the image to the mystery of the Creator alone, while the outward rite remained, the unbridled and dull multitude became quiet. Even if the weak are perhaps endangered by this and fall into a vast whirlpool of error, no scandal or foulness breaks forth from a mind that remains sound. 

From this one counsel, however, I hear it judged that provided the orthodox faith of Christ is brought to its fullness, it would not be a wrong, but rather a founding and laudable deed (unless perhaps the luxury of long-standing custom prevents it) if one were to construct temples and oracles stripped of the carvings of saints. Indeed, one would then exalt the minds of men to the hyperbolic and ethereal spirits of the saints, not to corporeal images made by hand. This would rescue the weak from the danger of scandal. Furthermore, it would impose silence on the barking of the detracting Jews and lead many of them, whom the worship of past images repels, to embrace the pious religion of Christ. Nevertheless, in all things, I commit myself to the sacred and unshakable edicts of the Church, which is ruled by a spirit that does not err. With her I go forward, with her I think, I live, and I shall rest forever.

<margin>21</margin> **You shall not make molten gods.** <note>Leviticus 19.</note>
That is, neither for others nor shall others make them for you.

<margin>22</margin> **You shall not make silver gods.** <note>Exodus 20.</note>
This means any prominent carved image, even for the sake of ornament, unless you leave the picture with a truncated limb <note>a reference to a legal loophole where an incomplete figure was not considered a forbidden idol.</note>.

# OF ARISTOPHANES

Accuser: But, men of the jury, it is the most terrible
of deeds that I have suffered, and, oh my <note>an exclamation of lament</note>,
for he got off into the corner and a large amount of cheese
he prepared and molded in the dark.

Phi. By Zeus, but he is clear to me at least,
this very wretched cheese-eater,
this glutton, and he did not share any shamefully with me,
and how will anyone be able to do this to you,
if someone does not throw something to me, the dog?

Accuser: He did not share anything even with me, the common dog.

Phi. For a hot man <note>impatient/angry man</note> is worth nothing for lentils <note>proverbial, meaning he is useless in a pinch</note>.

Bd. By the gods, do not judge beforehand, father,
until you have heard from both sides.
Phi. But, my good man,
the matter is obvious. For it cries out for itself.

Accuser: Do not let him go now as being the most
gluttonous of all the deaf ones,
who desires to enrich the mortar in a circle,
having devoured the curd from the cities.

Phi. And to me, he has shaped this insolence.

Dog <note>Labes</note>: Because of these things, even if you punish me, for no other
way will I be able to turn, one spear cannot steal for two,
so that I do not bark at things I have already bitten,
and if not, I will bark for what remains.

Phi. Look, look, how many accusers for these villainies,
a thieving thing is the man, which seems so to you,
oh rooster, by Zeus, go away <note>a sudden exclamation of annoyance</note>.
The magistrate, look there, let him give me the urinal.

Accuser: I will bring it down myself, for you are calling the witnesses,
let him bring the witnesses, a bowl,
a pestle, a cheese-grater, a hearth, a pot,
and the other scorched kitchenware.

<summary>The legal proceedings continue with the accuser presenting a list of kitchen items as evidence of the dog's gluttony and theft, while Philo grows impatient.</summary>

67. *Melitæi canes.*] In eos, qui propter solam oblectationem delicatè enutriuntur. Canum enim alij sunt indagatores, alij cum feris in pugnam congrediuntur, nonnulli domum & res ibidem custodiunt; alij denique qui solius voluptatis causa aluntur.

68. *Rutam mihi impertire, ne me fascines.*] Rutam enim aiunt aduersus fascinum esse amuletum, vt ait Aristoteles in Problematibus.

69. *Portio, non iugulatio.*] Cùm potentiores imbecilliorum victum raperent, illosque ea de causa iugularent, quòd se defendere illi non possent, excitata partitio est. Cumque æquam singuli partem caperent; exclamabant, Pars non iugulatio.

70. *Post Lesbium cantorem.*] Parœmia est apud Cratinum vsurpata de illis qui secundas ferunt. Lacedæmonij enim Lesbios citharœdos primi aduocarunt. Cùm enim illorum vrbs aliquando tumultuaretur, oraculum editum est, Lesbium cantorem esse aduocandum. Illi itaque Terpandrum ob cædem exulantem Antissa accersitum in Syssitijs cùm audiuissent, à tumultu cohibiti, & quieti pristinæ redditi fuerunt. Aut quod cùm Lacedæmonij in seditione essent, ex Lesbo musicum Terpandrum arcersierunt, qui illorum animos composuit, & seditionem sedauit. Si quando igitur postea Lacedæmonij musicum audirent, Post Lesbium cantorem dicebant.

71. *Cum Musis Corydus.*] De indoctis qui cum eruditis versantur. Cum gestu autem quodam legendum. Parœmia similis illi: *Carica Musa.*

He who produced the greater noise was praised; from this, therefore, comes <term>Methysocottabus</term> <gloss>wine-cottabus/drunken cottabus</gloss>.

67. *Melitean dogs.*] Concerning those who are daintily fed solely for the sake of amusement. For among dogs, some are trackers; others engage in battle with wild beasts; some are house-guardians of property; and others are kept solely for pleasure.

68. *Share your rue with me, so that you may not bewitch me.*] For they say that rue is an amulet against bewitchment, as Aristotle says in his *Problems*.

69. *Portion, not slaughter.*] When the powerful used to seize the food of the weaker, and slaughter them for that reason because they could not defend themselves, the partition was devised. And when each person took an equal share, they would exclaim, "A portion, not a slaughter."

70. *After the Lesbian singer.*] This is a proverb used by Cratinus concerning those who take second place. For the Lacedaemonians were the first to call upon the Lesbian cithara-players. For when their city was once in turmoil, an oracle was issued that a Lesbian singer should be summoned. They, therefore, summoned Terpander, who was in exile for manslaughter, from Antissa. Having heard him at the <term>Syssitia</term> <gloss>communal meals</gloss>, they were restrained from their turmoil and restored to their original peace. Or, because when the Lacedaemonians were in sedition, they summoned the musician Terpander from Lesbos, who harmonized their souls and stopped the sedition. If, therefore, at any time afterward the Lacedaemonians heard a musician, they would say, "After the Lesbian singer."

71. *With the Muses, a Lark.*] Concerning the uneducated who associate with the educated. It should be read with a certain gesture. It is similar to the proverb: *A Carian Muse.*

<header>PREFACE.</header>

But I do not wish to delay you with a longer Preface, benevolent reader. Farewell, therefore, and look favorably upon my Epicurus, whose *Letter to Menoeceus*, and the remaining Moral Fragments—which have escaped the shipwreck of time—collected from Laertius and other ancient writers, amended and illustrated, I am going to bring to light, if the best God grants me life and strength.

Written at Zurich of the Swiss, on the Ides of March, 1818.

Fuit et alius Sophocles nepos eius, et ipse Tragicus, qui docuit fabulas XL. vicit septies.

De charactere Sophoclis pauca iam attingam: in explicandis fabulae huius partibus agam copiosius, gravis et sublimis est: ita tamen ut, gravitatem iucunditate, et dulcedine perfundat in movendis affectibus, quamvis sit tragicus, vincit tamen Euripides. Est enim Euripides ut aliis rebus longe inferior, tamen τραγικώτατος, id est, maxime movens affectus, vel Aristotelis iudicio in Poetica. Quintilianus addit carmen Euripidis ad Oratorium genus magis, quam Sophocleum accedere, sed de Poeta, eiusque charactere satis: de Tragoedia, eiusque ortu iam agamus.

Tragoedia, Comoedia, atque adeo omnis poësis a natura fluxit: et ab ea suum ortum accepit. homo enim ad imitandum natus, aptusque est: id, quod etiam in ipsis statim infantibus facile cerni potest, qui imitatione discunt agere quaecunque agunt, imitatur autem homines res vel laetas, vel tristes. Vita enim hominum in his quasi duobus vertitur cardinibus, secundis (inquam) rebus, vel adversis. Primi itaque illi homines alij has, alij illas pro diversitate ingeniorum, sequuti, eas imitando exprimere sunt conati, casu primum hoc accidit ut Aristoteles etiam testatur: deinde re notata ab iis, qui erant solertiores, et ingenij acumine valebant, utraque res, Comoedia, Tragoediaque paulatim crevit, et progressus primum modicos, deinde magnos fecit. Ortus eius a rebus divinis manasse creditur. Solebant enim veteres pro frugibus sacra facere, et incensis altaribus, admotoque hirco carmen canere in Bacchi laudem: hoc carmen τραγῳδίαν vocabant ἀπὸ τοῦ τράγου καὶ τῆς ᾠδῆς, id est, ab hirco vinearum hoste, et cantu, vel, quod hirco sive utre musti pleno donabatur carminis author: vel quod cantores ora faecibus perlinirent, antequam Aeschylus personas reperisset. Ut cum faeces τρύγες Graece dicantur, τραγῳδία quasi τρυγῳδία carmen vocaretur, quod canerent agerentque peruncti faecibus ora: ut Horatius canit. Hunc in modum Tragoedia inventa in Peloponneso coepit agi, eiusque ortum (ut author est Aristoteles in Poëtica) Dorienses sibi vendicant. agere enim ipsi δρᾶν dicunt, unde

pages.translation:
There was also another Sophocles, his grandson, himself a tragic poet, who taught XL <note>40</note> plays and won seven times.

I shall now touch briefly on the character of Sophocles: I will treat it more fully when explaining the parts of this play. He is grave and sublime, yet in such a way that he infuses gravity with pleasantness and sweetness. In moving the affections, although he is tragic, Euripides nevertheless wins. For Euripides, although far inferior in other things, is nevertheless <term>tragikotatos</term> <gloss>most tragic</gloss>, that is, the one who most moves the affections, even by the judgment of Aristotle in his *Poetics*. Quintilian adds that the poetry of Euripides approaches the oratorical genre more than that of Sophocles. But enough about the poet and his character; let us now treat of tragedy and its origin.

Tragedy, Comedy, and indeed all poetry flowed from nature and received its origin from her. For man is born and apt for imitation: a thing which can be easily seen even in infants, who learn by imitation to do whatever they do. Moreover, one imitates people in either joyful or sad situations. For the life of men turns on these two hinges, so to speak: prosperous circumstances (I say) or adverse ones. Therefore, those first men, following some the one and others the other according to the diversity of their talents, attempted to express them by imitating them. At first, this happened by chance, as Aristotle also testifies. Then, the matter being noted by those who were more skillful and possessed keenness of mind, both things—Comedy and Tragedy—grew little by little and made progress: first modest, then great. Its origin is believed to have flowed from divine matters. For the ancients were accustomed to make sacrifices for their crops and, with smoking altars and a goat brought forward, to sing a song in praise of Bacchus. They called this song <term>tragodia</term> <gloss>tragedy</gloss> <term>apo tou tragou kai tes odes</term> <gloss>from the goat and the song</gloss>, that is, from the goat, the enemy of the vines, and the song; either because the author of the song was gifted with a goat or a wineskin full of must, or because the singers smeared their faces with dregs before Aeschylus had invented masks. So that, when dregs are called <term>truges</term> in Greek, <term>tragodia</term> would be called as if <term>trugodia</term> <gloss>dregs-song</gloss>, a song which they sang and performed with their faces smeared with dregs, as Horace sings. In this manner, tragedy, having been invented in the Peloponnese, began to be performed, and the Dorians claim its origin for themselves (as Aristotle is the author in his *Poetics*). For they say <term>dran</term> <gloss>to do</gloss> for to perform, whence

Ac primum Dissertationem quod adtinet Homericam, in ea id egi, quod e præmissa Epistola intelligi potest, ut rejectis Porphyrii mei nugis, quibus locum Poëtæ tenebris involverat potius quam illustraverat, novam Antri Nympharum explicationem proponerem, pulcræque Homeri descriptioni quam potui lucem adfunderem. <header>PREFACE.</header>
The second part of the Collectanea follows, which illustrates Porphyry, and contains excerpts:
- from Marsham’s *Chronic Canon* p. 72, 73.
- from Petitus *On the Sibyl*. p. 73—80.
- from G. Canterus’ *New Readings*. p. 80—82.
- then my own observations on the booklet of Porphyry on the Cave of the Nymphs. p. 83—122.
Three indices close the procession: the first critical. p. 123, 124. the second grammatical. p. 125, 126. the third of subjects. p. 127 and following.

I have a few things to say about these individually. And first, regarding the Homeric Dissertation, I have done in it what can be understood from the preceding Letter: namely, having rejected the trifles of my Porphyry, by which he had obscured rather than illuminated the Poet's passage, I proposed a new explanation of the Cave of the Nymphs and shed such light as I could on Homer’s beautiful description. But it is not irrelevant to warn here that my friend, the celebrated Ruhnkenius, disagreed with me somewhat on this matter. He believed that the <term>Homericos</term> <gloss>Homeric [poles/masts]</gloss> (*) should be understood differently than they had been accepted by me: namely, not as *masts of ships*, but (as the word equally expresses) as those timbers to which the ancients fastened their webs, which indeed are sometimes called *webs* themselves by the Latins; for the *stamen* <gloss>warp/thread</gloss> is the work which is woven. The ambiguous nature of the Poet’s words favors this opinion, if you understand the word to mean *masts*; for since the mention of <term>φαρεων</term> <gloss>fabrics/veils</gloss> follows immediately, woven by the Nymphs in the Cave, the double sense of <term>των ιστων</term> <gloss>of the looms/masts</gloss> seemed to him to demand that these should not be understood as *masts of ships*, but as those weaving instruments to which the warp is fastened. To this is added...

<margin>(*) See Dissertation on Porphyry, Chapter II, § 10.</margin>

ἡ ἐκ δευτέρας δὲ τοῦ τεύχεσθαι, τὸ ἐκ στεμφύλων ἀπόβρεγμα φέρει αὐτὸ μεῖζον.

Ὁ δὲ ῥητινίτης οἶνος παρὰ τὰ ἔθνη ὀνομάζεται, πλεονάζει δὲ ἐν Γαλατίᾳ διὰ τὸ ἀποξύνεσθαι

...are of similar power, styptic and good for the stomach, and suitable for fluxes of the stomach, intestines, and bladder, and for hemorrhages. They also cure all fluxing ulcers when poured on, and they stop fluxes of the uterus and anus when used as a sitz bath.

On Phoenician Wine. Chapter 43.

For Phoenician wine, take common ripe dates, throw them into a jar with a pipe <note>original: "siphon"</note> inserted at the bottom, bound with a reed and sealed. Stuff it with linen; for every ten <term>choinikes</term> <gloss>dry measures</gloss>, pour in 3 <term>choes</term> <gloss>liquid measures</gloss> of water. If you want it to be sweet, pour in five <term>choes</term>. Leave it for seven days. On the eleventh day, remove the cloth from the pipe, and draw off the thick, sweet, or strained wine. It is a flavoring and causes headaches; it works against fluxes due to its styptic property. Hence, it is suitable for stomach conditions, intestinal conditions, and for the stomach. They also mix water into it again and receive it, and make a weaker [wine], fourth, fifth, sixth, and finally it turns to vinegar.

On Katorxites Wine. Chapter 44.

Katorxites wine, which some call fig wine, is prepared in the same way as Phoenician wine. It differs because some add to it the juice of freshly pressed residues, adding as much as they want. Dried figs, which are called swallow figs, or black Phoenician [figs], are taken and soaked as previously said. After ten days, the liquid is taken. And from the second and sixth [pressings], it is done with the juice of the residues, and water is added. From the washings, the liquid is taken, and the washings turn to vinegar similarly. They use it as vinegar. It is deficient, flatulent, bad for the stomach, and destroys appetite. It is not laxative for the bowels. It suppresses menses and makes milk sparse. It creates bad blood and is stinging for elephantiasis, as is its nature. Some add salt to the jars, up to ten. Others add a jar of brine, which is difficult to change and not good. Others add thyme and fennel to the bottom, along with the figs, and they do this in turn until they fill the vessel.

On Sycamore Wine. Chapter 45.

It is prepared from sycamores as a vinegar wine, and it becomes sharp because the liquid does not penetrate, and it preserves the sweetness of the <note>original: "rhynes" (obscure)</note>.

On Resinous Wine. Chapter 46.

Resinous wine, as the nations prepare it, is more common in Galatia. Because of the souring, [they prepare] the wine by mixing it with pine resin. It is crushed with the bark and the resin. It is mixed with a <term>hemikotylion</term> of wine. And some boil it after soaking, removing the resin. Others leave it. When aged, they become smooth. All such wines cause headaches and vertigo. However, they are digestive and diuretic. They are suitable for those with fluxes and those who are constipated, for intestinal conditions, dysentery, dropsy, and women with flows. For internal ulcerations, [use it as an] injection. However, it is more styptic than the white one, as it turns black.

On Pine-Nut Wine. Chapter 47.

Pine-nut wine is prepared by soaking the fresh bark of pine nuts and crushing them. Press them with the resinous wine. If one soaks the pine nuts in sweet wine and mixes them, it is suitable for the phthisical <gloss>tuberculous</gloss> when drunk.

On Cedar Wine. Chapter 48.

Cedar, juniper, cypress, laurel, pine, and fir wine are prepared similarly. One must [use] the woody parts...

->Just as when from her bed beside noble Tithonus,<- 
->Dawn arose to bring light to immortals and mortals alike,<-

Zeus sent down <term>Eris</term> <gloss>Strife</gloss> to the swift ships of the Achaeans, 
cruel, holding in her hands the sign of war. 
She stood upon the black, cavernous ship of Odysseus, 
which was in the middle so that a shout could reach both sides, 
both to the tents of Ajax, son of Telamon, 
and to those of Achilles, for they had hauled their balanced ships 
to the furthest edges, trusting in their bravery and the strength of their hands. 
Standing there, the goddess shouted great and terrible 
shrieks to the Achaeans, and she cast great strength into each 
man’s heart to wage war and fight unceasingly. 
For them, battle suddenly became sweeter than returning 
in their hollow ships to their beloved native land. 
The son of Atreus <note>Agamemnon</note> shouted and commanded the Argives 
to arm themselves, and he himself donned the gleaming bronze. 
First he put the greaves around his shins, 
beautiful, fitted with silver ankle-clasps. 
Next, he put the breastplate around his chest, 
which Cinyras once gave him as a guest-gift; 
for he heard in Cyprus the great report that the Achaeans 
intended to sail to Troy in their ships,

It resounded horribly, and <term>Penelope</term> laughed.
Immediately she addressed <term>Eumaeus</term> with winged words:
"Go, call the guest here to me in person.
Do you not see that my son has sneezed at all my words?
Therefore, death shall not be imperfect for the suitors
At all, nor shall anyone avoid death and fate.
Another thing I tell you, and you place it in your mind:
If I recognize him telling all things truly,
I will clothe him in a cloak and an under-tunic, beautiful garments."
She spoke, he went, the swineherd, after he heard the word.
Standing near, he addressed him with winged words:
"Father guest, the prudent <term>Penelope</term>,
Mother of <term>Telemachus</term>, calls you; her mind commands her to inquire
Something about her husband, even though she has suffered sorrows.
But if she recognizes that you tell all things truly,
She will clothe you in a cloak and an under-tunic, of which you most
Have need. And asking for bread among the people,
You will feed your belly, and he will give to you whoever wishes."
The much-enduring divine <term>Ulysses</term> answered him:
"<term>Eumaeus</term>, I will quickly tell all things truly
To the daughter of <term>Icarius</term>, the very prudent <term>Penelope</term>.

# ORPHEUS

Prayer, blessed goddess, war-shaking, strong-hearted.
Unspeakable, wind-rushing, great-named, cave-dweller.
You who move through the high-necked hills of the mountain-peaks.
And shady mountains, and delight your mind in the valleys.
Lover of arms, driving the souls of mortals into madness.
Training hands, having a terrifying spirit.
Slayer of the Gorgon, runaway from marriage, mother of many-blessed arts.
Urger, to friends evils, but to the good, wisdom.
Male and female you were born, war-defender, counsel.
Varied-formed, dragon-like, divinity-loving, bright-honored.
Destroyer of the Phlegraean <note>referring to the site of the war against the Giants</note> giants, rider of horses.
Tritogeneia <note>an epithet of Athena of uncertain origin</note>, releaser of evils, victory-bringing spirit.
Days and nights always in the final seasons,
hear me praying, and give peace rich in blessings.
And plenty, and health, in prosperous seasons.
Grey-eyed, discoverer of arts, highly-prayed-to queen.

->Incense for Victory: manna.<-

Come, blessed, good Victory, desired by mortals.
You who alone release the competitive urge of mortals,
and painful sedition, in battles against opponents.
Judging in wars upon victory-bearing works.
To whomsoever you urge on, you bring the sweetest glory.
For you rule all, and all the noble fame of strife.
Victory lies upon glorious things, swelling with feasts.
But, blessed one, come with a desired, bright eye.
Always leading noble fame upon glorious works.

->Incense for Apollo: manna.<-

Come, blessed Paean, Tityus-slayer, Phoebus, Lycoreus.

# GALEN ON THE AFFECTED PARTS, BOOK 1

<margin>Edition of Chartier, Volume 7, page 400.</margin>
<margin>Edition of Basel, Volume 3, page 259.</margin>

...ronment happens often. For the vapors rising from the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: γαστρὸς / ventriculo; in Galenic medicine, the stomach was considered a source of vapors that could ascend to the brain and affect the nervous system.</note> certainly alter them. However, not everyone perceives such a small change. It is only noticed by those who possess a <term>precise sensory power</term> <note>original: αἰσθητικὴν δύναμιν ἀκριβῆ / exquisitam sensificam facultatem; the functional capacity of the nerves to detect and transmit sensory information.</note>. # ISAAC CASAUBON’S COMMENTARY AND CASTIGATIONS ON BOOK 15 OF STRABO’S GEOGRAPHY.

<meta>A small decorative woodcut initial 'A' marks the beginning of the commentary on Book 15.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>the regions of Asia outside the Taurus</margin> Since the Geographer had divided Asia into that which is on this side of the Taurus and that which is across the Taurus, it seemed best to him to begin from that which is called <margin>within the Taurus</margin> <note>original: "entos Taurou"</note>. He has explained this to us in the three previous books. The other part, which is called <margin>outside the Taurus</margin> <note>original: "ektos Taurou"</note>, has remained untouched until now, if you except a very few things which he included in the previous book concerning Cilicia, Pamphylia, and Lycia. These regions are so intertwined with the roots of the Taurus mountains that they can be said to be situated in the mountains themselves rather than strictly <margin>outside</margin> or <margin>inside</margin> the Taurus. Now, therefore, Strabo approaches the description of the regions that are across the Taurus. To these he will add the remaining part of Asia in which Syria and Egypt are located; finally, he will explain Africa in a few words. And to embrace the matter briefly, there remains to be discussed whatever lies <margin>toward the south</margin> <note>original: "pros notion"</note> of the Taurus mountain and our sea (which is in the same straight line with that mountain).
<margin>and many first by their voyage</margin> The first who opened India to the Greeks were the companions of Alexander in his Indian expedition. Those who followed them were the Greeks who attempted to snatch the East from the Macedonian kings, and even took away a part of it. Strabo says in the eleventh book that these people advanced much further than had been done by Alexander. Finally, many began to sail to India for the sake of conducting trade. And from all of these, it seemed possible to learn the truth of Indian affairs. Yet Strabo rightly complains now that this was not done. For Alexander's companions, and those who followed them, could only perceive the character and nature of the places in passing and on the run. The merchants who later sailed there, as Pliny says, measure the journey for the sake of profit, not for the sake of knowledge. There is the same complaint from Marinus in Ptolemy; in that passage, he says that merchants <margin>do not care to examine the truths, being always occupied with trade, and often even increasing accounts through boastfulness</margin>. Since these things are so, Strabo deservedly asks that the reader take it in good part if he finds anything in the following pages that seems less probable or even less true.
<margin>looking over the Greeks with the Bactrian</margin> See the notes to Book 1.
<margin>PAGE 473. as if an uneducated life</margin> who was one of those Greeks <margin>from-</margin>

For it seems it should be taken in this way in this place, as a direct antithesis; although the things that follow concerning the cities seem to refer to the Greeks. Therefore, this passage is not sound. A passage from Pliny pertains here: "The companions of Alexander the Great in that region of India which they had subdued wrote that there was no town smaller than five thousand, and of nine nations."

διεψεύσθημεν γὰρ ἄν, οἷον φέρε κρίναντες τὸ ἀναπνοῇ χρώμενον μόνον ζῶον εἶναι· ἢ πῶς ἂν τὸ ἀρχικὸν εἶεν αἱ ἔννοιαι; ἀναμνηστικῶς οὖν νοοῦμεν ἀπὸ μικρῶν αἰθυγμάτων, ἀπό τινων κατὰ μέρος ὑποπεσόντων ἀναμιμνησκόμενοι τῶν πάλαι ἐγνωσμένων, ὧν λήθην ἐλάβομεν ἐνσωματωθέντες. ἔτι δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ οὐ φθείρεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας κακίας, οὐδὲ ὑπὸ τῆς ἄλλου φθείροιτ’ ἄν, οὐδ’ ἁπλῶς ὑπ’ ἄλλου, οὕτω δὲ ἔχουσα ἄφθαρτον ἂν εἴη. τό γε μὴν αὐτοκίνητον ἀρχικῶς ἀεικίνητον, τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον ἀθάνατον· αὐτοκίνητον δὲ ἡ ψυχή, τὸ δὲ αὐτοκίνητον ἀρχὴ πάσης κινήσεως καὶ γενέσεως, ἀρχὴ δὲ ἀγέννητον καὶ ἀνώλεθρον· ὥστε ἥ τε τῶν ὅλων ψυχὴ τοιαύτη ἂν εἴη καὶ ἡ ἀνθρωπίνη, τοῦ αὐτοῦ γε κράματος ἀμφότεραι μεταλαβοῦσαι. αὐτοκίνητον δέ φησι τὴν ψυχήν, ὅτι σύμφυτον ἔχει τὴν ζωὴν ἀεὶ ἐνεργοῦσαν καθ’ αὑτήν. ὅτι μὲν οὖν αἱ λογικαὶ ψυχαὶ ἀθάνατοι ὑπάρχουσι κατὰ τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον, βεβαιώσαιτ’ ἄν τις· εἰ δὲ καὶ αἱ ἄλογοι, τοῦτο τῶν ἀμφισβητουμένων ὑπάρχει. πιθανὸν γὰρ τὰς ἀλόγους ψυχάς, ψιλῇ τε φαντασίᾳ ἐλαυνομένας καὶ οὔτε λογισμῷ οὔτε κρίσει χρωμένας, οὔτε θεωρήμασι καὶ τῇ τούτων συναγωγῇ οὔτε καθολικαῖς διαλήψεσι, παντελῶς δὲ ἀνεννοήτους οὔσας καὶ τῆς νοητῆς φύσεως, μήτε τῆς αὐτῆς οὐσίας εἶναι ταῖς λογικαῖς, θνητάς τε καὶ φθαρτὰς ὑπάρχειν. τῷ δὲ ἀθανάτους εἶναι τὰς ψυχὰς λόγῳ ἠκολούθησε τὸ εἰσκρίνεσθαι αὐτὰς τοῖς σώμασι, παρεμφυομένας ταῖς τῶν ἐμβρύων διαπλαστικαῖς φύσεσι, καὶ διαμείβειν πολλὰ σώματα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώπινα, ἢ ἀριθμοὺς μενούσας ἢ βουλήσει θεῶν ἢ δι’ ἀκολασίαν ἢ διὰ φιλοσωματίαν· ἔχει δέ πως οἰκειότητα πρὸς ἄλληλα σῶμα καὶ ψυχή, ὡς πῦρ καὶ ἄσφαλτος. καὶ ἡ θεῶν δὲ ψυχὴ κέκτηται καὶ αὐτὴ τό τε κριτικόν, ὃ καὶ γνωστικὸν ἂν καλοῖτο, καὶ μὴν τὸ ὁρμητικόν τε, ὃ καὶ παραστατικὸν ἄν τις ὀνομάσειε, καὶ τὸ οἰκειωτικόν· αἵτινες δυνάμεις οὖσαι καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἀνθρωπίναις ψυχαῖς μετὰ τὸ ἐνσωματωθῆναι οἷον μεταβολὴν λαμβάνουσιν, ἡ μὲν οἰκειωτική εἰς τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν, ἡ δὲ ὁρμητικὴ εἰς τὸ θυμοειδές.

<header>ALCINOUS 34</header>

...would be immortal. We might be led to the conclusion that learning is recollection in this way: for learning could not exist otherwise than by the recollection of things known long ago. For if we conceived of generalities from particulars, how could we traverse particulars when they are infinite, or how could we do so from a few? For we would be deceived, as if we judged that only an animal using respiration is a living thing. Or how could the concepts be the governing principles? We think, then, through recollection from small sparks, remembering from certain particulars that fall under our notice things known long ago, of which we suffered forgetfulness when we were embodied. Furthermore, the soul is not destroyed by its own vice, nor would it be destroyed by the vice of another, nor simply by anything else; having this nature, it would be incorruptible. Moreover, that which is primarily self-moving is always in motion, and such a thing is immortal. The soul is self-moving, and the self-moving is the principle of all motion and generation; a principle is ungenerated and imperishable. So both the soul of the universe would be of this kind and the human soul, both sharing in the same mixture. He says the soul is self-moving because it has life naturally inherent, always acting by itself.

That the rational souls are immortal according to this man <note>referring to Plato</note> one might confirm; but whether the irrational souls are also immortal is among the things disputed. For it is persuasive that the irrational souls, driven by bare imagination and using neither reason nor judgment, nor contemplations and their collection, nor universal perceptions, and being entirely without thought of the intelligible nature, are not of the same essence as the rational souls, and are mortal and corruptible. Following the argument that souls are immortal is the idea that they are inserted into bodies, being implanted in the formative natures of embryos, and that they exchange many bodies, both human and non-human, either waiting for certain numbers of years or by the will of the gods, or because of licentiousness, or through a love for the body. Body and soul have a certain kinship to each other, like fire and asphalt. Even the soul of the gods possesses both the critical power, which might also be called cognitive, and the impulsive power, which one might name representational, and the power of appropriation. These powers, which are also in human souls, undergo a kind of change after being embodied: the power of appropriation becomes the appetitive part, and the impulsive power becomes the spirited part.

## ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΧΟΡΙΑΜΒΙΚΟΥ ΜΕΤΡΟΥ.

ΤΟ χοριαμβικὸν συντίθεται μὲν καὶ καθαρόν, συντίθεται δὲ καὶ ἐπίμικτον πρὸς τὰς ἰαμβικάς· ὡς ἐπίπαν δὲ ὅτε καταληκτικόν ἐστιν εἰς τὴν ἰαμβικὴν κατακλεῖδα παράγεται, τοῦτ' ἔστιν εἰς ἀμφίβραχυν, ἢ βακχεῖον διὰ τὴν ἀδιάφορον. παράγεται μὲν γὰρ καὶ εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν, τὸν δάκτυλον, ἢ κρητικόν, οἷον, δίμετρον μὲν ὅ,

"And of those answering in turn," <note>original: "Τῶν δ' ἀπαμειβομένων"</note> a <term>trochee</term> <gloss>a foot of a long and short syllable</gloss>, and a remaining <term>iamb</term> <gloss>a foot of a short and long syllable</gloss>, and <term>anapaests</term> <gloss>feet of two shorts and a long</gloss>,

-> ˘ ˘ - ˘ ˘ - ˘ ˘ - <-
"swift-footed Achilles addressed him." <note>original: "προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς"</note> It contains an iamb. He says this because the words <term>ereo</term> <gloss>I will say</gloss> and <term>phileein</term> <gloss>to love</gloss> become iambs through <term>synizesis</term> <gloss>the merging of two vowel sounds into one</gloss> when they become <term>ero</term> and <term>philein</term>. This is, as it seems, an Ionic division; for this reason, he used the example of the anapaest at the beginning purely in these cases alone. "It might fall under" <note>original: "Ὑποσέλλοιτο αὖ"</note>: instead of "it might fall into," because when the long syllable of the anapaest is resolved, the <term>proceleusmatic</term> <gloss>a foot of four short syllables</gloss> is formed. "Into the proceleusmatic": for from the first two proceleusmatics one anapaestic <term>syzygy</term> <gloss>a pair of feet</gloss> is formed, and from the following proceleusmatic and the final foot being an anapaest, the second syzygy is formed. Thus it becomes an <term>acatalectic dimeter</term> <gloss>a line of two measures with a complete ending</gloss> measured by <term>dipody</term> <gloss>pairs of feet</gloss>, provided it has four complete anapaests. It is reasonable that he placed an anapaest ending among the proceleusmatics, because while a resolved <term>ion</term> <gloss>Ionic foot</gloss> is perhaps a <term>dactyl</term> <gloss>a long and two shorts</gloss>, or at least equal in time, the anapaest is not. "Having a <term>bacchius</term> <gloss>a foot of a short and two longs</gloss>": it will therefore be found with a complete <term>amphibrach</term> <gloss>short-long-short</gloss> and one syllable, so that it is <term>catalectic</term> <gloss>shortened at the end</gloss> into a disyllable. Since the anapaest delights in the iamb, as it begins from a short syllable, just as the dactyl delights in the trochee because of the long syllable.

---

## ON CHORIAMBIC METER.

The <term>choriambic</term> <gloss>a foot of a long, two shorts, and a long</gloss> is composed both in a pure form and mixed with iambic measures. Generally, when it is catalectic, it is brought to an iambic closing, that is, into an <term>amphibrach</term> or a <term>bacchius</term> due to the <term>indifferent syllable</term> <gloss>the final syllable which can be long or short</gloss>. For it is also brought to its own closing, the dactyl or the <term>cretic</term> <gloss>long-short-long</gloss>, such as this dimeter:

> ⁝ Equal-spirited | youths. <note>original: "Ἰσοπνόοι μείρακες"</note> And a trimeter, such as:
> ⁝ Neither the lions' | strength nor | their rearing. <note>original: "Οὐδὲ λεόντων σθένος οὐδὲ τροφαί"</note> And a tetrameter:
> ⁝ You who breathe | upon the | works of white- | armed Cytherea. <note>original: "Αἳ κυθερείας ἐπιπνεῖτ' ἔργια λευκωλένου"</note>

But such forms are more continuous and less distinct. Those ending in an amphibrach or bacchius include dimeters from the *Aeolosicon* of Aristophanes:

> ⁝ Not in vain, O | women <note>original: "Οὐκ ἔτος ὦ γυναῖκες"</note>

<summary>This page discusses the resolution of anapaestic feet into proceleusmatics and introduces the rules of choriambic meter, including its pure and mixed forms.</summary>
<keywords>anapaest, proceleusmatic, synizesis, choriambic meter, Aristophanes, Aeolosicon, dimeter, trimeter, tetrameter</keywords>

desires, a steady contemplation knows how to refer every choice and avoidance to the health of the body and the tranquility <term>ataraxia</term> <gloss>freedom from disturbance</gloss> of the soul, since this is the goal of a blessed life. For we do everything for the sake of this: so that we may feel no pain and no fear. Once this state is achieved for us, every storm of the soul is dissolved, as the living being has no need to wander as if seeking something missing, or to search for something else by which the good of the soul and the body would be completed. For we have need of pleasure only when we feel pain because pleasure is absent. When we do not feel pain, we no longer need pleasure. Because of this, we say that pleasure is the beginning and the end of a blessed life. For we recognize this as the first and innate good, and from this we begin every choice and avoidance. We return to this, using the feeling of pleasure as a rule to judge every good thing. And since this is the first and natural good, we do not choose every pleasure. Instead, there are times when we pass over many pleasures when a greater difficulty follows from them. We also consider many pains to be better than pleasures when a greater pleasure follows for us after we have endured the pains for a long time. Every pleasure, therefore, because it has a nature that is familiar to us, is a good thing, yet not every pleasure is to be chosen. In the same way, every pain is an evil, yet not

# GALEN TO PISO
## ON THE BOOK OF THERIAC

<margin>Ed. Chart. XIII. [943.]</margin>
<margin>Ed. Bas. II. (462.)</margin>

### Chapter 10
#### [How harmful things can sometimes be beneficial; and how a single quality arises from many in compound medicines.]

It is more necessary to investigate through reason that which seems worthy of wonder to many people. For how is it that those very wild animals, being enemies to our bodies and killing humans so quickly, are in turn able to help those who have been bitten by them? How can they alone preserve a person from such an evil? There is an ancient saying <note>original: "archaios logos" (ἀρχαῖος λόγος)</note> that certain animals kill the person they bite when they come into contact with the human blood discharged from the wound. Yet, if they have not tasted the blood, but are instead eaten in this state, they are naturally suited to save those who have been bitten. 

This is just like what is recorded about the plant called *helenium* <note>original: "elenion" (ἑλένιον), often identified as elecampane, though here used as a term for a toxic plant</note> by the Greeks, but called *nikos* <note>original: "nikou" (νίκου)</note> or *ninos* <note>original: "ninou" (νίνου)</note> by the local inhabitants. They say that the Dacians and the Dalmatians smear this substance on the tips of their arrows. In this way, when it comes into contact with the blood of those who are wounded, it has the power to kill. However, if it is eaten by them, it is harmless, and 

<summary>Galen discusses why venomous animals and toxic plants like helenium can be lethal when they enter the bloodstream through a bite or wound but medicinal or harmless when ingested.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s Letter 44 to John. Synesius is weighing the gravity of the accusations against John regarding the death of Aemilius, using the classical personification of "Rumor" to explore the relationship between public reputation and private guilt.</meta>

# EPISTLES

...acting as my strength daily allowed. So now, regarding the circumstances that have befallen you, it pleases me to offer some counsel, since I cannot offer a practical remedy. For it is not right for Synesius, as long as he breathes and has the power, not to be ready in every way to serve his friends. Listen, then, to what is honorable for me to discuss with you.

If Rumor <note>original: "fama"; the Latin translation of the Greek "Pheme," the personification of gossip and public report.</note> is a Goddess, as one of our poets <margin>Hesiod, Book 2, at the end <note>A reference to the final lines of Hesiod's *Works and Days*, where he warns that Rumor is a "mischievous deity" who is easy to raise but hard to bear.</note></margin> suggests, then you have killed the late Aemilius—not by a deed committed with your own hand, but by a murder you planned and deliberated. You have composed a "barbaric tragedy" <note>A rhetorical metaphor comparing the orchestrated assassination to a staged, cruel play.</note> of assassins, sending the most savage of your own subordinates to strike. Rumor tells these things, and for her to lie would be a sin, since she is a Goddess.

But if Hesiod is indeed talking nonsense, and many things are reported falsely—and if this story about you is just one of many such falsehoods—then that is what I would hope to be true. For I value a loss of money far less than the loss of a friend. And if you are now being spoken of poorly without being a party to the crime, you are certainly unfortunate, but you are not a wicked man.

<summary>Synesius addresses the rumor that his friend John orchestrated the murder of Aemilius using a soldier, weighing the poetic idea of "Rumor" as an infallible goddess against the possibility that John is an innocent victim of slander.</summary>

<keywords>Synesius of Cyrene, John, Aemilius, Rumor, Hesiod, friendship, murder accusation, ethics, slander</keywords>

pages.translation:
When you find Admetus <note>a King of the Molossians</note> saving his enemy and remaining so far from doing harm to Themistocles that he even assisted him in reaching his destination as quickly as possible—even though it was clear that helping him would grieve those demanding his surrender, who were the greatest of the Greek cities—nevertheless, he respected the supplication of his enemy more than he feared the danger. Do you then consider the King of the Molossians to be senseless because of his philanthropy, or do you regard him as admirable for his magnanimity? Do you think he should be considered more blessed for this quality than for his actual rule? 4. Now I ask you to imitate what you admire: either set aside your anger toward this man for the sake of your friends, or, by maintaining it, cause your friends distress. 5. Lucianus did wrong: he says so himself, so there is no need for an accuser. For why would anyone need to prove the guilt of one who confesses? This is the right time for pardon, when the one under accusation does not deny it but instead consumes himself with regret, and when those who wish for your good reputation join us in our petition. It would be reasonable for you not to dishonor us and not to seek a penalty from this man greater than the conviction he already feels within himself: namely, that he owes the ultimate penalty. 6. It would have been very easy for me to extend the length of this letter, but I feared it might not seem to be the proper length for a letter from one friend to another.

<margin>
Textual variants regarding the name of the Molossians and the Greek word for "magnanimity."

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the fable of the Ringdove (here identified as a "partridge" due to a variation in the Greek manuscript or OCR error) and the Mouse from the "Stephanites and Ichnelates." The Mouse has just finished gnawing the net to free the birds, and the Crow, observing this act of loyalty, now seeks to befriend the Mouse.</meta>

### Page 71

"If indeed the partridge <note>original: πέρδιξ. While the standard version of this fable features a Ringdove, this manuscript uses the word for partridge.</note> is a lure, I have reached a point where I can do no more; I have given up. I shall leave these things. For if I am to release you, I would be left behind until I have loosed your bonds." The mouse said: "These are the words: I desire more for you and your kin than what you desire for yourself." Having said these things, he loosed every one of the bonds. Once loosed, the partridge departed. When the **crow** saw what had been done, he was struck <gloss>with amazement</gloss> by the mouse’s extraordinary management and way of life. Coming forward, he said to him, "O dearest one!" But the mouse said to him, "Who are you?" "I am the crow. Having seen your disposition toward your friends, I wished to establish a friendship with you; and for this reason I have approached." But the mouse said: "What common ground could there be for me and you? For it is necessary for the mouse to [live on] the earth, but for you to travel the air <note>The mouse is highlighting the natural enmity or "otherness" between a ground-dweller and a bird of prey.</note>. When I frequent such places, it is like oil upon water, or <unclear>piamas</unclear>—and like a ship on dry land. How can I be a friend to you, when my nature is [your prey]?" But the crow said: "Let us discern the truth and do what is fitting. For nothing is more important to me than to be sustained by you. How much more beneficial it is for us to live our lives together, that we might benefit one another! I will not allow you to send me away from the fulfillment of my hope, for I have seen your goodwill toward your friends. If you accept these things from me—for the honor of a virtuous man is like the image of musk <note>original: μόσχου. While this can mean "calf," in Byzantine Greek it often refers to musk, the perfume. The metaphor describes a virtue so potent it cannot be hidden.</note>, which does not merely adorn, but spreads its scent and becomes manifest to all." The mouse spoke, still regarding him as an enemy: "<unclear>Dingga</unclear>! O you who shines like a lion or an elephant! But the flight and the pursuit <gloss>between us</gloss> is like that of the mouse and the weasel,"

<column-break/>

"and sharp to enemies. For how can water, even if heated by fire, not eventually lose its [borrowed] nature? For when it is poured out, it extinguishes the very fire <gloss>that heated it</gloss>." The crow said: "You speak [rightly]; but my friendship toward you will not be like a ceramic vessel. Rather, it is like a vessel of gold, which is difficult to break and easy to repair. For a clay vessel is easily shattered and therefore beyond repair; but the greatness of my friendship is difficult to change. The friendship of the <unclear>pure</unclear> is easily broken and hard to heal." The mouse said: "I accept then this friendship; never have I honored a mouse <gloss>as a friend</gloss> nor have you sent me away. But let us make these words into a defense <gloss>of our bond</gloss>. Let me make a [promise] to all mice. For if ever the time comes that I should keep these daily agreements, when you have me [with you]... <unclear>tommia</unclear>... you have lured me." Then he peeked out from his own hole. The crow said: "Why do you not come out further toward me?" and he said, "I am still [wary] of a crow. Those who live their lives in error... <unclear>terpois</unclear> with one another as friends. For I think [of friends] in terms of the soul; but some are friends only for utility and not for the soul itself. For they embrace the 'friendship' but not the soul itself. Those who are friends for utility, how could they... <unclear>komper</unclear>... establish our friendship? You seem to be throwing yourself into this boldly; those who [pursue] the bait... for such ones are not friends of mine, but are merely providing for their own advantage. I, for my part, have become a friend to you for no other reason than yourself. But nothing prevents me from coming out to you; it is only that I fear your kin..." <note>The text ends mid-sentence with a catchword.</note>

<summary>The Crow, impressed by the Mouse's loyalty in freeing the trapped birds, attempts to negotiate a friendship. Despite the Mouse's initial skepticism and warnings about natural enmities, the two discuss the nature of true friendship versus friendship based on utility.</summary>
<keywords>Stephanites and Ichnelates, fables, friendship, metaphors, gold vs clay, Michael Psellos, Byzantine literature</keywords>

pages.translation:
"Practicing and repeatedly practicing." If one can from time to time think and reflect, and eventually everything is harmonized within, then there is joy. This saying appears in the <term>Analects</term>. Scholars, regarding the matters they learn, should from time to time think and reflect so that they do not deviate from the path. When one extends goodness to others, and people believe and follow the principles, one is harmonized within and naturally joyful. When one extends goodness to others and the believers are many, those who return to the goodness are many; therefore, one can be happy. The meaning of "goodness is within oneself, sufficient to extend to others, and those who believe..." is like this. Even if one is happy, if others do not see it, and one is not worried, this is what is called a superior person. The superior person is a name for one who has completed their virtue. Even if one is happy to extend goodness to others, if people do not yet believe, one is still at peace with one's own position. The scholars of antiquity learned for their own sake, wanting to attain it within themselves. The scholars of today learn for the sake of others, wanting it to be seen by others. This saying appears in the <term>Analects</term>. Learning for the sake of others is like seeking satiety when eating or warmth when wearing clothes; if it is not for others, the satiety is within oneself; it is not for the sake of others. Those who learn for the sake of others only seek external beauty; if it is not for others, it is within oneself. What one should be diligent about is to truly attain learning and goodness. The key lies in oneself. If one seeks practical application, then learning will penetrate the heart; how much more so if one’s intention is to seek external things, deceiving oneself while hoping for goodness.

<summary>This page explores the joy of learning, the distinction between learning for oneself versus for the sake of reputation, and the importance of internalizing virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Analects, Joy, Learning, Superior Person, Self-reflection, Virtue</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Continues the entry for Lei Gong Teng (Thunder-god Vine) from the previous page.</meta>

It sprouts at the foot of northern-facing mountains around the <term>Lixia</term> <gloss>Start of Summer</gloss> solar term. It grows as a single stem with creeping vines; the stem pierces the center of the leaves. Leaves grow from the upper stem. The leaves are round at the bottom and pointed at the top, resembling a plow or rake. They also resemble <term>Sanjiao Feng</term> <gloss>Three-cornered Wind</gloss>. The branches have thorns. 

According to the <term>Wuli Xiaoshi</term> <gloss>Small Records of Natural Principles</gloss>, it is called <term>Liutou Citeng</term> <gloss>Plow-head Thorn Vine</gloss>. Its leaves are triangular like a plow head and it often grows along fences. It can treat <term>luoli</term> <gloss>scrofula/neck lumps</gloss> and can also intercept malaria. Its other names are: <term>Pili Mu</term> <gloss>Thunderbolt Wood</gloss>, <term>Fang Sheng Ban</term>, <term>Dao Jin Gou</term> <gloss>Inverted Golden Hook</gloss>, <term>Laotie Cao</term> <gloss>Branding Iron Herb</gloss>, <term>Daogua Zijin Gou</term> <gloss>Hanging Inverted Purple-Gold Hook</gloss>, <term>He Bai Cao</term>, <term>Li Jian Cao</term> <gloss>Plow-tip Herb</gloss>, <term>Kua Pa Cao</term> <gloss>Rake Herb</gloss>, <term>Long Xian Cao</term> <gloss>Dragon Immortal Herb</gloss>, <term>Yuwei Hua</term> <gloss>Fish-tail Flower</gloss>, and <term>San Mu Mian</term> <gloss>Three Cotton</gloss>. Those produced in Jiangxi are the most potent. Locals gather it to poison fish; clams and snails of the same type also die. Its nature is extremely intense. If the smoke from this herb is used to fumigate silkworm eggs, they will not hatch; sericulture families avoid it. Mountain dwellers gather it to fumigate wall lice. It treats <term>guzhang</term> <gloss>tympanites/abdominal bloating</gloss>, edema, <term>juji</term> <gloss>abdominal masses/accumulations</gloss>, jaundice, malaria that has persisted for a long time, <term>yu kou</term> <gloss>carbuncles near the mouth</gloss>, <term>biandu</term> <gloss>venereal sores/buboes</gloss>, scrofula, and falls or injuries. It eliminates wall lice, and the stems can be burned under the bed to ward off all kinds of poisonous snake bites; it is a remedy for ten thousand ailments.

The master, because he offered sacrifices to the Arhats, a monk asked, "Danxia burned the wooden Buddha; why do you, Master, offer sacrifices to the Arhats?" The master said, "Burning them does not touch them; offering sacrifices is also fine." The monk said, "Have the Arhats come?" The master said, "Do you eat your rice every day?" The monk was silent. The master said, "Few are clever."

Chan Master Xingkong of Xiaoyi Temple in Jizhou extended his hands to show the monk. The monk went forward and then stepped back. The master said, "With both parents dead, you do not show sorrow." The monk laughed loudly. The master said, "I will ask you about the matter shortly." The monk turned a somersault and left. The master said, "Heavens, heavens!" After the monk finished paying his respects, the master said, "If you go on like this, is there any truth of the Buddha-dharma left?" He replied, "I am tongue-tied."

<header>Journey to the West</header>

The lyre-hall's fragrant wolves act as clerks. Lions, elephants, <term>naoseng</term> <gloss>macaque-like</gloss> kings, tigers, and leopards all act as guards. Wild boars carry the luggage. Water monsters move to the front. After encountering a many-year-old stone, it harbors anger there. You ask that acquaintance, he knows the road to the West.

Hearing these words, the Pilgrim <note>Sun Wukong</note> sneered and said, "We are going; there is no need to ask him. Just ask me." Tripitaka still did not understand the intent. The Zen Master transformed into a golden light and headed straight to the bird's nest. The Elder bowed to thank him. The Pilgrim was furious in his heart and raised his iron staff,搗 <note>pounding or smashing</note> upwards wildly. He only saw ten thousand lotus flowers bloom and a thousand layers of auspicious mist protecting it. Even with the strength to churn the seas and topple rivers, the Pilgrim could not hope to grab even a single strand of the bird's nest. When Tripitaka saw this, he pulled on the Pilgrim and said, "Wukong, this is a Bodhisattva. Why are you smashing his nest?" The Pilgrim replied, "He scolded my brother and me for a while before leaving." Tripitaka said, "He was explaining the path to the Western Heaven; how did he scold you?" The Pilgrim said, "You do not understand. He spoke of a wild boar carrying the luggage."

<summary>Sun Wukong reacts with anger to the Zen Master's warnings and perceived insults, leading to a confrontation that highlights the difference in understanding between the master and his disciple.</summary>

The <term>Yangsheng Fang</term> <gloss>Prescriptions for Nourishing Life</gloss> states: Click the teeth together morning and evening, and the teeth will not decay.
It also states: After eating, one must rinse the mouth several times; otherwise, it will cause the person to suffer from tooth decay.

->Tooth Decay Condition<-

"Tooth decay" is when insects eat the teeth until they break, with pus and rot, and fluids that smell like the decay of a gathered pile. Thus it is called "tooth decay."

->Exposed Tooth Condition<-

The branch meridians of the Hand Yangming enter the teeth. If wind-cold in the head and face is transmitted into these meridians, it causes the teeth to break, and the interstitial fluids transform into pus and fluids. Because the blood and qi are deficient and exhausted, they cannot nourish the teeth, so the tooth roots are exposed.

### Flower Hairpin
> According to the *Verified Prescriptions* of Yang Chunya, to treat the onset of breast abscesses: Take a woman's flower hairpin and face it toward the sun. Trace a circle in the air and silently recite: "In the sky, a patch of black clouds; on the earth, a woman suffers breast pain. I now specifically bestow this golden hairpin; once the golden hairpin dissolves, the pain will never return." Perform this seven times, then hand the hairpin to the woman to draw a circle around the affected area, and it will heal.

They attacked him, even though Sim Ui-gyeom, despite being a royal relative, had previously contributed to forcing out treacherous ministers and supporting the scholar class. The older and higher-ranking officials protected Sim Ui-gyeom. Thus, a rift grew between the senior and junior generations, moving from a subtle disagreement to a prominent one. 

In the years of <term>Gyemi</term> <gloss>1583</gloss> and <term>Gapsin</term> <gloss>1584</gloss>, the names "East" and "West" were first divided. Because Kim Hyo-won's house was in the eastern part of the city, his followers were called <term>Dongin</term> <gloss>Easterners</gloss>. Because Sim Ui-gyeom's house was in the west, his followers were called <term>Seoin</term> <gloss>Westerners</gloss>. The Easterners promoted Kim Hyo-won, Yu Seong-ryong, Kim U-ong, Yi San-hae, Jeong Ji-yeon, Jeong Yu-gil, Heo Bong, and Yi Bal. The Westerners promoted Sim Ui-gyeom, Park Sun, Jeong Cheol, Yun Du-su, Yun Geun-su, and Ki Sa-maeng. This was the beginning of the <term>Pungdang</term> <gloss>factions</gloss>. 

Before this, when Prime Minister Yi Jun-gyeong was dying, his final memorial to the King stated that a gradual trend of factionalism would appear among the officials. Yi I <note>The famous scholar Yulgok</note>, who was then in the <term>Okdang</term> <gloss>Office of Special Advisors</gloss>, submitted a petition criticizing this. He considered it an attempt to drive a wedge between the King and his ministers. He even went so far as to insult him, saying that when a man is about to die, his words are usually good, but when Jun-gyeong was about to die, his words were evil. By this time, Yi I feared that the words would prove true. He put all his effort into mediating and resolving the conflict between the two sides. However, the nation had suffered through many literati purges, all caused by royal relatives. The scholars had accumulated resentment toward royal relatives, and Sim Ui-gyeom happened to be caught in that trap. 

Just as the public anger was rising, Queen Ingun, the Great Dowager, passed away. King Seonjo had succeeded to the throne as a member of a branch of the royal family. Sim Ui-gyeom then firmly cut off his support from within the palace. However, the Easterners held onto an empty reputation...

<summary>This page details the formal split of the Joseon court into the Eastern and Western factions based on the residences of Kim Hyo-won and Sim Ui-gyeom. It also mentions Yi I's initial dismissal and later desperate mediation of the growing divide.</summary>
<keywords>Dongin, Seoin, Easterners, Westerners, Yi I, Yulgok, Yi Jun-gyeong, factionalism, royal relatives, King Seonjo</keywords>

## 9. No Eating at Improper Times

From the appearance of the morning light until high noon is called "the time." From when the sun begins to tilt until the morning light appears the next day is called "the improper time." Eating during the improper time is called breaking the fast. A sin is incurred for every swallow. However, drinking "improper time liquids," "dissolvable-in-the-mouth medicines," or "lifelong medicines" is not a violation. 

"Improper time liquids" refer to fruit juices, honey water, etc., which are clear and free of dregs. "Dissolvable-in-the-mouth medicines" refer to honey sugar, rock sugar, or clarified butter, which also have no dregs. "Lifelong medicines" refer to ginger, cinnamon, pepper, plum, and all pill medicines,

# Diagram of the Palace House Five-Frame Structure / Diagram of the Mansion House Five-Frame Structure

<note>Two architectural floor plans and structural diagrams. The right diagram illustrates a "Palace House" with a central hall, side rooms, and a complex roof frame. The left diagram illustrates a "Mansion House" with a similar five-bay layout, specifying areas for the shrine and the porch. Lines indicate the internal support structures and roof pitch.</note>

...can be seen, but I suspect a word was omitted under the "porch" <note>original: <term>seo</term></note>. To its front is the eastern face, and behind it is the western side chamber. This is the layout of the ground. The ridgepole covers the three middle bays. According to the indicated points, from the west reaching to the top of the western porch, the cover connects to this ridgepole above and meets the lower "thunder ridge" <note>original: <term>noe-gyeok</term></note>. This is the system for the upper bays, called the "four-sloped roof" <note>original: <term>sa-a</term></note>. The ridgepole is a horizontal beam. The front and back of the ridgepole form the north and south ridges. To the sides of these, which are the exterior, are the eastern and western lower beams. These four lower beams each connect to their respective directions and descend. The four edges depict the covering of the hall. The parts that extend beyond the steps are called the verandas <note>original: <term>mu</term></note>. The text below says the veranda corresponds to the system for the lower half of this house.
The Mansion-style house represents the system for the lower half. In a Mansion-style house, there are five bays in the front and four in the back, with no western room. Outside the three bays of the central hall, the back is divided into two bays each. The five eastern bays all use horizontal ridgepoles like the Palace-style system. However, the hanging eaves that block the wind are called "wind-blockers" <note>original: <term>byeok-pung</term></note>. Below the wind-blockers, there are also two verandas.

<column-break/>

# Doubts

The north and south are connected only to cover the side steps. Looking at the verandas, they do not extend beyond the wind-blocker boards. According to the commentary on the *Book of Etiquette and Ceremonials* by Master Zheng, the Mansion-style house has slopes that connect down to form verandas. Because the roof of such a house has many eaves, the eaves all receive the name "veranda." "Thunder" <note>original: <term>noe</term></note> is a name for the same roof; the southern eaves are also called "thunder." Since it is the same as the Palace-style house, the northern eaves are also called "thunder." The two verandas under the ridgepole are "waist eaves" <note>original: <term>yo-cheom</term></note> and are not connected. Some also do not extend beyond the wind-blocker. Or they are called "wings" <note>original: <term>ik</term></note> and are not called by the name "thunder." "Wings" is the name for the waist eaves, so simply calling it "wind" <note>original: <term>pung</term></note> is an error.

Reviewing the system of the rear chamber <note>original: <term>hu-chim</term></note>, if one makes left and right rooms, the two-bay system is clear. However, now that it is made with an eastern room and a western chamber, I suspect it should also be two bays. The shrine system is the same. I have now added dots where the pillars stand, but I do not know if this is correct. Furthermore, the term "two pillars" <note>original: <term>ryang-yeong</term></note>...

# Gathering and Storage
<note>original: "収貯" (shū zhù). Gathering and storing the harvest.</note>

<note>Below the title are two red square seals, likely identifying the artist or the collection.</note>

<vocab>Gathering and Storage, agriculture, traditional labor, water buffalo</vocab>

<margin>
Reaping Grain
<note>original: "刈禾" (yì hé). Followed by two red artist seals.</note>
</margin>

-># Reaping the Grain<-

This intricate scene is a quintessential example of the <term>Pictures of Tilling and Weaving<gloss>the *Gengzhi Tu*, a genre of didactic art used by Chinese emperors to emphasize the importance of agriculture and sericulture</gloss></term>. Having nurtured the rice through the seasons of planting and weeding, the focus now shifts to the frantic and rewarding labor of the harvest. 

In the upper left of the composition, groups of farmers are bent low over the golden stalks, using hand sickles to cut the rice at the base. Their rhythmic labor is the foundation of the empire's food security.

<column-break/>

The logistics of the harvest are illustrated with great detail:

*   **Manual Transport:** In the lower left, laborers utilize shoulder poles to carry heavy, balanced bundles of harvested grain. This method was essential for navigating the narrow paths between paddies where carts could not reach.
*   **The Buffalo Cart:** On the right side of the spread, the scale of the operation increases. A large wooden cart, laden with the bounty of the fields, is being prepared for transport. 
*   **Draft Animals:** The scene highlights the vital role of the <term>water buffalo<gloss>the primary draft animal in southern Chinese rice cultivation, prized for its strength in muddy terrain</gloss></term>, shown here pulling the heavy cart across the landscape.

The backdrop of soft hills and a small wooden bridge crossing a quiet stream serves as a reminder of the natural environment that sustains these agricultural efforts. The scene captures the transition from "Reaping" (cutting the grain) to the broader category of "Gathering and Storage," where the fruits of a year's labor are finally secured.

<summary>This page illustrates the crucial harvest stage of the agricultural cycle, depicting the manual reaping of rice and its transport via shoulder poles and buffalo-drawn carts. It highlights the transition from field labor to the systematic collection and storage of the empire's food supply.</summary>

<keywords>agriculture, rice harvest, water buffalo, Gengzhi Tu, manual labor, transport, food security, gathering and storage</keywords>

# [Illustration of the Jade Chariot]
<note>This page consists of a detailed woodcut illustration with no accompanying text. It is the left half of a double-page spread depicting the Emperor’s ceremonial transport.</note>

->**Visual Description**<-

The woodcut displays the side and rear profile of the **Jade Chariot** <note>original: *yulu* (玉輅)</note>. As the most prestigious of the five imperial carriages, every element shown here serves as a symbol of state authority:

*   **The Wheel:** A large, heavy wheel is depicted with intricate carvings on its spokes and rim, designed to support the massive weight of the ritual carriage.
*   **The Canopy:** The upper portion of the carriage features a highly decorated canopy. It is embellished with **floral and geometric patterns**, reflecting the sophisticated textile and woodworking crafts of the period.
*   **Drapery:** Ornate silken draperies hang from the roof of the carriage, shielding the interior and adding to the visual spectacle of the imperial procession.

<note>The right side of this illustration is missing from this specific folio; in the original complete work, the right-hand page would have shown the front of the vehicle and the mechanical "South-Pointing" figure standing atop the carriage head.</note>
