<meta>This page continues the discussion on astrological prognostications, shifting from the specific lunar periods (Vishti) discussed on page 15 to the broader influences of the Sun’s transit (Sankranti) into different signs, and the specific effects based on the day of the week the transit occurs.</meta>

# 16
## Br. Da. Ga.

...favor. Through wakefulness, the "Boar" <note>original: "kola," likely referring to a specific astrological posture or omen</note>, and the dwelling of sleep, the astrological periods of **Bava** and **Balava** <note>two of the eleven "Karanas" or half-lunar days used in Vedic astrology to determine the auspiciousness of an action</note> are established. These bring about the loss of wealth for those who are joined with them, yet for others, they create stability and fearlessness <unclear>....</unclear> otherwise, they bring disease and suffering to the common people. 

The growth of all things, including abundant grain and rice, will be seen, leading to festivals for the king. Even in this time, rain will fall according to the season, and the laws of the kingdom will remain firm. In this particular year, a **favorable transit** <term>Sankranti</term> <note>the moment the Sun moves from one zodiac sign to another</note> shall arise. However, if the transit is unfavorable, there will be an increase in enemies, conflicts within one's own home, and a "disease of duels" <note>likely referring to civil unrest or social strife</note>. There will be a loss of prosperity in the world.

### The Seated Transit

When the transit is "seated" <note>an astrological classification based on the specific time of day the transit occurs</note>, the world will be swarmed by **thieves and insects**, and there will be great winds and **earthquakes**. One may see deformed births and an absence of medicine. The kings will have "frowning brows" <note>an expression of anger or worry</note> and fickle minds; there will be great fear among them. This transit brings the affliction of dust and the constant threat of thieves. 

### Sun in the Signs of the Fish and the Ram

The hardships previously mentioned will be moderate for those who are thirsty for success. When the transit occurs at the end of the day or at night, it fulfills all purposes. 

*   When the **Sun** enters **Pisces** <note>original: "Ravi meena," the transit marking the solar month of Meena</note>, one should examine the results carefully. 
*   When the transit occurs in **Aries** <note>original: "Mesha"</note> during the bright fortnight or during the day, there will be an abundance of crops. The earth will become truly lush with vegetation.

### Influences of the Planets and Days

The fruits of the Sun's transit are halved if the son of the Earth <note>original: "Mahisuta," a name for the planet Mars</note> is lacking in strength. If the transit coincides with a full moon or a powerful planet, it may be fruitless. At such times, there may be a "rain of weapons" <note>a metaphor for war or violent conflict</note>, anxiety for the king, and loss of rice and grain. While there is a wealth of crops, the subjects may still suffer. 

The effects based on the day of the transit:
*   **Sunday:** If the transit falls on Sunday, there is fear of thieves and enemies.
*   **Monday:** Known as the "water-carrier," it brings coolness and cleansing rains.
*   **Tuesday:** Influenced by Mars, it brings distress from the king and constant restlessness.
*   **Wednesday/Thursday:** Known as the path of the celestial Ganges; when associated with **Jupiter**, it produces an abundance of all crops.

<summary>This page details the astrological consequences of the Sun's transit (Sankranti), predicting social, political, and agricultural outcomes—ranging from earthquakes and war to bountiful harvests—based on the timing and the day of the week.</summary>

Дорогой другъ мой, Макаръ Алексѣевичъ!
Я вамъ уже третій день, мой другъ, ничего не писала, а у меня было много-много заботъ, много тревоги.

Третьяго дня былъ у меня Быковъ. Я была одна, Ѳедора куда-то ходила. Я отворила ему и такъ испугалась, когда его увидала, что не могла тронуться съ мѣста. Я чувствовала, что я поблѣднѣла. Онъ вошелъ, по своему обыкновенію, съ громкимъ смѣхомъ, взялъ стулъ и сѣлъ. Я долго не могла опомниться, наконецъ, сѣла въ уголъ за работу. Онъ скоро пересталъ смѣяться. Кажется, мой видъ поразилъ его. Я такъ похудѣла въ послѣднее время; щеки и глаза мои ввалились, я была блѣдна какъ платокъ... дѣйствительно, меня трудно узнать тому, кто зналъ меня годъ тому назадъ. Онъ долго и пристально смотрѣлъ на меня, наконецъ, опять развеселился. Сказалъ что-то такое; я не помню что отвѣчала ему, и онъ опять засмѣялся. Онъ сидѣлъ у меня цѣлый часъ; долго говорилъ со мной; кой о чемъ разспрашивалъ. Наконецъ, передъ прощаніемъ, онъ взялъ меня за руку и сказалъ (я вамъ пишу отъ слова и до слова): «Варвара Алексѣевна! Между нами сказать, Анна Ѳедоровна, ваша родственница, а моя короткая знакомая и пріятельница, преподлая женщина». (Тутъ онъ еще назвалъ ее однимъ неприличнымъ словомъ). Совратила она и двоюродную вашу сестрицу съ пути, и васъ погубила. Съ моей стороны и я въ этомъ случаѣ подлецомъ оказался; да вѣдь, что, дѣло житейское». Тутъ онъ захохоталъ что есть мочи. Потомъ замѣтилъ, что онъ красно говорить не мастеръ, и что, главное, что объяснить было нужно, и объ чемъ обязанности благородства повелѣвали ему не умалчивать, ужъ онъ объявилъ, и что въ короткихъ словахъ приступаетъ къ остальному. My dear friend, Makar Alekseevich!
I have not written to you for three days now, my friend, and I have had many, many worries, much anxiety.

The day before yesterday, Bykov was here. I was alone; Fedora had gone somewhere. I opened the door for him and was so frightened when I saw him that I could not move from my spot. I felt myself turn pale. He entered with his usual loud laugh, took a chair, and sat down. I could not recover for a long time; finally, I sat in the corner to work. He soon stopped laughing. It seems my appearance struck him. I have become so thin lately; my cheeks and eyes are sunken, and I was pale as a handkerchief... indeed, it would be difficult for anyone who knew me a year ago to recognize me. He looked at me long and intently, and finally, became cheerful again. He said something; I do not remember what I answered, and he started laughing again. He sat with me for a whole hour; he spoke with me for a long time; he asked about various things. Finally, before saying goodbye, he took my hand and said (I am writing to you word for word): "Varvara Alekseevna! Between us, Anna Fedorovna, your relative and my close acquaintance and friend, is a vile woman." (Here he also called her an indecent name). "She led your cousin astray and ruined you. For my part, I turned out to be a scoundrel in this matter too; but then again, that is just life." Here he roared with laughter as hard as he could. Then he remarked that he was not a master of eloquent speech, and that what was important—what needed to be explained, and what the obligations of nobility forbade him from keeping silent about—he had already declared, and that in short words he was proceeding to the rest. Then he declared to me that he was seeking my hand, that he considered it his duty to restore my honor, that he is rich, that he would take me after the wedding to his

Онъ пишетъ: «Если я точно въ своей жизни дѣлаю одно дурное и не дѣлаюсь хоть на волосокъ лучше, т.-е. не начинаю дѣлать немножечко поменьше дурного, то я непремѣнно лгу, говоря, что я хочу дѣлать доброе. Если человѣкъ хочетъ точно не для людей, а для Бога, дѣлать хорошее, то онъ всегда подвигается на пути добра... жизнь вся есть движеніе по этому пути». Далѣе онъ ссылается на милосердіе и всепрощеніе Божіе, «на несуществованіе грѣховъ передъ Богомъ для человѣка, любящаго Его», и даже приводитъ такой аргументъ, чтобы отстранить идею искупленія: «не проще ли Богу прямо простить мои грѣхи?..» «Вы говорите, что помощь эта произошла 1880 лѣтъ назадъ, а я думаю, что Богъ какимъ былъ всегда, такой и теперь, и всегда оказываетъ помощь людямъ» $^1$). На основаніи этихъ и другихъ сужденій подобнаго же содержанія можно бы предположить у Толстого вообще слабое сознаніе грѣха и его ядовитой силы подъ предлогомъ Божія милосердія, иначе говоря, можно понять это какъ ученіе о милосердіи Бога не къ человѣку, но къ грѣху, что есть, конечно, скрытое безбожіе, хотя оно нерѣдко и проповѣдуется въ качествѣ христіанства. И однако, въ примѣненіи къ Толстому это было бы несправедливо. Онъ слишкомъ глубоко заглянулъ въ человѣческую душу, онъ слишкомъ много позналъ опытомъ своей собственной жизни, чтобы вмѣстѣ съ оптимистами совершенно отвергать силу грѣха, провозглашать нравственное здоровье естественнаго человѣка. Напротивъ, ни въ чемъ такъ не близокъ Толстой къ христіанству церковному, какъ въ сознаніи грѣха, его силы и непобѣдимости, передъ которой дѣтскимъ лепетомъ кажутся толки о самоспасеніи. Толстой слишкомъ хорошо зналъ въ надменномъ человѣкобогѣ грязнаго человѣкозвѣря. Вотъ какъ говоритъ онъ о грѣхѣ въ послѣднемъ своемъ сборникѣ «Путь Жизни»: «Человѣкъ рожденъ въ грѣхахъ. Отъ тѣла всѣ грѣхи, но духъ живетъ въ человѣкѣ и борется съ тѣломъ. Вся жизнь человѣка — это борьба духа съ тѣломъ. Большая ошибка думать, что отъ грѣха можно освободиться вѣрой или прощеніемъ отъ людей. Отъ грѣха ничѣмъ нельзя освободиться. Можно только сознавать свой грѣхъ и стараться не повторять его.

---
$^1$) Ibid. 54—5.

<page-break/>

<page-num>25</page-num>
<meta>catchwords: 1) Путь Жизни, вып. 6: Грѣхи, соблазны, суевѣрія, 14—15. 2) Христіанское ученіе, 13.</meta>

Если же впредь отказываешься отъ борьбы, то отказываешься отъ главнаго дѣла жизни... Горе тому человѣку, который скажетъ себѣ, что освободился отъ грѣховъ» $^1$). «Человѣкъ ни звѣрь, ни ангелъ, но ангелъ, рождающійся отъ звѣря, — духовное существо, рождающееся отъ животнаго, и все наше пребываніе въ этомъ мірѣ есть не что иное, какъ это рожденіе» $^2$). Въ этомъ ученіи Толстой дѣйствительно переходитъ на сторону ученій о «радикальномъ злѣ» въ человѣческой природѣ. Оставляя въ сторонѣ вопросъ, насколько могутъ быть согласованы обѣ части этого ученія, посмотримъ, что же даетъ ему эта духовная зрячесть, вѣдающая силу грѣха и все человѣческое безсиліе до конца его побороть? Толстой моралистъ и проповѣдникъ не устаетъ повторять, что самый путь борьбы съ грѣхомъ исполненъ чувства приближенія къ Богу и поэтому радостенъ, — о радости и покоѣ, какъ о чемъ-то уже достигнутомъ, онъ нерѣдко говоритъ по разнымъ поводамъ. Напримѣръ, въ цитированномъ уже письмѣ къ А. А. Толстой мы читаемъ: «Движеніе это радостно, во-первыхъ тѣмъ, что чѣмъ ближе къ свѣту, тѣмъ лучше; во-вторыхъ тѣмъ, что при каждомъ новомъ шагѣ видишь, какъ мало ты сдѣлалъ и какъ много еще этого радостнаго пути впереди... человѣкъ, начавшій эту истинную жизнь, всегда знаетъ и можетъ повѣрить, оглянувшись назадъ, что онъ какъ ни медленно, но приближается къ свѣту и узнаетъ это направленіе, и въ движеніи въ этомъ направленіи полагаетъ жизнь».

Въ этомъ главный нервъ религіозной проповѣди Толстого и ея паѳосъ: *радость пути* и радость сознанія, какъ много этого пути осталось. Радость есть сила всякой религіи. Радостью побѣдило міръ христіанство въ сердцахъ богоизбранныхъ. Конечно, это совсѣмъ иная радость и объ иномъ, нежели у Толстого, но настоящая радость о «Духѣ Святомъ» есть, можетъ быть, единственный документъ религіозной подлинности вообще. И Толстой хорошо понималъ это, а потому онъ часто и настойчиво говорилъ о достигнутой имъ радости, какъ будто стараясь въ этомъ кого-то увѣрить, можетъ быть,

---
$^1$) Путь Жизни, вып. 6: Грѣхи, соблазны, суевѣрія, 14—15.
$^2$) Христіанское ученіе, 13.

<vocab>Л. Н. Толстой, грѣхъ, искупленіе, Путь Жизни, христіанство, радость, борьба духа съ тѣломъ</vocab>

redemption. He writes: "If I actually do one evil thing in my life and do not become even a hair better, that is, if I do not begin to do a little bit less of what is evil, then I am certainly lying when I say that I want to do good. If a person wants to do good truly for God, and not for people, then he is always advancing on the path of good... life is entirely movement along this path." Further, he refers to the mercy and total forgiveness of God, "to the non-existence of sins before God for a person who loves Him," and even brings up this argument to dismiss the idea of redemption: "would it not be simpler for God to just forgive my sins directly?.." "You say that this help occurred 1880 years ago, but I think that God is now as He has always been, and He is always providing help to people" <note>1</note>. On the basis of these and other judgments of similar content, one could assume that Tolstoy had a generally weak consciousness of sin and its poisonous power under the guise of God's mercy; in other words, one can understand this as a teaching of God's mercy not toward the person, but toward the sin, which is, of course, a hidden atheism, although it is often preached as Christianity. And yet, when applied to Tolstoy, this would be unfair. He looked too deeply into the human soul, he learned too much from the experience of his own life, to completely reject the power of sin along with the optimists, to proclaim the moral health of the natural man. On the contrary, Tolstoy is nowhere so close to Church Christianity as in the consciousness of sin, its power and invincibility, before which talk of self-salvation seems like childish babble. Tolstoy knew the dirty man-beast inside the arrogant man-god all too well. Here is how he speaks about sin in his last collection, "The Way of Life": "Man is born in sins. All sins come from the body, but the spirit lives in man and fights with the body. A person's whole life is a struggle of the spirit with the body. It is a big mistake to think that one can be freed from sin by faith or forgiveness from people. One can never be freed from sin by anything. One can only realize one's sin and try not to repeat it.

<note>1) Ibid. 54—5.</note>

<header>БРАТЬЯ КАРАМАЗОВЫ.</header>

ее? Вѣдь красавица. Да не тѣмъ она красива тогда была. Красива была она тѣмъ, въ ту минуту, что она благородная, а я подлецъ, что она въ величіи своего великодушія и жертвы своей за отца, а я клопъ. И вотъ отъ меня, клопа и подлеца, она вся зависитъ, вся, вся кругомъ и съ душой и съ тѣломъ. Очерчена. Я тебѣ прямо скажу: эта мысль, мысль фаланги, до такой степени захватила мнѣ сердце, что оно чуть не истекло отъ одного томленія. Казалось-бы и борьбы не могло уже быть никакой: именно-бы поступить какъ клопу, какъ злому тарантулу, безо всякаго сожалѣнія... Пересѣкло у меня духъ даже. Слушай: вѣдь я, разумѣется, завтра-же пріѣхалъ-бы руки просить, чтобы все это благороднѣйшимъ, такъ сказать, образомъ завершить и чтобы никто, стало быть, этого не зналъ и не могъ-бы знать. Потому что вѣдь я человѣкъ, хоть и низкихъ желаній, но честный. И вотъ вдругъ мнѣ тогда въ ту-же секунду кто-то и шепни на ухо: «Да вѣдь завтра-то этакая, какъ пріѣдешь съ предложеніемъ руки, и не выйдетъ къ тебѣ, а велитъ кучеру со двора тебя вытолкать. Ославляй, дескать, по всему городу, не боюсь тебя!» Взглянулъ я на дѣвицу, не совралъ мой голосъ: такъ, конечно, такъ оно и будетъ. Меня выгонятъ въ шею, по теперешнему лицу уже судить можно. Закипѣла во мнѣ злость, захотѣлось подлѣйшую, поросячью, купеческую штучку выкинуть: поглядѣть это на нее съ насмѣшкой, и тутъ-же пока стоитъ передъ тобой и огорошить ее, съ интонаціей, съ какою только купчикъ умѣетъ сказать:

— Это четыре-то тысячи! Да я пошутилъ-съ, что вы это? Слишкомъ легковѣрно, сударыня, сосчитали. Сотенки двѣ я, пожалуй, съ моимъ даже удовольствіемъ и охотою, а четыре тысячи это деньги не такія, барышня, чтобъ ихъ на такое легкомысліе кидать. Обезпокоить себя напрасно изволили.

Видишь, я-бы, конечно, все потерялъ, она-бы убѣжала, но зато инфернально, мстительно вышло-бы, всего остальнаго стоило-бы. Вылъ-бы потомъ всю жизнь отъ раскаянія, но только чтобы теперь эту штучку отмочить! Вѣришь-ли, никогда этого у меня ни съ какой не бывало, ни съ единою женщиной, чтобы въ этакую минуту я на нее глядѣлъ съ ненавистью, — и вотъ крестъ кладу: я на эту глядѣлъ тогда секунды три или пять со страшною ненавистью, — съ тою самою ненавистью, отъ которой до любви, до безумнѣйшей любви — одинъ волосокъ! Я подошелъ къ окну, приложилъ лобъ къ мерзлому стеклу и, помню, что мнѣ лобъ обожгло льдомъ какъ огнемъ. Долго не задержалъ, не безпокойся, обернулся, подошелъ къ столу, отворилъ ящикъ и досталъ пятитысячный пятипроцентный безъименный билетъ (въ лексиконѣ французскомъ лежалъ у меня). Затѣмъ молча ей показалъ, сложилъ, отдалъ, самъ отворилъ ей дверь въ

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Dmitri Karamazov’s confession regarding his encounter with Katerina Ivanovna, who has come to his lodgings to ask for the money to save her father.</meta>

<header>THE BROTHERS KARAMAZOV.</header>

her? After all, she is a beauty. But she was not beautiful because of that at that moment. She was beautiful in that moment because she was noble and I was a scoundrel, because she was in the majesty of her magnanimity and her sacrifice for her father, and I was a louse. And now, this woman depends entirely upon me, a louse and a scoundrel, entirely, completely, body and soul. She is trapped. I will tell you frankly: this thought, the thought of the <term>phalanx</term> <gloss>a tightly ordered formation, here symbolizing Dmitri’s perceived power over her</gloss>, so gripped my heart that it nearly burst from the mere yearning of it. It seemed as though there could be no struggle anymore: one should just act like a louse, like a wicked tarantula, without any regret. My breath even hitched. Listen: after all, I would, of course, have come to ask for her hand the very next day, to finish it all in the most noble manner, so to speak, so that no one would know or could ever know. Because, after all, I am a man who, though possessed of low desires, is an honest one. And then, suddenly, at that very second, someone whispered in my ear: "But tomorrow, when you arrive with a proposal of marriage, she will not come out to you, but will order the coachman to throw you out of the courtyard. 'Let him spread his scandals all over town, I am not afraid of him!' she will say." I looked at the young lady, and my inner voice did not lie: yes, of course, that is exactly how it will be. I will be kicked out, one can judge that by her face as it is now. Anger boiled within me, I wanted to play a most base, piggish, merchant-like trick: to look at her with mockery, and right there while she stands before you, to stun her with the intonation that only a petty merchant knows how to use:

— That four thousand! Why, I was joking, what is this? You counted too gullibly, my dear lady. Two hundred or so, I might, perhaps, with my own pleasure and willingness, but four thousand is not the kind of money, young lady, to throw away on such frivolity. You have troubled yourself in vain.

You see, I would, of course, have lost everything, she would have run away, but it would have turned out infernal, vengeful; it would have been worth more than anything else. I would have howled for the rest of my life from remorse, but only to pull that stunt right now! Believe me, this has never happened to me with anyone, not with a single woman, that in such a moment I looked at her with hatred, — and I swear it: I looked at that one then for three or five seconds with terrible hatred, — with that very hatred from which, to love, to the most insane love, there is but a single hair’s breadth! I approached the window, pressed my forehead against the frosted glass, and I remember that my forehead was seared by the ice as if by fire. I did not linger long, do not worry; I turned around, went to the table, opened the drawer, and took out a five-thousand-ruble five-percent bearer bond (it was lying inside my French lexicon). Then I showed it to her in silence, folded it, gave it to her, and opened the door for her myself into

<summary>Dmitri recounts the intense internal conflict and sadistic impulse he felt while Katerina Ivanovna stood before him, ultimately describing his decision to provide her with the money.</summary>

Ввечеру приказъ данъ Полиціи, за подписаніемъ Губернаторскимъ, чтобъ, по случаю недостатка въ сѣнѣ <gloss>¹)</gloss>, каждый житель объявилъ, сколько имѣетъ у себя на дворѣ сѣна, и оное бъ безъ всякой утайки отдавалъ на команду Яицкихъ казаковъ, для защищенія города находящихся.

На 10-е число въ ночи пойманъ на рѣкѣ Яикѣ крещеный Калмыкъ; у него найдено 7 или 8 фунтовъ пороха и фитиль; который въ допросѣ между прочаго показалъ, что онъ отъ злодѣевъ съ тѣмъ и посланъ въ городъ, дабы въ тѣхъ самыхъ мѣстахъ, гдѣ больше и чаще строенье, зажечь и причинить пожаръ, а въ то-де время злодѣи хотѣли приступъ сдѣлать къ городу. Поутру хотя и учинена была за городомъ высылка, чтобъ схватить нѣкоторые злодѣйскіе разъѣзды; но за великимъ морозомъ и вѣтромъ, возвращена была въ городъ. А послѣ полудня еще была высылка, въ которую командировано было Яицкихъ казаковъ до 300 человѣкъ; злодѣи, усмотря оную команду, начали противъ ее выѣзжать изъ своего лагеря, и выѣхало ихъ тысячи съ полторы человѣкъ, причемъ имѣли они у себя пушки, на дровняхъ укрѣпленныя, изъ коихъ сдѣлавъ 4 выстрѣла, принудили означенной небольшой командѣ, неимѣвшей при себѣ ни одной пушки, возвратиться въ городъ, а какъ по онымъ злодѣямъ выпалено изъ города изъ трехъ пушекъ, то они отдалясь, возвратились въ свой лагерь. Яицкіе казаки сказывали, что при первомъ на злодѣевъ нападеніи, пока они еще не умножились, закололи у нихъ одного человѣка, на которомъ-де былъ красный кафтанъ съ золотыми широкими галунами, и черезъ съ деньгами (сказывали, что онъ былъ изъ Яицкихъ казаковъ, по прозванію Серебрецовъ, и за его наѣздничество отъ злодѣя сдѣланъ старшиною), да одному

at night, so during the day, nothing was seen of the villains. Only around noon were three cannon shots heard in their camp, though the reason remained unknown. In the evening, an order was given to the Police, signed by the Governor, stating that due to a shortage of hay <gloss>¹)</gloss>, every resident must declare how much hay they have in their courtyard and turn it over without any concealment to the detachment of Yaik Cossacks who are stationed there for the defense of the city.

On the 10th, at night, a baptized Kalmyk was caught on the Yaik River. 7 or 8 pounds of gunpowder and a fuse were found on him. During interrogation, he testified, among other things, that he had been sent by the villains to the city specifically to set fire to those places where the buildings were dense and frequent, and at that time, the villains wanted to make an assault on the city. In the morning, although a dispatch was sent out of the city to seize some villainous patrols, it was returned to the city due to the severe frost and wind. After noon, there was another dispatch, to which about 300 Yaik Cossacks were assigned. He loved the Christians more than other Muslims love them; in his life, there was one great event from which a kind feeling could not cool until the grave.

He was still very young when his father gave him a charming Greek orphan girl as a slave, taken captive on the islands during the struggle for the independence of Hellas.

She was only fourteen years old, and her name was Marigo. When Shekir, himself still almost a boy, was left alone with her, Marigo wept and, stretching out her hands to him, said: "My master, I am yours. I have no father, no mother; they were killed; do with me what you want. I will only say one word to you. Have pity on me, I am afraid!"

Shekir left her in peace; later, through affection, gifts, and brotherly care, he persuaded her to become close. Once having overcome her childish fear, the slave became attached to Shekir with all the strength of her soul. No one touched her beliefs: she continued to go to church, and during fasts, she was fed separately. Shekir’s old parents rejoiced at their son's kindness, at the childish initial fear, and later at the submissive affection of the little Greek girl. "Children, little children!" Shekir’s father and mother would say to each other, laughing. When they married Shekir-Bey off to a wealthy girl, the slave's life, of course, became worse, but not for long. "Not at all."

"Do you want to help me untangle some wool? Come here, to me."

She nodded to me and walked out of the living room.

I followed her.

In the room we entered, the furniture was a little better and arranged with greater taste. However, at that moment I could notice almost nothing: I was moving as if in a dream and felt in my whole being a kind of foolishly intense well-being.

The princess's daughter sat down, took out a skein of red wool, and, pointing me to a chair opposite her, carefully untied the skein and placed it on my hands. She did all this in silence, with a kind of amusing slowness and the same bright and mischievous smirk on her slightly parted lips. She began to wind the wool onto a folded card and suddenly shone upon me with such a clear and quick glance that I involuntarily looked down. When her eyes, usually half-squinted, opened to their full size, her face changed completely: it was as if light were flooding over it.

"What did you think of me yesterday, Monsieur Voldemar?" she asked after a little while. "You surely judged me?"

"I... princess... I did not think anything... how could I..." I answered with embarrassment.

"Listen," she countered. "You do not know me yet: I am very strange; I want you to always tell me the truth. You, I heard, are sixteen, and I am twenty-one: you see, I am much older than you, and therefore you must always tell me the truth... and obey me," she added. "Look at me: why do you not look at me?"

I became even more embarrassed; however, I lifted my eyes to her. She smiled, but not with the previous smile, but another, approving one. "Look at me," she said, lowering her voice affectionately: "I do not find it unpleasant. I like your face; I have a premonition that we will be friends. And do you like me?" she added mischievously.

А что изъ твоего слова сдѣлаешь? Шубу не сошьешь. Да оно отчего бы не дать! Деньги не велики. Кабы вы только могли чувствовать.

Мы васъ и уважаемъ, и будемъ уважать.

pages.translation:
->Anna Pavlovna.<-

And even those two thousand were scraped together with great difficulty. Now we only need to borrow three hundred rubles for a short time.

->Khryukov.<-

I know this "short time." If I give you three hundred rubles now, you will come asking for just as much again in a week; or perhaps even more.

->Anna Pavlovna.<-

We will not. We will return this money to you with gratitude. I give you my word.

->Khryukov.<-

You give your word? And what can I take from you for it?

->Anna Pavlovna.<-

I pledge it to you with my word.

->Khryukov.<-

And what can one do with your word? You cannot sew a fur coat out of it. And yet, why not give it! The money is not a great sum. If only you could show some feeling.

->Anna Pavlovna.<-

What does that mean? How, show feeling?

->Khryukov.<-

Just that. Show feeling. Respect your benefactors; that is how you show feeling.

->Anna Pavlovna.<-

We do respect you, and we will continue to respect you.

->Khryukov.<-

Well, we shall see! (*He approaches. He pats Anna Pavlovna on the head*). Look at you, how smoothly your hair is combed: hair by hair! So, how much money do you need?

Sed caufa hujuf-modi accipitur ex canone primo cum ejus figura, ubi oculus eft in medio fubtiliori, & res in medio denfiori, cujus concavitas eft verfus oculum & oculus eft inter centrum & rem vifam. Si objiciatur quod imago minor eft quam res, propter quod diceret aliquis, quod minor deberet videri; Dicendum eft, quod majoritas anguli cum propinquitate prævalet in hac parte. Res e-nim propinquior cæteris paribus apparet evidentius in fua quantitate, & præcipue quando fub majori angulo videtur. Si iterum dicatur, quod radii ftellarum inveniunt vapores & nubes non folum in horizonte & prope, fed verfus medium cœli & in illo medio; fed folo quando eft prope medium cœli vel in medio non apparet infolitæ quantitatis; ergo nec prope or-tum & occafum. Et quidam probabiliter inftructi in rebus perfpectivis æftimaverunt vapores non effe caufam hujus rei, propter hanc objectionem. Sed decepti funt, quia aliam caufam dare non poffunt: nam illa quæ pri-us affignata eft de magnitudine ftellarum in horizonte eft perpetua, hæc autem appericatio magnitudinis eft ad tempus, nec femper, & ideo habet caufam temporalem. falsity: the cause of which is manifest from the aforementioned canons, namely the first concerning planes and the fifth concerning concaves. For because the eye is in a rarer medium and the object is in a denser one, the object must appear closer and more elevated toward the eye, where the visual ray meets the perpendicular <note>a line drawn from the object at a right angle to the surface</note>, and it will appear larger. Wherefore it will seem to the sight that the object <note>p</note> placed in a vessel is elevated <note>q</note> from the bottom of the vessel to the surface of the water; nor is this a different figuration than what was done in the aforementioned places, and therefore that suffices. 

If, however, we look at the sun, the moon, or the stars in the east and west while watery vapors intervene, as often happens in summer and autumn, we see these luminaries of an unusual size, as anyone experiences. But the cause of this is taken from the first canon with its figure, where the eye is in the rarer medium and the object is in the denser medium, whose concavity is toward the eye, and the eye is between the center and the visible object. For vapors of this kind are spherical and concentric to the world, because they recede equally from the center, and therefore their concavity will be toward the eye, and the eye will be between them and their center, which is the center of the world. And so, as appeared from that figuration, the image of the object is closer, and it is seen under a larger angle, and therefore the object appears larger and closer. 

If it is objected that the image is smaller than the object, for which reason someone might say that it ought to look smaller, it must be said that the magnitude of the angle together with the proximity prevails in this part. For an object that is closer, all other things being equal, appears more evidently in its quantity, and especially when it is seen under a larger angle. If it is said again that the rays of the stars find vapors and clouds not only on the horizon and nearby, but toward the middle of the sky and in that middle, but the sun, when it is near the middle of the sky or in the middle, does not appear of unusual size, and therefore neither does it near the rising and setting. And certain men, probably instructed in matters of perspective, thought that vapors were not the cause of this thing, because of this objection. But they are deceived, because they cannot give another cause: for the one that was previously assigned concerning the magnitude of the stars on the horizon is perpetual, whereas this appearance of magnitude is for a time, and not always, and therefore it has a temporary cause. And we see that when the air is clear and dry at sunrise and sunset, lacking vapors, then the stars have their usual magnitudes; but when it is vaporous, in those times an appearance of unusual magnitude occurs. It is manifest, therefore, that vapors are the cause. The objection, however, is solved by the fact that the rays of the stars near the rising and setting fall entirely at oblique angles and therefore are refracted on the surface of the air according to the tenor of the said canon. But when a star tends toward the middle of the sky, the rays approach the rectitude of the angles, for which reason they are not refracted as they are when the star is in the east. And if <note>r</note> it is objected that all the rays of the planets are refracted around the tropic of Cancer, as has been held before, because they do not fall toward the center of the world but toward the horizon, it must be conceded: but yet they are refracted much less, and they approach more toward perpendicularity when the star is toward the middle of the sky, and therefore although it then appears...

If, therefore, their office, as we see, has become obsolete, and nothing but an empty name is left to them, while the secretaries have taken their place and perform those things before the Pontiff that were performed by them, let the advocates bear with the same patience that the secretaries are preferred to them in honor as the bishops long ago bore that the notaries were preferred to them. Especially since the episcopal order far surpasses notaries in dignity, while the advocates do not surpass the secretaries in dignity; indeed, they are not even their equals, and they are surpassed in terms of convenience, as we have proven.

<meta>A blue decorative initial L.</meta>Leonardo sends greetings to Guarino. O Guarino, best of men, and even most learned, what now should I answer you, or in what way should I excuse this tardiness and procrastination of mine? That I was occupied. What was the occupation so great through which there was no opportunity for responding? That it was deeper. I call God as my witness that you have always been most dear to me, even though some have attempted to stir up things against me. What then was the cause, if not a certain habit of mine that is rather slow in writing? You, therefore, bear with an equal mind that I have done to you what I am accustomed to do to others, my dearest friend. I have two letters from you. One, very old, regarding the controversy of the spiteful ones who were striving to make us conflict with one another. The other, filled with benevolence and congratulation for this new dignity of mine. 3 février 1629. rencontres de rimes, ou autres cadances, quasi inopinées. Il faut qu'il
ayt bien changé d'humeur, car il estoit merveilleusement humble en ce
païs icy, et d'une conversation doulce et complaisante, quasi comme
celle de Mʳ Rubens au reste homme de grande probité et syncérité, et
grandement timoré, de sorte que j'aurois peine à me persuader qu'il se
laissast porter à des suppositions. Il m'escript qu'on avoit trouvé sa
manière si approchante de celle de Antoine More, disciple de Titian,
qui vivoit il y a 70 ans qu'on avoit revocqué en doubte si le portraict
de son frère n'estoit point de cette main là. Mais il m'allègue en
tesmoings deux peintres bien galants hommes que j'ay veus icy, qui
le cognoissent luy et son frère utérin qui est représenté en ce portraict.
Bien veux-je croire qu'il l'a si longuement pené, et tant à son aise,
son frère luy prestant le collet qu'il n'en feroit pas si aisément un
pareil, et de faict il me dict que selon le payement on faict plus ou
moings de travail, et que pour estre payé à la douzaine il ne seroit pas
raisonable d'y apporter tant d'art et tant de soing. Mʳ Rubens me parle
de luy en une de ses lettres (1), et me dit qu'il a veu de ses portraicts
si exactement ressemblants, et de si bonne manière, qu'il le louoit
grandement, ce qui me faict croire qu'il avoit possible veu la personne
mesmes de son frère utérin qui est représentée en ce portraict ; tant y
a que j'en sçauray la vérité, car j'en feray escrire ces deux peintres
qu'il m'allègue. Et quand cette piece ne seroit pas de luy, toujours
seray-je bien aise d'avoir de sa main le portraict de M. Saulmaise (2)
et quelqu'autre comme il m'a promis, et me contenterois bien de la
bonté de la manière qu'il avoit autres foys icy, à plus forte raison s'il
l'a bonifiée comme il dict. Aydez-moy envers Mʳ de Saulmaise pour luy
faire donner le temps, et prester le collet. Et s'il faict M. Grotius, je
le prieray de m'en faire une coppie, car celuy que j'ay ressemble si
peu à mon gré que j'avois peine de le recognoistre quand je le receus.

3 February 1629. <note>He is referring to</note> accidental rhymes, or other cadences, almost unexpected. He must have changed his mood a great deal, for he was wonderfully humble in this country, and of a gentle and compliant conversation, almost like that of Mr. Rubens; furthermore a man of great integrity and sincerity, and greatly timid, so that I would have difficulty persuading myself that he would let himself be led to suppositions. He writes to me that his manner had been found so close to that of Antoine More, a disciple of Titian, who lived 70 years ago, that it had been called into doubt whether his brother's portrait was not by that hand. But he cites as witnesses two painters, very gallant men whom I have seen here, who know him and his uterine brother who is represented in this portrait. I am very willing to believe that he labored over it for so long, and at his ease, with his brother lending him the collar, that he would not so easily make another like it; and in fact he tells me that according to the payment, more or less work is done, and that to be paid by the dozen it would not be reasonable to put so much art and care into it. Mr. Rubens speaks to me of him in one of his letters (1), and tells me that he has seen portraits of his that were so exactly resembling, and in such a good style, that he praised him greatly, which makes me believe that he had perhaps seen the very person of his uterine brother who is represented in this portrait; suffice it to say that I will know the truth of it, for I will have these two painters he cites to me write about it. And even if this piece were not by him, I would still be very happy to have the portrait of Mr. Saumaise (2) by his hand and some other as he promised me, and I would be quite satisfied with the quality of the style he used to have here, and even more so if he has improved it as he says. Help me with Mr. de Saumaise to make him give the time, and lend the collar. And if he makes Mr. Grotius, I will ask him to make me a copy, for the one I have resembles him so little to my liking that I had trouble recognizing him when I received it.

PH. TAMIZEY DE LARROQUE. *Letters of Peiresc to the Dupuy brothers*, Vol. II, pp. 15-16.

The sole evidence for referring any of the prose treatises to the twelfth or thirteenth century is external. It consists in the assertions† of Messrs. Jean Paul Perrin, Samuel Morland, and Jean Leger, that certain MSS. of them exhibited the dates of 1100, 1120, and 1230. But no such documents so dated are now to be met with. Neither does it appear certain that any one, save Perrin, ever saw the date of 1120; for Theodore Tronchin’s attestation in 1656 purports only that Perrin showed him “divers *original* MSS.,” words entirely devoid of meaning, and calculated to give a vague semblance of authentication, without saying anything. Perrin was, however, silent as to the date of the catechism which he printed; and it was reserved for Jean Leger to reprint it, with the daring assertion that its date was A. D. 1100.

A deep mystery and ugly suspicions hang over all the dealings of these people with Waldensian books. The written volumes which were “remises entre‡ les mains de Monsieur Morland, Commissaire Extraordinaire de Millord Oliver Cromwell, Protecteur de la Grande Bretagne, par Messrs. Antoine et Jean Leger, pasteurs originaires des vallées,” were presented by Morland “to the public library of the famous University of Cambridge, in August, 1658.” One of the pieces in volume A was expressly dated 1230, which might excite some degree of presumption that the whole volume was of that date.

Since Martin Luther did not declare himself a reformer until 1517, and Zuingli not until 1519, it is reasonable to suppose that whatever contents of these volumes are found—upon strict examination—to belong to the "New Learning" (the Reformation) rather than to the ancient Lugdunensian sect, are either original autographs or very early copies.

The sole evidence for attributing any of these prose treatises to the twelfth or thirteenth century is external. It consists of the assertions <note>Perrin, "Hist. Vaud.," p. 57; Morland, "Evang. Churches," pp. 9, 30, 142; Leger, "Hist. Gen.," pp. 24, 58, 71, 83, 87, 92.</note> of Messrs. Jean Paul Perrin, Samuel Morland, and Jean Leger that certain manuscripts exhibited the dates 1100, 1120, and 1230. But no such documents bearing these dates can be found today. Furthermore, it does not appear certain that anyone other than Perrin ever saw the date 1120; for Theodore Tronchin’s attestation in 1656 only claims that Perrin showed him "diverse *original* manuscripts"—words entirely devoid of specific meaning, calculated to provide a vague semblance of authentication while saying nothing of substance. Perrin, however, remained silent regarding the date of the catechism he printed; it was left to Jean Leger to reprint it with the daring assertion that its date was 1100 A.D.

A deep mystery and ugly suspicions hang over all the dealings these men had with Waldensian books. The written volumes which were "delivered into the hands of Mr. Morland, Commissioner Extraordinary of Lord Oliver Cromwell, Protector of Great Britain, by Messrs. Antoine and Jean Leger, pastors originating from the valleys," were presented by Morland to the public library of the famous University of Cambridge in August 1658. <note>Leger, "Histoire Generale," p. 21.</note> One of the pieces in Volume A was explicitly dated 1230, which might raise a presumption that the entire volume was of that age.

<summary>This page challenges the reliability of early Vaudois scholars like Perrin, Morland, and Leger, who claimed ancient dates for their manuscripts without providing verifiable evidence, noting the suspicious history of these documents' movements.</summary>

walking, fatigue, receiving food, which can neither help nor harm, are indeed neither good nor evil. The best moderation of laws is divided into three parts: First, if the laws themselves are excellent and optimal. Second, if the citizens observe with all diligence those laws which have been laid down. Third, if the republic is well administered according to the customs and studies of whoever has established the laws. Therefore, the first part of this moderation is that the laws are best; the second, that one remains within them; the third, that one lives according to excellent customs and gods. The iniquity contrary to this laudable moderation of laws is likewise split into three: one is if the laws are the worst and harmful to foreigners and citizens; another if those which are the least followed are not obeyed; the third, if there is no law at all. The contrary is divided into three ways, for example, we say good is contrary to evil, as justice is to injustice, wisdom to foolishness, and other such things. Evils, however, are contrary to evils, as prodigality to avarice and unjust punishment to unjust impunity and other evils of that kind are contrary to evils. Furthermore, light things are said to be contrary to heavy, slow to fast, and black to white, these being intermediate contraries. 

There are three genera of goods: some exist to be held, others to be shared, others to subsist. The first are those that can exist, such as justice and health. The following are those that cannot be held, but we can be participants in them; for example, it is not possible to possess "the good itself," but it is not impossible to enjoy participation in it. A substance, however, that neither admits participation nor is possible to hold, but rather must "be," such as being honest and being just, is good; yet one cannot hold it nor participate in it, but it suffices to be honest and just. This is the distribution of goods. 

Counsel is likewise tripartite. One part takes from the past, another from the future, another from the present time. The past time provides examples when one attends to what care and what people have suffered, so that we may beware, or what they have done prudently, so that we may imitate them, as for instance what the Lacedaemonians suffered while they were confident. It advises one to consider the thing itself which is at hand, for example, weak walls, timid men, a scarcity of grain, and other things of this sort. It urges one to look to the future so that nothing is done rashly, keeping in mind the consideration of good reputation, so that embassies are not to be violated by suspicions, lest the grace of honor be lost. 

Voice is divided into two: for it is either animate or inanimate. Animate is indeed vocal; inanimate is truly that of sounds and rattles. Furthermore, animate is split into two; for it is either literate or illiterate. Literate, such as that of humans; illiterate, such as that of animals. Of those things which exist, we say some are divisible, others are indivisible. Of the divisible ones, some have a finite part; others are dissimilar and truly indivisible.

<summary>This page explores the moderation of laws, the three types of goods, the tripartite nature of counsel, and the division of voice and divisible things.</summary>

First of all, concerning the Lacedaemonians, because they were both common and equal to me regarding their angers <note>i.e., their mutual grievances</note>, and to make an alliance of parts. For an earthquake having occurred around Cyprus at the time their assembly was harmed, on the following day the city, victorious in the Lacedaemonian assembly itself, and he himself having come from his homeland to the autocrat to reach an agreement. Whence, with the Lacedaemonians, it shifted that it was necessary to be a friend rather than an enemy, and trust between one another is sent so that they might give whatever they can. To say that they themselves, regarding their own affairs, [would act] for the sake of those things which would most aid the war, but if they were to withdraw from affairs, just as the multitude would seem to care for the sake of private necessity. And in common, he asserted that their own things were being risked for the sake of all. It was voted, all being persuaded, to give them the punishment of the Lacedaemonians. Because they were not the first ones themselves, but the Lacedaemonians [were] to give back for many things and to be with the allies. It would seem to be of the absurd things, just as wisdom on account of the opinion regarding foreign parts. And if anyone agrees with them that they themselves are no less worthy, indeed also being in need of having made allies. But as they came past for the sake of this very thing, already they call another nation. And having sent away the embassies toward the city to others. And they having arrived, they brought back the rest. And the others, as well as the holy ones, came to the alliance of the Athenians, and they make it in the treaties, and they themselves there [made] an alliance of parts. On the following day, the Lacedaemonians, shouting, said they would not give, with the elder <term>ephors</term> <gloss>overseers</gloss> prevailing that these things should happen, and as many others as are persuaded by these. And by that release of theirs, they swore the treaties. But the first, in the whole time, they held it incomplete and were harmed because it seems to them that the apology to the Lacedaemonians is invalid, on account of his provision. Just as the Athenians also [had] nothing from the Lacedaemonians, at any time, legal, and so they held them in anger. And thinking themselves to be wronged, but indeed the Argives and the allies present stepped aside otherwise, as it was not possible for the treaties [to hold].

<margin>

set within a year: -
</margin>
And their alliance was as follows. They made treaties according to the Athenians and Lacedaemonians and Mantineans and Eleans toward themselves and the allies over whom each rules, without deceit and harmless, both by land and by sea. Let it not be permitted to bring weapons for harm, neither [may] the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans and the allies over whom they rule [bring them] upon the Athenians, nor the Athenians and the allies over whom they rule upon the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans and the allies over whom they rule, by no art nor by any contrivance. Upon these terms, the Athenians and Argives and Eleans and Mantineans [made an] alliance for one hundred years. If enemies go upon the land of the Athenians, the Argives and Eleans and Mantineans are to assist the Athenians, according to whatever the Athenians may summon, in whatever way they can, most strongly according to the possible. But if they go away having ravaged, that city is to be an enemy to the Argives and Mantineans and Eleans and Athenians, and to suffer evil by all these cities. And it is not to be permitted to dissolve the treaty, this city [may not] by any one of the cities, nor by all, unless it seems so to all. And the Athenians are to assist to Argos and Mantinea and Elis, if enemies go...

...is such that the townspeople buy grain from neighboring countries. If a situation arises where travel routes in various directions become difficult, one should mix yams and millet with rice and barley to satisfy hunger. Make sure to learn how to cultivate yams and how the vines grow quickly, doing so uniformly across all villages. Learn how to manage water during times of severe drought. As for the production of yams, if the mountain forest administration is carried out well and millet is planted widely in areas where it grows within the mountains, even if the trees and shrubs where millet grows within the tangled vines are numerous, it will suffice for the consumption of the rice and barley in the villages and even for the low-ranking personnel in the capital, provided one mixes in the various types of millet.

Regarding defense preparations in the villages, they were discussed with the district office in years past and recorded in the meeting articles regarding the regulations for firearms <note>original: 鐵炮格式</note>. I have heard that for defense preparations in the capital, the senior ministers held meetings and put it in writing. It is certain that the framework of the legal system is well-prepared. I shall now record the grand boundary, thinking of the capital's defense based on the standards for village defense. In times when the western provinces are not peaceful, the capital's troops should be prepared for the capital's defense, and village troops should be prepared for the defense of the villages.

When the poor scholar encounters his birthday, he often becomes a debtor. His purse cannot sustain him, and the world feels narrow around him.
He does not allow his children to be close, so he causes his friends to be distant. Alas, the scholar. If one is poor, why seek to fill a hundred years?
When the rich man encounters his birthday, he returns home from distant travels. He spends a hundred pieces of gold on a single cup; a thousand coins settle a theatrical performance.
Rare delicacies exhaust the mountains and seas; he searches everywhere with no strategy left out. With this, he sounds his own satisfaction, saying, "I have exceeded the common standard."
He does not fail the years Heaven has granted; year after year he expands his household. Seeing this shocks the human spirit; it is more than just black and white <note>a reference to the stark contrast between wealth and poverty</note>.
Just observe the life of the rich; it is often planned by Heaven. It is not like the meager years of the poor; the Creator does not cherish them.
Could it be that Heaven also envies extravagance, and thus cuts away the lifeline of longevity? Now, as you celebrate the day of your birth, the plates contain only fruit pits.
Your resentment does not reach the chicken or the pig; your fate has not harmed the ants or crickets. You have no intention of conforming to the worldly; you are tranquil, like an immortal or a recluse.

If one fears it is too thick and adds water, this is not like adding water to congee; it is like adding water to wine. When water is added, the wine becomes dregs. Can its taste still be savored? Therefore, those who are good at managing the kitchen must limit the water by measure when adding it. If one ensures not a single drop can be added or removed, and then applies heat, adjusting it evenly, then whether it is congee or rice, it will not seek to be different yet will naturally surpass that of others.

When hosting guests, the rice served must be slightly more refined than that eaten at home. What is the method for refinement? I say: just make it fragrant. I once instructed my maid to prepare a bottle of floral essence. As soon as the rice was cooked, I sprinkled it over. After sprinkling, I closed the lid for a moment, stirred it well, and then served it in bowls. The guests praised the quality of the grain, marvelling at it as a rare species, and when asked, they did not know it was just ordinary grain. This method has been kept secret for a long time; today I reveal it to the world. One does not need to fill the whole pot with this method.

<header>First General Star Map of the Visible Hemisphere</header>

The General Star Map of the Visible Hemisphere uses the North Pole of the celestial equator as its center, the celestial equator as its middle circle, and the visible horizon as its boundary. By the term "visible horizon," we mean the limit defined by the North Pole appearing thirty degrees above the horizon. Thus, all stars visible from the North Pole northward are fully contained herein. South of this, it is difficult to add more, as this represents a spherical <term>huntian</term> <gloss>celestial sphere</gloss> model. South of the celestial equator, the celestial degrees gradually narrow, whereas on the map, they appear to widen. This distortion in shape means there is no way to include them on the same map. We must use the celestial equator as the boundary, divide the work into two maps, and use both poles as centers to ensure the physical properties correspond correctly. Therefore, we present the two general maps of the northern and southern celestial equator thereafter. The outer boundary of this map is divided into three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees, representing the longitudinal degrees of the celestial equator. The straight vertical line from north to south is called the meridian line. On this line, the poles are marked, with one fixed star plotted every degree north and south of the equator, forming the chart of stellar longitude and latitude.

There was a woman's voice. Peering into the room, he saw three or four young women sitting on the ground, with several maids setting out wine and food; all were of exceptional beauty. One woman said, "Lady Qin, Lady Qin, why has Aying not come?" The one sitting lower down replied, "She came from Hangu <note>a historical strategic pass, often used in literature to signify a distant or rugged place</note> yesterday and was injured in her right arm by a villain; she cannot join the excursion. I am deeply resentful." Another woman said, "I had a terrible dream last night; even now I am sweating and trembling." The one sitting lower down took her hand and said, "Do not speak of it, do not speak of it. Tonight, we sisters shall gather; let us speak of the sorrowful, not the unpleasant." The woman smiled and said, "You maids are too timid. Even if tigers or wolves were to carry you away, you must not speak of it—you must sing a song to toast the lady." The woman hummed in a low voice: "The peach blossoms by the idle steps open one after another; our little appointment to walk in the green fields yesterday should not have gone awry. I instruct the girl from the eastern neighbor to wait a little longer, do not urge me; as soon as I see my phoenix-head shoes, I shall come." After the singing, everyone present sighed in admiration. During the conversation and laughter, suddenly a magnificent man of imposing stature entered from outside, with hawk-like eyes and an eagle-like stance.

### Memorial for the New Year

Holding a post in the territory of Gija <note>Korea</note>, I am prevented from attending the golden steps of the palace. Looking toward the halls of the Emperor, I offer a toast of celebration. The jade flute announces the return of spring, and the three "yang" <note>positive forces</note> open the auspicious omens. At the vermilion court, good fortune gathers, and all nations look up to the Dragon Throne. Where his teachings reach, every corner of the world is pleased. I respectfully reflect:

His Majesty the Emperor's merit participates in the nurturing of all things. His way is one of continuous respect. He grants the calendar to the people, initiating the work of the officials and making the various tasks flourish. He achieves the Great Harmony and bestows the Five Blessings upon the people. As we face the start of the year, he receives the joy of the new beginning. Your humble servant, residing in a remote wasteland, wishes to imagine the grand ceremonies. Though I am far from the Emperor's light, my prayers for the Sage's longevity are doubled.

The investigation revealed that Ham I-wan’s report and the subsequent designs were exactly as expected. Yun Jang-do and Yi Ui-jing were implicated, and Mok Chang-myeong was restored to his post. Gwak Han was arrested due to his connection to Yi Si-do. Separate punishments were ordered for the officials. Cao Seok-an was dismissed. Jo Tae-dong and Yi Ui-jing were arrested. It was revealed that Yun Jang, Yi Ui-jing, and others had plotted to harm the <term>Kon-gung</term> <gloss>Queen's Palace</gloss> <note>Queen Inhyeon</note> and falsely initiated a massive trial. For this, they were sentenced to death. 

Nam Gu-man was appointed as the <term>Yeong-sang</term> <gloss>Chief State Councilor</gloss>. Nam Gu-man had been living at home since the years of <term>Mu-gi</term> <note>1688–1689</note>. Now, the King specially ordered his recruitment. The decree said: "The state cannot go a single day without a Chief State Councilor." A royal messenger was sent with a warm message, but Nam declined. He submitted another memorial to resign. The King replied: "I have already explained my intentions in the previous reply. Why must I say more? A great minister is the limbs of the King. Even in peaceful times, you should not retire. How much more so now, when the court is nearly empty and the nation faces difficulties? Why do you not think of your loyalty to the state? Your refusal is too much. Please follow my will, set your mind at ease, and come to court quickly." 

Special orders were given to arrest Gwak Han and Jo Sa-gi. During the reign of King Hyojong, Jo Sa-gi had criticized Jo Yi. He always harbored resentment. Later, as the magistrate of Pyeongchang, he visited Song Jun-gil in the capital. He spoke disparagingly of Song. People said: "When Jo Sa-gi sees me, he starts to choke." He was a man with a nature like a fox, a true "small man" <note>an unprincipled person</note>. Not long after, Jo Sa-gi entered the Secretariat wearing a red robe and presented a secret memorial. This concerned the funeral rites of 1659 and the matter of the royal coffin. In 1674, Jo Sa-gi gained influence and did many evil things. By 1683, the Queen Mother’s status was not maintained for even a few months. Jo Sa-gi and Bak Pung worked together to submit memorials that insulted the previous reign and slandered the Queen Mother. This caused deep hatred in the King’s heart. Even from his place of exile, Jo Sa-gi continued to submit memorials comparing the late Queen to Empress Wu <note>original: "the words of Mun-jeong"</note> and interfering in the inner palace. He was the chief culprit behind the disaster of the deposition of the Queen. Though many ministers tried to save him, and the King initially did not punish him severely, the King was now enraged. He issued a memorandum: "The traitor Jo Sa-gi committed the crime of insulting the late Queen. This must be resolved."

The withered scholar waits for the first awakening. The sleeping monk does not know the flavor. The clouds and flowers pass the wrist. The evening moon comes to the corner of the tower. The tea is different. The bell strikes, reaching the three times of service <note>referring to the scheduled Buddhist prayers or rituals</note>. In the silence of summer, I chant. I come to write a "white war" poem <note>original: "白戰詩"; a poetic competition where certain common words are forbidden to challenge the writers</note>. Fortunately, I met someone to ask about the Way. The stream in front points to the fragrance of yesterday. The scenery is beautiful. Alone and drunk, I have many poetic lines. The forest birds are close. Little right or wrong. I stroke the tall pine with my hand. My body is as it was before. I climb the sheer peak. When it is time to fly back, the west wind blows. The smoke of the incense on the furnace does not stop. When the guest arrives, the flowers tip their heads.

今は紛やの孫右衛門商ひ冥利、女房限つて此文見せず、我一人披見して、起請共に火に入る。誓文に違はない「少ア、忝い。夫で私が立ます」と又伏しづめば、治「ハアくハアうぬが立の立ぬとは人がまましい。是兄者人、片時も彼奴が面見ともなし。いざ御座れ。去ながら此無念口惜さどふもたまらぬ。今生の思ひ出、女が面一ツ踏、御免あれ」と、つと寄て地団太踏、「エ、、く、しなしたり。足かけ三年恋し床しも最愛可愛も、今日といふ今日、たつた此足一本の暇乞」と額ぎはをはつたと蹴て、「わつ」と泣出し兄弟つれ帰る姿もいたく敷、跡を見送り声を上、歎く小春も酷らしき、無心中か心中か、誠の心は女房の、其一筆の奥深く、誰が文も見ぬ恋の道、別れてこそは三重帰りけれ。

# 中之巻

福徳に天満神の名を直に、天神橋と行通ふ、所も神のお前町、営む業も紙店に、紙屋治兵衛と名を付て、千早振程買に来る、かみは正直、商賣は、所がらなり老舗なり。夫が火燵に轉寐を、枕屏風で風ふせぐ、外は十夜の人通り、見世と内とを一緒に、女房おさの心配り。「さん」「日は短かし夕飯時、市の側迄使にいて、玉は何して居る事ぞ。此三五郎

"Now Magoemon will follow his merchant's pride. I will not show this letter to any woman, not even a wife. I alone will read it and then cast it into the fire along with the vow-papers. I will not break my oath." Koharu replied, "I am grateful. Then I will stand as proof," and she prostrated herself again. Jihei said, "Hah! Whether you stand or not is nothing to me. Brother, I cannot bear to see that person's face for another moment. Let us go. However, this resentment and regret are unbearable. As a memory of this life, let me kick her face once. Permit me this!" He suddenly stepped forward and stamped his feet. "Oh, I have failed! For three years I loved you and longed for you, but today, this very day, this one foot is all that remains to say goodbye!" He kicked her squarely in the forehead. She cried out as the brothers left together, a pitiful sight. Koharu looked after them and wailed, a cruel sound. Was it heartless or was it love? The true heart lay deep within that single letter from the wife. In the path of love where no one else's letter is seen, they have parted, yet she returns three times over.

# Volume Two

The God of Tenma, whose name is synonymous with fortune, lends his name to the Tenjin Bridge where people pass. This is the town before the god. The business here is a paper shop, and the man's name is Kamiya Jihei. People come to buy from him in great numbers. A paper merchant must be honest; his business depends on his reputation and the history of his shop. He was dozing by the <term>kotatsu</term> <gloss>hearth</gloss>, with a pillow screen shielding him from the draft. Outside, people were passing by for the ten nights of prayer. His wife, Osan, was managing both the shop and the household. "The days are short and it is already dinner time. I sent Tama to the market, but what is she doing? And this Sangoro..."

...was reappointed as Vice Director. He addressed the King: "In the affairs of the state, many in the central government do not act with sincerity, and they cannot avoid using words of temporary expediency. If one can plan for the nation with sincerity, why would there be a need for expedient words?"

He also said: "If the ruler is firm in his will to seek the virtuous, even if he cannot obtain many, obtaining just one virtuous person will cause others of their kind to come forward together."

He also said: "The virtuous person only knows righteousness and principle <term>uiri</term>. Poverty or success, long life or early death—none of these external things can move their heart. They only exert effort in learning and set their will on the correct path. How could they have any intention regarding personal success or failure? Whether they are used or not depends on the ruler, not themselves."

He also said: "Recently, those who do not respond to the regular examinations do so because they have been encouraged by the court and the National Academy <term>Pan-gung</term>. During the era of the deposed king <note>referring to the tyrant Yeonsangun</note>, Confucian scholars were made to pull palanquins, yet they accepted it calmly. Because people were selected through literary composition at irregular times, scholars used to always carry pens and ink, waiting for the king's every move. Such people only wish to bring glory to themselves and enrich their own lives. What else is there? Even if we obtain such people, what benefit would they bring to the nation?"

# The Great Announcement

All those who hew flames of fire, the subduing and the excommunications of our masters, the geniuses of the land, regarding the printing of the book <term>Etz Chaim</term> <gloss>Tree of Life</gloss>, they are for a safeguard under the hand of the one who brings it upon the beds of the printing press. The wise and distinguished, our teacher Rabbi Abraham Isaac... and this is their seal of truth and justice. And we were not given permission to write in the book due to the expenses of printing, for they are great; also due to the great effort. But this is to let it be known, that the young lion is in his den, with a vow of strictness in holy matters, over all printers, whether in this country or another. For a duration of ten years from the completion of the printing, none shall be printed or opened for use. And the one who passes over... this hidden thing... and to place his way... and the abundance of blessing and success will reach them.

# Sabbath Repairs by the Queen

...the soul of the gods, etc., that they go up and down. A rooster that flew—he who sees it until it sets, [they are] still going up and down... and a woman who is in pain with her son, etc. Judah, a man of Kefar Gevoni, who takes one and leaves one, beside if he were scraping, it is forbidden. 

B. They do not help an animal [to give birth] on the festival day, but they support and walk the woman on the Sabbath, and they call a midwife for her from place to place, and they desecrate the Sabbath for her, and they tie the navel. Rabbi Yose says: They even cut. All requirements of circumcision are done on the Sabbath.

**"My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her. Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners? I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished and the pomegranates budded. Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib."**

### Chapter 19
Rabbi Eliezer says: If he did not bring a tool from before the Sabbath, he brings it on the Sabbath uncovered, and in danger he covers it. According to the witnesses, Rabbi Eliezer also said: They may cut wood to make charcoal and to make iron tools. Akiva stated a general rule: Any work that it is possible to do before the Sabbath does not override the Sabbath, and that which is impossible to do before [the Sabbath] overrides the Sabbath. B. All requirements of circumcision are done on the Sabbath: circumcising, uncovering [the corona], sucking [the blood], and placing upon it a plaster and cumin. And if he did not grind [them] before the Sabbath, he chews [them] with his teeth and places [them]. And if he did not mix wine and oil before the Sabbath, he gives this by itself and this by itself. And they do not make a bandage for it in the first instance, but he wraps a rag upon it. If he did not prepare [it] before the Sabbath, he wraps [it] on his finger and brings [it], even from another courtyard. C. They bathe a small child on the third day that happens to fall on the Sabbath, for it is said: "And it came to pass on the third day, when they were in pain." A person of doubtful sex and an <term>androgynos</term> <gloss>hermaphrodite</gloss>—they do not desecrate the Sabbath on their behalf. Rabbi Judah permits [it] regarding an <term>androgynos</term>. D. He who had two infants, one to be circumcised after the Sabbath and one to be circumcised on the Sabbath, and he forgot and circumcised the one of after the Sabbath on the Sabbath—he is liable. [If he had] one to be circumcised on the Eve of Sabbath and one on the Sabbath, and he forgot and circumcised the one of the Eve of Sabbath on the Sabbath—Rabbi Eliezer holds him liable for a sin-offering, and Rabbi Joshua exempts [him]. E. A small child is circumcised on the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth [day], no less and no more. How so? According to the norm, on the eighth. Born between the suns [twilight], he is circumcised on the ninth. [Born] between the suns of the Eve of Sabbath, he is circumcised on the tenth. A festival day after the Sabbath, he is circumcised on the eleventh. Two days of the New Year, he is circumcised on the twelfth. A sick child—they do not circumcise him until he recovers. F. These are the shreds [of the foreskin] that invalidate the circumcision: flesh that covers most of the corona, and he does not eat of the heave-offering. And if he was a fleshy person, he corrects it because of appearances. He circumcised but did not cut the circumcision—it is as if he did not circumcise.

**"Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies. How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter! The joints of thy thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman. Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies. Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins."**

### Chapter 20
Rabbi Eliezer says: They may hang the strainer on the festival day and pour into the hanging one on the Sabbath. And the Sages say: They do not hang the strainer on the festival day, and they do not pour into the hanging one on the Sabbath, but they may pour into the hanging one on the festival day. B. They pour water over the dregs so that they may clarify, and they strain the wine in cloths and in an Egyptian basket, and they put an egg into a mustard-strainer, and they make <term>inomelin</term> <gloss>honey-wine mixture</gloss> on the Sabbath. Rabbi Judah says: On the Sabbath, in a cup; on the festival day, in a pitcher; and on the intermediate days, in a barrel. Rabbi Tzadok says: Everything [is done] according to the guests. C. They do not soak asafoetida in lukewarm water, but one may put it into vinegar. And they do not soak vetches, nor do they rub them, but one puts [them] into the sieve or into the basket.

<summary>This page continues the halakhic regulations for the Sabbath from the Mishnah (Chapters 19 and 20), focusing on the laws of circumcision and the preparation of food and drinks.</summary>
<keywords>Sabbath, circumcision, Halakhah, Song of Songs, Mishnah, Chapter 19, Chapter 20, Sabbath repairs</keywords>

<meta>The previous page concluded a section on specific talismans for repelling pests (rats, mosquitoes, and flies) using zodiacal decans and specific planetary metals. This page begins Chapter 10, which shifts focus to the "lapidary" aspect of astral magic—the correspondence between the seven planets and various gemstones and minerals—and introduces the visual forms of the planets as described in ancient sources.</meta>

<page-num>106</page-num>

# Chapter (10) on Stones

Among these are: **"Saturn"**, to which belong the stones: iron, diamond <note>original: "al-mas"; also refers to adamant</note>, antimony, onyx, and jet 
<margin>3</margin> (the clear black variety), turquoise, and magnet <note>lodestone</note>, and magnesia. It shares an affinity with gold, red ruby, golden marcasite, and hematite.

**"Jupiter"** has the stones: lead <note>original: "al-anak"</note>, and white and yellow ruby. It shares 
<margin>6</margin> an affinity with carnelian, gold, peridot <note>original: "zabaryad"</note>, rock crystal <note>original: "al-maha"</note>, and crystal; it governs every bright, white-colored stone.

**"Mars"** has the stones: red copper, the "cat-eye" stone <note>original: "al-sunnuri"</note>, and sulfur of all kinds. It shares an affinity with marcasite, bloodstone <note>original: "hajar al-dam"</note>, magnet, glass, carnelian, 
<margin>9</margin> and onyx; it governs every red stone that has a dark or dusky hue.

**"The Sun"** has the stones: gold, arsenic, garnet <note>original: "al-bijadi"</note>, diamond, "Pharaonic" glass, red shell, and every bright stone. It shares an affinity with hematite, 
<margin>12</margin> emery <note>original: "al-sunabadhaj"</note>, and red ruby.

**"Venus"** has the stones: red copper, lapis lazuli, pearls, shell, malachite <note>original: "al-dahnaj"</note>, and coral. It shares an affinity with silver, rock crystal <note>original: "al-maha"</note>, glass, and magnesia.

<margin>15</margin> **"Mercury"** has the stones: "hydrargyros" <note>original: "idramus," from the Greek for quicksilver/mercury</note>, "sabadhaj" <note>an unidentified stone, possibly a corruption of a Greek term</note>, emerald, and quicksilver. It shares an affinity with peridot, tin, glass, and marble.

---

Now that we have mentioned this, I shall begin describing the forms of the planets according to what we have transmitted from *The Book of the Benefits of Stones* by Mercury the Scribe, from the book of 
<margin>9</margin> *Apollonius the Sage* <note>original: "Abalous al-Hakim"; referring to Apollonius of Tyana</note>, and from the book *The Interpretation of Spiritual Talismans* translated by Baqratis.

-> First of these <-

<margin>12</margin> The Sun

In the book of *Apollonius the Sage*, its form is a woman standing upon a chariot pulled by four horses. In her right hand is a mirror, and in the left, held against her chest, is a whip. Upon her head is her radiance <note>a crown of rays</note>. We have already mentioned her form.
<margin>15</margin> From the book *The Benefits of Stones* by Mercury: it is the form of a man standing as if greeting whoever is opposite him. In his left hand is a shield, and beneath his feet is the form of a dragon.

סוד הרוח הוא מן הדברים העמוקים ואין להשיג בו אלא בדרך הקבלה והעיון. ודע כי הרוח הוא כלי לכל הנשמות ובו יתחברו הנשמות אל הגוף. וזהו סוד מה שאמרו רבותינו זכרונם לברכה כי הרוח הוא המקשר בין הנשמה ובין הגוף. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת האמצעי בין הנפש ובין הנשמה.

והנה הרוח הוא בחינת הלב והוא מקום משכן הנשמה. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת האויר והוא בחינת החיים. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ויהי האדם לנפש חיה. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת המלאך הממונה על האדם. וזהו סוד מה שאמרו רבותינו זכרונם לברכה כי לכל אדם יש מלאך ממונה עליו.

ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת השכל והוא בחינת הבינה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח חכמה ובינה. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת האור והוא בחינת הזיו. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ואור צדיקים ישמח. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת הקדושה והוא בחינת הטהרה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח קדשך אל תקח ממני.

ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת התפלה והוא בחינת הבקשה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח תפלה ותחנונים. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת התשובה והוא בחינת החרטה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח נשברה לב נשבר. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת האהבה והוא בחינת היראה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח יראת ה'.

ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת השמחה והוא בחינת הגילה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח שמחה. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת השלום והוא בחינת האחדות. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח שלום. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת החיים והוא בחינת הנצחיות. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח חיים.

ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת האמת והוא בחינת האמונה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח אמת. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת החסד והוא בחינת הרחמים. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח חסד. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת הגבורה והוא בחינת הדין. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח גבורה.

ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת התפארת והוא בחינת האמת. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח תפארת. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת הנצח והוא בחינת ההוד. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח נצח והוד. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת היסוד והוא בחינת הצדיק. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח יסוד. ודע כי הרוח הוא בחינת המלכות והוא בחינת השכינה. וזהו סוד מה שכתוב ורוח מלכות.
